title: cypher: data loss when using list_transform and regexp_replace

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
Only seen with `regexp_replace`:
```py
db = kuzu.Database(":memory:")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

conn.execute("""
    CREATE NODE TABLE Node (
        id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
        cities STRING[]
    );
""")

d = json.dumps([{"cities": ["New York", "Los Angeles"]}, {"cities": ["Tokyo", "Osaka"]}])
print("Input: ", d)
conn.execute("""
    UNWIND CAST($data AS STRUCT(cities STRING[])[]) as data
    CREATE (n:Node)
    SET n.cities = list_transform(data.cities, label -> regexp_replace(label, 'New', 'Old'));
""", {"data": d})

res = conn.execute("""
    MATCH (n:Node)
    RETURN n;
""")
for row in res.rows_as_dict():
    print("Output: ", row["n"]["cities"])
```
```
Input:  [{"cities": ["New York", "Los Angeles"]}, {"cities": ["Tokyo", "Osaka"]}]                                                                                           
Output:  ['Old York', 'Los Angeles']
Output:  ['Old York', 'Los Angeles']
```
Works when using other functions:
```cypher
SET n.cities = list_transform(data.cities, label -> lower(label))
```
```
Input:  [{"cities": ["New York", "Los Angeles"]}, {"cities": ["Tokyo", "Osaka"]}]
Output:  ['"new york"', '"los angeles"']
Output:  ['"tokyo"', '"osaka"']
```

title: cypher: casting map to struct should not depend on the order of the map entries

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
```cypher
kuzu> return cast({
  names: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dan'],
  age: 50,
  description: {height: 2}}
AS struct(
  age int64,
  names string[],
  description struct(height int64))) as r;
Error: Conversion exception: Unsupported casting function from STRUCT(names STRING[], age INT64, description STRUCT(height INT64)) to STRUCT(age INT64, names STRING[], description STRUCT(height INT64)).
```
After flipping `age`, it works:
```cypher
kuzu> return cast({
  age: 50,
  names: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dan'],
  description: {height: 2}}
AS struct(
  age int64,
  names string[],
  description struct(height int64))) as r;
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ r                                                                   │
│ STRUCT(age INT64, names STRING[], description STRUCT(height INT64)) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {age: 50, names: [Alice,Bob,Carol,Dan], description: {height: 2}}   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
Using a string for the map also works:
```cypher
kuzu> return cast("{names: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dan'], age: 50, description: {height: 2}}" as struct(age int64, names string[], description struct(height int64))) as r;
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ r                                                                         │
│ STRUCT(age INT64, names STRING[], description STRUCT(height INT64))       │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {age: 50, names: ['Alice','Bob','Carol','Dan'], description: {height: 2}} │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
This is especially problematic if the map is coming from Python as a parameter.

kuzu> return cast({
  age: 50,
  names: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Carol', 'Dan'],
  description: {height: 2}}
AS struct(
  age int64,
  names string[],
  description struct(height int64))) as r;
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ r                                                                   │
│ STRUCT(age INT64, names STRING[], description STRUCT(height INT64)) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {age: 50, names: [Alice,Bob,Carol,Dan], description: {height: 2}}   │

title: algo: implement spanning forest
body:
# Description

Implements single threaded [Kruskal's algorithm ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal's_algorithm) with [DSU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint-set_data_structure) to track components. 

Closes #5412
Associated docs https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu-docs/pull/626

Syntax
```
CALL SPANNING_FOREST
(
    '{Projected Graph}', 
    weight_property:='{property on Rel Table}',
    variant:={'min'|'max'})(default 'min')
)
RETURN src, dst, rel, forest_id
```
Note that omitting the `weight_property` will run the algorithm by assigning all edges the same weight. 

After https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/5853

The returned table should look like this 
```

│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: Node, id: 4} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: Node, id: 9} │ (0:0)-{_LABEL: Edge, _ID: 1:0, weight: 2}->(0:1)   │ 0         │
│ {_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: Node, id: 2} │ {_ID: 0:4, _LABEL: Node, id: 3} │ (0:2)-{_LABEL: Edge, _ID: 1:3, weight: 3}->(0:4)   │ 0         │
│ {_ID: 0:4, _LABEL: Node, id: 3} │ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: Node, id: 4} │ (0:4)-{_LABEL: Edge, _ID: 1:2, weight: 3}->(0:0)   │ 0         │
│ {_ID: 0:7, _LABEL: Node, id: 8} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: Node, id: 9} │ (0:7)-{_LABEL: Edge, _ID: 1:7, weight: 3}->(0:1)   │ 0         │
│ {_ID: 0:9, _LABEL: Node, id: 6} │ {_ID: 0:8, _LABEL: Node, id: 7} │ (0:9)-{_LABEL: Edge, _ID: 1:9, weight: 3}->(0:8)   │ 0         │
│ {_ID: 0:6, _LABEL: Node, id: 0} │ {_ID: 0:5, _LABEL: Node, id: 1} │ (0:6)-{_LABEL: Edge, _ID: 1:6, weight: 5}->(0:5)   │ 0         │

│ {_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: Node, id: 5} │ {_ID: 0:8, _LABEL: Node, id: 7} │ (0:3)-{_LABEL: Edge, _ID: 1:10, weight: 10}->(0:8) │ 0         │
```

title: Bug: Incorrect lowercasing of word-final Greek capital Sigma (Σ)

labels.name: type: feature

labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
### Kuzu version

v0.10.0

### What operating system are you using?

Windows 11

### What happened?

When applying UPPER() to the Greek word 'κόσμος', KuzuDB returns 'ΚΌΣΜΟΣ'. However, applying LOWER() to that result returns 'κόσμοσ' instead of the original 'κόσμος'.

According to wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma), there are two forms of lowercase for Greek capital Sigma (Σ):
- If Σ is at the end of a word, it should lowercase to ς
- If Σ is in the middle of a word, it should lowercase to σ

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```cypher
return LOWER(UPPER('κόσμος'))
```

code_snippets.code: return LOWER(UPPER('κόσμος'))

body:
If a timeout of a query is triggered or the query is interrupted by the caller, we'd throw a runtime error with "RuntimeError: Interrupted".  However, this is not clear enough on what triggers this interrupted behaviour. 

We should consider: 1) provide more information in the error message on what can potentially trigger this; 2) if possible, differentiate different causes of this error, so the error message is more clear. e.g., "The query is interrupted due to time out after xxx seconds. Please try the query with a larger ......".

```python
import kuzu
import polars as pl


def main():

    conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

    conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE TestNode(id INT64, bool_field BOOLEAN, PRIMARY KEY(id))")

    df = pl.DataFrame({
        "id": [1, 2, 3],
        "bool_field": [None, None, None]
    })

    df.write_parquet(parquet_path)

    except Exception as e:

if __name__ == "__main__":
```

# Description
Parsing only considered magnitude when validating bounds. This is faulty logic. It resulted in an out of bounds error on i128 min. 

This fix pushes the sign down to the number literal subtree of the parse tree so that it can be used for parsing. 
Closes #5805

title: Improve behaviour of `INSTALL extension; LOAD extension`

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
### Kuzu version

v0.11.1dev12 (master)

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

The current behaviour of raising a `RuntimeError` for trying to load an extension that's already loaded is quite tedious - users have to include this try-except block _everywhere_ in their Python code where anything to do with the extension is called. Below is an example for the vector extension.
```py
    try:
        conn.execute("INSTALL vector; LOAD vector;")
    except RuntimeError:
        pass
```
In a realistic code base, the user might have multiple scripts where they create a vector index, maybe even create multiple vector indices in different scripts. And the query vector index functionality would be in a totally different script that also requires the user to use these try-except blocks as boilerplate everywhere in their codebase.

## Align with user expectation

Why don't we instead silently handle the `RuntimeError` on our end and avoid the user having to explicitly handle it themselves? Or provide some alternate syntax to help them not worry about this on the client language side.

How about some syntax like this?
```sql
INSTALL vector; LOAD IF NOT EXISTS vector;
```

code_snippets.code: INSTALL vector; LOAD IF NOT EXISTS vector;

title: Feature: public API and documentation for storage format extesnions

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

C++

### Description

**tldr**
It would be very helpful to have a public API and documentation for creating third-party extensions for Kuzu to support additional storage formats.

**Context**
Apache GraphAr (incubating) is a project focused on property graph storage, using YAML metadata and data in formats like CSV, Parquet, and ORC. GAR already provides an Arrow-based C++ API and a Spark DataSource for working with its format.

Since Kuzu is also Arrow-based, written in C++, and optimized for in-memory graph processing, it seems feasible to develop a Kuzu extension for reading and writing GAR data. While there are extension examples in the Kuzu repository (such as the [Iceberg](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/tree/master/extension/iceberg)), clear documentation on the required APIs and extension structure would make it much easier to build and integrate new format support.

[Link to the corresponding issue in GraphAr.](https://github.com/apache/incubator-graphar/issues/679)

Thanks in advance!

# Description

Commonly used functions in the Python API (iterators, Pandas/Polars DataFrames) currently produce a ton of linter errors. Only one test was changed for the `rows_as_dict` function, to address the FBT001 ruff linting error [here](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/boolean-type-hint-positional-argument/).

title: Add scripts to build from source for uv-managed Python
body:
# Description

This PR adds scripts to allow users to build from source using uv-managed Python rather than system, brew, or pyenv-managed Python. **It's non-intrusive** and does not force users to use uv (it's totally opt-in).

uv has become the defacto standard to manage Python installations and virtual environment for many users, and its most recent release 0.8.0 is a landmark one, because it can [now manage Python installs globally](https://pydevtools.com/blog/uv-0-8-release-automatic-python-installation-to-path/) without conflicting with system Python in any way. It's also orders of magnitude faster to install things in uv than with any other method in Python, for both installing new Python versions, and for downloading packages from PyPI.

The shell scripts provided allow users who choose to use uv to build Python from source (includes a `README.md` to help). Users who prefer doing things the old way don't need to use these scripts.

## How did I test?

I completely uninstalled `pyenv` which I used before to manage global Python (which pybind11 and cmake relied upon). The build process broke, as expected. The system Python installation I have on my mac is far too old to be usable by Kuzu, so the build didn't happen. Then, I ran the scripts included in this PR, and cmake and pybind11 now locate the global uv installation correctly, and the entire build process for Kuzu and Python works seamlessly, end-to-end.

Example commands (includes option for parallel builds):
```bash
# Configure and build everything with uv Python
./scripts/uv-make build

# Build only Python API
./scripts/uv-make python

# Build and run tests
./scripts/uv-make pytest

# Configure only (no build)
./scripts/uv-make configure

# Clean build directory
./scripts/uv-make clean

# Show help
./scripts/uv-make help

# Parallel builds (much faster!)
NUM_THREADS=20 ./scripts/uv-make build
NUM_THREADS=8 ./scripts/uv-make python
```

# Contributor agreement

- [x] I have read and agree to the [Contributor Agreement](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/master/CLA.md).

title: migration-testing: update script with option to split test files
body:
# Description

Example usage
`python scripts/export-import-test.py --base-commit=b0c573c --test-commit=master --test-dir=test/test_files/copy/ --output-dir=tmp`

This will create a file structure at tmp as follows 
```
your-project-root/
├── scripts/
│ └── export-import-test.py
├── tmp/
│ ├── db/ 
│ ├── export/ 
│ └── import/ 
```

All test cases in `test-dir` that have a split comment (#SPLIT) will be divided into export and import tests (that is, for every case with \#SPLIT there are 2 new .test files being created). 

The export tests are everything from the --CASE line to \#SPLIT. The import tests include everything after SPLIT till the EOF or the start of a new CASE. We also follow the Kuzu testing framework to ensure every test is a valid test file (test files have a header, at least one --CASE...). 

The script then builds kuzu at `base-commit`and runs the export tests with its e2e test executable, placing any created dbs in the db folder.

Finally the script then builds kuzu at `test-commit` and runs the import tests with its e2e test executable, importing any needed dbs from the db folder. 

# Contributor agreement

title: Create default values for union during copying / runtime
body:
In `Value::createDefaultValue` we were initializing a union value with a single `null` value as the default child. This resulted in the child lacking required information when copying from certain types. For example, `childrenSize` of the child would be `0`, and so if the selected field turned out to be a struct (with more than one field), none of its fields would be copied, resulting in an empty output. E.g.
```
return union_value(a := struct_pack(b := 2))
{}
```
when the correct output should be `{b: 2}`

The solution implemented here was to just set up default union values with no children, and create the default child value during copying once we know the selected field.

title: Add compatible version specifications for Kuzu Neo4j extension
body:
### Description

Thanks for the amazing work on this project - it's been great to see it evolve. I was excited to see the Neo4j extension because of the opportunities that Kuzu provides and how difficult it can be to manually export nodes and relationships. That said, some of the databases I'm working with use various versions of Neo4j and upgrading is not always an option due to how complex that can get for Neo4j.

I noticed there are no version ranges mentioned on the [Kuzu Neo4j docs (https://docs.kuzudb.com/extensions/neo4j/) but experienced that there is likely a minimum version based on how the API accesses Neo4j. The [line here](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/34b1eb7aafd8c4b4ade5709f685d674f8031f2c6/extension/neo4j/src/function/neo4j_migrate.cpp#L43) suggests that only versions of Neo4j >= 4.x are compatible with the Kuzu Neo4j extension. My understanding is that from Neo4j 3.x -> Neo4j 4.x there was an API change from using `/db/data/transaction/commit` to `/db/neo4j/tx/commit` for requests. If one attempts to connect Kuzu to a Neo4j 3.x version it seems to fail because of this change.

This all being said, it'd also be great to have compatibility with Neo4j 3.x (which still includes APOC) at some point if possible! Let me know if I may create another issue to this effect.

### Link

https://docs.kuzudb.com/extensions/neo4j/

title: Implement casting between unions, fix issues with nested unions and union lists/arrays
body:
This PR does a few things:
#### Support casting between unions
A cast between two unions is valid if for every variant of the source union, there is a variant in the target union with the same name and there exists an implicit cast between the variant types.
```cypher
cast(union_value(a := 23) as union(x string, b bool, a int32))
-> 23

cast(union_value(a := 23) as union(x string, a float, y int64))
-> 23.000000

cast(union_value(q := [3, 2, 13, 4]) as union(s string, q float[]))
-> [3.000000,2.000000,13.000000,4.000000]
```
Resolves https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/3150

#### Fix casting nested type to union
```cypher
cast({q: 12, b: "abc"} as union(x struct(q float, b string), y bool))
-> {q: 12.000000, b: abc}

cast([2, 3, 4] as union(a int8[]))
-> [2,3,4]
```

#### Support unions contained in other nested types
```cypher
cast([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5, 6]] as union(a float[])[])
-> [[1.000000,2.000000],[3.000000],[4.000000,5.000000,6.000000]]

cast({a: {b: 123}} as struct(a union(x bool, y struct(b float))))
-> {a: {b: 123.000000}}
```

title: test-tools: update rewriter behaviour for error (regex)
body:
# Description
[Do not review; in test]
Update the rewriter to do the following for error(regex)

1. If the query succeeds (no error). Replace the output with 
`---- ok`

2. If the query fails and matches the regex.
Leave the output as is (i.e write the same expected error back).
`---- error(regex)`
`{old error regex}`

3. If the query fails and does not match the regex
Overwrite the output with 
`---- error`
`{query error msg}`

Closes #5739

title: Optimization: Storage Efficiency on a Billion edges scale dataset
body:
### Description

I would like to be able to process a graph with a billion edges on a 32GB laptop.

Here is my input:

```
du -sh graph.parquet
3.7G    graph.parquet
D select count(1) from read_parquet('graph.parquet');
┌──────────────────┐
│     count(1)     │
│      int64       │
├──────────────────┤
│    827497855     │
│ (827.50 million) │
└──────────────────┘
```

When it's imported into kuzu:

```
kuzu> match (a: node)-[b: rel]-(c: node) return count(1);
┌────────────┐
│ COUNT(1)   │
│ INT64      │
├────────────┤
│ 1654995710 │
└────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 4.40ms (compiling), 3588.53ms (executing)

kuzu> CALL storage_info('rel') RETURN sum(num_values);
┌─────────────────┐
│ SUM(num_values) │
│ INT128          │
├─────────────────┤
│ 4599560202      │
└─────────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
kuzu> CALL storage_info('rel') RETURN sum(num_pages) * 4096 as num_bytes;
┌─────────────┐
│ num_bytes   │
│ INT128      │
├─────────────┤
│ 86016495616 │
└─────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 3.95ms (compiling), 36.56ms (executing)
```

In other words the table takes 86GB on disk. Queries that I want to run kill kuzu due to OOM.

In theory it should be possible to store this using:

827e6 * 4bytes + compressed COL and ROW pointers.

This is further exacerbated by the cost of reading this graph into memory for the purpose of running a graph algorithm. Most parallel libraries such as networkit or ParClusterers don't do [zero copy optimizations](https://github.com/adsharma/supercsr/commit/4d139047b7ca4d920a4f0cf010e6aafda7a30608). 

The ask here is two fold:

* More compact disk storage
* Example queries to read graph into memory in arrow format using CSR or SuperCSR that could be used by a parallel algorithm library with zero-copy C++20 features.

Related: #5050, https://github.com/networkit/networkit/issues/1331

title: Bug: Update Test Rewriter
body:
### Kuzu version

0.10.0.6

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS

### What happened?

For post 0.11.0
I experienced this using the test rewriter to update the badkeys test in the llm extension.

The test rewriter has an unreasonable way of handling error regex. What it should do is attempt to match the actual error message with the expected error regex. 

If the message does not fix the regex it should update the test with the produced error message (overwriting the regex in the process).

What it currently does is keep the regex so long as the actual output is an error (no matching attempts are made). This is unreasonable and can mask away issues like tests needing updates. 

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Fix list_contains type sniffing

# Description

The type sniffing for list_contains is incorrect, we blindly use the child type of list as the comparison type. For cases like `INT64 IN LIST[INT8]`, we will try to cast INT64 to INT8 which may not succeed. This PR extracts the common type between list and input element.

title: Bug: Overflow error when using IN with serial id
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.10.1

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS

### What happened?

When executing a query with a parameter list compared using IN operator with serial id, Kuzu throws an overflow exception. 

Expected behavior:
The query should execute successfully and return the matching nodes

Actual behavior:
RuntimeError: Overflow exception: Value 128 is not within INT8 range

The error occurs when:
- there are at least  256 nodes
- node.id is compared using IN operator with an binded array
- all array elements are in INT8 range

Using hardcoded values in the query works fine:
`MATCH (node:Chunk) WHERE node.id IN [1] RETURN node.id`
as well as adding element outside INT8 range to parameters:
```python
conn.execute(
    "MATCH (node:Chunk) WHERE node.id IN $chunk_ids RETURN node.id",
    {"chunk_ids": [1, -1_000_000]},
)
```

Detected on Python 3.13.5



### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```python
import kuzu

db = kuzu.Database("./bug.db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Chunk(id SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY(id))")

for _ in range(256):
    conn.execute("CREATE (c:Chunk)")

conn.execute(
    "MATCH (node:Chunk) WHERE node.id IN $chunk_ids RETURN node.id",
    {"chunk_ids": [1]},
)

# RuntimeError: Overflow exception: Value 128 is not within INT8 range
```

GDS functions support `optionalArgName := optionalArg`.

title: Bug: type conversion issue / no type validation when scanning from pandas
body:
```python
df = pd.DataFrame({'test': [{'a': 1}, {'a': 2}, {'a': 3}, {'b': "abc"}], 'qwe': [1, 2, 3, False]})
res = conn.execute("LOAD FROM df RETURN test, qwe")
while res.has_next():
    print(res.get_next())
```
The above snippet succeeds and produces the following output:
```
[{'b': '\x00'}, '1']
[{'b': '\x00\x00\x00'}, '2']
[{'b': ''}, '3']
[{'b': 'abc'}, 'False']
```
It seems like we should convert to string when a column has inconsistent types (e.g. `qwe` column), but in this case it is attempting to convert the `test` column to the same type as the last entry: `STRUCT(b STRING)`.

It works fine with lists:
```python
df = pd.DataFrame([[1, "a"], [2, "b"], [3, "c"], [4, "d"], [{"x": "yyyz"}, 3]])
res = conn.execute("LOAD FROM df RETURN *")
for r in res:
    print(r)
```

```
['2', 'b']
['3', 'c']
['4', 'd']
["{'x': 'yyyz'}", '3']
```

title: 8 Byte hash slot for AggregateHashTable
body:
I've reduced the slot size in the AggregateHashTable from 16 bytes to 8 bytes by using the most significant 7 bits of the entry pointer to store a fingerprint (rather than the full hash). This generally should be fine since most operating systems don't use more than 48 bits as far as I can tell. The largest is [Intel's 5-level paging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel_5-level_paging) which increases the size of pointers to 57 bits (also supported by some AMD processors). As far as I can tell is an optional feature on processors that support it, so I'm not sure if we need to handle this case, but since there was no noticeable performance difference between the 7 and 8 bit versions I thought it would be prudent to use a 7 bit fingerprint.

Clickbench on 128 threads 2x AMD EPYC 7551:

`MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.UserID, h.SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) LIMIT 10`: before: 3.1s 5.5GB peak memory, after: 2.7s, 5.0GB peak memory

`MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.URL, COUNT(*) as c ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10;`: before: 6.4s, 13.3GB peak memory, after:5.4s, 13.0GB peak memory

```python
def install_algo_extension(conn: kuzu.Connection) -> None:
    conn.execute("INSTALL ALGO; LOAD ALGO;")
    logger.info("Kuzu algorithm extension installed successfully.")

def compute_page_rank(
    conn: kuzu.Connection, projected_graph: ProjectedGraph, params: PageRankParams, batch_size: int = 10000
) -> Generator[pd.DataFrame, Any, None]:
    """
    Returns:
        a generator that yields DataFrames containing the columns: "rank", "node_group", and "node_id".
    """
    install_algo_extension(conn)
    projected_graph.create(conn)

    node_groups_info = __get_node_groups_info__(conn)

    offset = 0
    while True:
        query = f"""
        CALL page_rank(
            '{projected_graph.name}',
            dampingFactor := {params.damping_factor},
            maxIterations := {params.max_iterations},
            tolerance := {params.tolerance},
            normalizeInitial := {params.normalizeInitial}
        )
        RETURN node, rank
        ORDER BY rank DESC
        SKIP {offset}
        LIMIT {batch_size};

            df.drop(columns=["node"], inplace=True)

            yield df
            offset += batch_size
        else:
```

def install_algo_extension(conn: kuzu.Connection) -> None:
    conn.execute("INSTALL ALGO; LOAD ALGO;")
    logger.info("Kuzu algorithm extension installed successfully.")

def compute_page_rank(
    conn: kuzu.Connection, projected_graph: ProjectedGraph, params: PageRankParams, batch_size: int = 10000
) -> Generator[pd.DataFrame, Any, None]:
    """
    Returns:
        a generator that yields DataFrames containing the columns: "rank", "node_group", and "node_id".
    """
    install_algo_extension(conn)
    projected_graph.create(conn)

    node_groups_info = __get_node_groups_info__(conn)

    offset = 0
    while True:
        query = f"""
        CALL page_rank(
            '{projected_graph.name}',
            dampingFactor := {params.damping_factor},
            maxIterations := {params.max_iterations},
            tolerance := {params.tolerance},
            normalizeInitial := {params.normalizeInitial}
        )
        RETURN node, rank
        ORDER BY rank DESC
        SKIP {offset}
        LIMIT {batch_size};
        """
        result = conn.execute(query)
        if isinstance(result, kuzu.QueryResult):
            df = result.get_as_df()
            if df.empty:
                break

            df["node_group"] = df["node"].apply(lambda x: x.get("_label") if isinstance(x, dict) else pd.NA)
            df["node_id"] = df["node"].apply(
                lambda x: x.get(node_groups_info.get(x.get("_label"))) if isinstance(x, dict) else pd.NA  # type: ignore
            )

            df.drop(columns=["node"], inplace=True)

            yield df
            offset += batch_size
        else:
            raise Exception("Unexpected kuzu result type. This is likely a bug.")

title: Fix attempting to free mmapped memory when spilling to disk
body:
`MemoryBuffer::setSpilledToDisk` was always using `std::free` to free the memory, even if it was allocated using our buffer manager.

I don't think this is currently reproduce-able since we only spill data in the partitioner and that data has a fixed capacity of 2048 which even for a 16 byte value is going to be much smaller than the 256KB `TEMP_PAGE_SIZE` (which is the only size for which the memory manager will use the buffer manager to allocate space).

But since we plan to extend the spilling system to more situations I thought I should address this before it becomes a problem.

The way the buffer manager frees data makes this more complicated than it was before, as spilling will just unpin the pages to be evicted via the eviction queue, instead of freeing the memory directly.

title: Fix bypassing the shadow pages in the overflow file
body:
The `lastPageOnDisk` variable was no longer being updated, so all pages were bypassing the shadow pages and being written directly. This was causing problems with checkpointing since for existing pages there might be a cached buffer manager page in memory which does would not be updated to include new changes or invalidated.

I've removed the `lastPageOnDisk` variable (which doesn't work well now that we re-use pages) and instead have the page write cache store whether or not the page is a newly added page.

title: InMemHashIndex rework for strings
body:
# Description

Slots in the `InMemHashIndex` now stores `std::string` instead of `ku_string_t`. This allows us to avoid needing access to an overflow file in the `InMemHashIndex`, which has a few benefits:

1. We had a handle to the persistent overflow file in the `InMemHashIndex` before. This change removes the need for this and thus we don't need to pass in a `PageAllocator` to `InMemHashIndex` calls (which is needed to allocate new pages for the overflow file). The persistent overflow file is now only touched during checkpoint.
2. We save a round of copies during node batch insert. Before, the dataflow was `index buffer -(copy string data)-> in mem hash index -(copy ku_string_t)-> persistent hash index`. Now, it is `index buffer -(move string data)-> in mem hash index -(copy string data)-> persistent hash index`.

This PR also introduces FSM reclaiming on rollback for the overflow file.

This can come at the cost of a small overhead for each string depending on the implementation for `std::string`. For example, on my system it has a slightly larger small string buffer (16 bytes compared to 12 bytes for `ku_string_t`) and stores a 64-bit length field (instead of 32-bit for `ku_string_t`). It also has a capacity field since `std::string` is resizeable (this overhead doesn't apply to small strings). If we wish to optimize further we can write a wrapper around `ku_string_t` that allocates on the heap but for now we're using `std::string` for simplicity..

As a quick microbenchmark, I ran a copy of ldbc-sf100 Comment with the ID column set to `STRING` type:

branch|copy time|peak memory usage
-|-|-
master|162.1s|23.7GB
new|128.1s|34.8GB

# Contributor agreement

body:
### Kuzu version

v0.9.0

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS Sequoia 15.5

### What happened?

Running queries on large datasets with multihop traversals is not performant. Discussion discord is [here](https://discord.com/channels/1196510116388806837/1349045216623067157)
The dataset can be replicated [here](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4953#issuecomment-2708380062)
I sent the database to @prrao87 as well.

## Nonperformant query
```cypher
MATCH (s:Sub{sic:6311})<-[:FILED_IN]-(n:Num{tag:'NetIncomeLoss'})-[c:COMPONENT_OF* SHORTEST 1..10 
    (r,n | where not r.is_prior_value)]->(n2:Num)
    return n.id, n2.id
```

The above query just hangs after a while. Executing on a smaller subset of the data works but is long relative to the number of records obtained.

## Comment from Discord
"Hi @Luxord, you are right, the performance overhead indeed comes from the SINGLE_SHORTEST_PATH. Let me explain here, internally we form a parallel BFS computation which requires pre-allocating a dense array with size up to number of nodes. In your case there are 300M nodes so this initialization takes about 100ms (on my M1 pro mbp). And compute 155 source nodes (as u can see in the profiler) takes about 100ms * 155 ~= 15s.
We should be able to optimize this because in your use a case a dense data structure is not needed. The connectivity seems to be pretty sparse. So we can save that initialization overhead until the frontier gets bigger.
Though this is not a one day fix. I might need a few days to get this out."



### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: FSM reclaim on rollback
body:
# Description

The FSM now reclaims optimistically-allocated pages (e.g. from COPY) if a transaction is rolled back. The exception is that we don't reclaim for rollback on the overflow file because doing so may require larger changes to the overflow file (so that will come in a future PR). We also don't reclaim if a checkpoint fails. This is because sometimes freeing pages isn't safe if we have already flushed a column chunk to disk + updated its on-disk metadata, which is a more complicated problem that should be addressed separately.

## Design

Introduces a new abstract class `PageAllocator`. This class is responsible for allocating/freeing pages in the data file for use. In general, storage classes should be going through this class for handling allocations instead of directly going through `FileHandle` or `PageManager` which gives higher-level mechanisms such as operators + checkpointer more flexibility in how it wants to handle page allocations. This class currently has two implementations:

1. A new `OptimisticAllocator` class. This wraps the `PageManager`, storing optimistically-allocated pages that can still be rolled back. On rollback, all optimistically-allocated pages will be freed and made immediately rewritable. This class is designed to be thread-local.
2. The existing `PageManager` which can be used directly if we want to handle rollback logic differently from the `OptimisticAllocator`. Currently, this is only needed by `addColumn` functionality as rollback is already automatically handled during checkpoint in this case.

Additional notes/changes:
- During transactions, all `OptimisticAllocators` should be owned by `LocalStorage`. If an operator wishes to use an allocator, it can go through `LocalStorage::addOptimisticAllocator()` to create a new allocator + grab its handle.
- During checkpoint, an `OptimisticAllocator` is owned by `Checkpointer` handles all the allocations.
- Updated all storage structures (e.g. tables, hash index, disk arrays) so that instead of owning a file handle/page allocator that is passed in at construction, they are passed in an allocator during checkpoint or any operator that performs optimistic writing. This gives the operator flexibility in choosing which allocator they pass in (the allocator implementation is no longer coupled to the storage structure).

title: Transaction local wal
body:
# Description

This PR introduces a transaction local WAL that writes records into a local buffer and flush to the global WAL file until COMMIT.
This ensures that the global WAL file doesn't record any transactions that were rolled back except for that last one. This guarantee simplifies the replay of WAL during recovery.

Also, the WAL and shadow files are only created when actually needed now, instead of always created during the initialization of the Database object.

More tests are added to simulate recover from partially corrupted WAL or missing WAL/shadow files. Also added a bunch of flaky checkpointer tests to simulate recover from various checkpoint failures.

The downside of the changes in this PR is that the men usage for write transactions can potentially go up as wal records are logged in memory first. This should be addressed later to get rid of the local WAL, instead loop over undo buffer to write to the global WAL file.

title: Refactor how UUIDs are stored internally
body:
The physical type of a UUID is a signed `int128_t`. Internally, we store it with the MSB flipped. This is so we can sort lexicographically correctly when using `ORDER BY` (i.e. UUIDs with a `1` as the MSB will appear first, since it is flipped to `0` and interpreted as positive). We flip the bit back only for the `toString` and `fromString` methods.

This took a while to notice when implementing UUID creation for the Java API.

To avoid further confusion, we shouldn't store UUIDs with the MSB flipped, rather we should just flip the bit whenever we want to sort. Alternatively, we can implement a `uint128_t` type and use that for UUIDs.

title: Fix FileHandle::writePagesToFile in IN_MEMORY mode
body:
`FileHandle::writePagesToFile` in IN_MEMORY_MODE was assuming that the frames were all contiguous in memory.
That's actually often the case when using mmap (as long as you don't write across a frame group boundary), and might be soon always the case when using mmap (when we merge the files and get rid of frame groups), and segmentation might also work around the problem when writing segments at least since we'll need contiguous memory for the segments even with the malloc buffer manager (the function is also used by spill to disk though).

To try and catch similar issues in future, I've made the `BM_MALLOC` mode be set by a CMake option, and enabled it for the ASAN tests (since ASAN won't catch out of bounds writes within the mmapped region anyway) and also added an in-memory test run to the webassembly tests.

### API

### Description

This is an observation of kuzu's implementation. title: Feature: Support for H3 (geospatial) indexing

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

The [H3 index](https://h3geo.org/) is a (mostly) hexagonal grid that offers indexing over existing geographical coordinate systems. Its positioning is fixed and it can therefore translate a given point (say in the WGS84 CRS) to a grid reference that is basically a very long number. For example: [Lat./Lng.: 51.50413559, -0.01645872472 is cell 8a194ad2291ffff](https://h3geo.org/#hex=8a194ad2291ffff).

One very useful application of H3 is in performing quick distance calculations. This is because, the adjacency of the hexagons at different scales is known and therefore, instead of performing relative [great circle distance calcluations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great-circle_distance), it is much faster to perform relative [distance calculations through the use of the index](https://h3geo.org/docs/api/traversal/).

If Kuzu had this ability (as an Extension), even if it was just for geographical points, then it would also be possible to take into account geospatial data in queries to order results given their relative distance from a specific point and aggregate counts of "events" over the grid itself.

body:
# Description

Add the option `cache_embeddings` to `CREATE_HNSW_INDEX`. This setting defaults to true, and if set to false we will skip caching the embedding column and read the embeddings straight from disk. This comes with a performance penalty but reduces the memory requirements.

I repurposed `OnDiskEmbeddings` to implement the interface `HNSWIndexEmbeddings` which is used to read embeddings during the creation of the HNSW index.

We also had some bugs managing the lifetime of scanned on disk embeddings, and our pattern of getting raw embedding ptrs was prone to lifetime issues in general. I reworked this so that `getEmbedding()` returns an `EmbeddingHandle`, which is a unique reference to an offset in the scanned output data chunk for the embeddings. When an `EmbeddingHandle` goes out of scope, the scan state will automatically reclaim space in the output data chunk allocated to that embedding.

**Microbenchmarks**

All benchmarks are on `CREATE_VECTOR_INDEX`.

title: Bug: kuzu_connection_query has a lot of segfault potential for callers
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.10.0

### What operating system are you using?

Fedora 40 X86_64

### What happened?

Royi asked me to report a issue though perhaps he meant it as a documentation or feature issue and not a bug.  We were having a discord discussion about the behavior of `kuzu_connection_query` and whether or not users are expected to call ` kuzu_query_result_get_error_message` when the return value is KuzuError.   Here are some notes I'd written on the issue from an API perspective, with specific callouts to some of the problems in `kuzu_connection_query`.

---

Many of the Kuzu APIs have signatures like this:

    `kuzu_state result = some_kuzu_call(... args ..., some_kuzu_struct* output_argument)`

Where kuzu_state is basically zero for success, one for KuzuError
and output_argument is really inout, pass a pointer to a struct that _may_
be filled in by the call.

There are some unanswered questions about the protocols that follow.

1. Will the output argument be modified if kuzu_state == KuzuError?
2. If the output argument is used across multiple calls, does it need to be
   re-initialized by each call?

Unfortunately the answer to each question seems to be yes, which put a burden on
callers because:

- Callers potentially need to examine the output parameter regardless
  of the kuzu_state return values.
- Callers aren't advised about whether they need to reinitialize the in-out
  parameter, possibly resulting stale state problems.

Let's look at kuzu_query_connection as an example.
```
    typedef struct {
        void* _query_result;
        bool _is_owned_by_cpp;
    } kuzu_query_result;

    /**
     * @brief Executes the given query and returns the result.
     * @param connection The connection instance to execute the query.
     * @param query The query to execute.
     * @param[out] out_query_result The output parameter that will hold the result of the query.
     * @return The state indicating the success or failure of the operation.
     */
    KUZU_C_API kuzu_state kuzu_connection_query(kuzu_connection* connection, const char* query,
        kuzu_query_result* out_query_result);
```

In the simplest case the caller might have:
```
    kuzu_connection conn ;
    kuzu_query_result query_result ;
    kuzu_state result = kuzu_connection_query(&conn, "CREATE ...", &result)
```

`kuzu_connection_query` looks like this:
```
    kuzu_state kuzu_connection_query(kuzu_connection* connection, const char* query,
        kuzu_query_result* out_query_result) {
        if (connection == nullptr || connection->_connection == nullptr) {
          return KuzuError;                                     // (1)
        }
        try {
            auto query_result =
                static_cast<Connection*>(connection->_connection)->query(query).release();
            if (query_result == nullptr) {
                return KuzuError;                               // (2)
            }
            out_query_result->_query_result = query_result;     // (3)
            out_query_result->_is_owned_by_cpp = false;
            if (!query_result->isSuccess()) {
                return KuzuError;                               // (4)
            }
            return KuzuSuccess;
        } catch (Exception& e) {
            return KuzuError;                                   // (5)
        }
    }
```

So there are 4 cases where the function returns KuzuError. However only one
of them in any way initializes or sets the out_query_result content
(marker 3).

If users are supposed to call kuzu_query_result_get_error_message when
KuzuError is returned and don't take extra steps to provide content of the output struct beforehand, then the content of out_query_result is unknown (initialized to potentially anything for an on-stack struct, for example).

The kuzu_query_result content would also be stale if the structure were
reused in repeated calls to kuzu_connection_query without setting them to
some known state, so if the intent is that users should call
`kuzu-query-result-get-error-message` when the return value is KuzuError,
the looks like segfault conditions to me.

It would probably be best to

- set the inout members to known state in all APIs using inout parameters.
- document the semantics of the inout parameters w.r.t. kuzu_state return
  values

Related wishlist items:
It would be really useful if the APIs could give error message
information _any_ time `kuzu_state` is `KuzuError`.  Trying to understand
why some functions return KuzuError is an enigma (even with access to the
source code), such as the values of `kuzu_system_config` on
`kuzu_database_init`, which took me a day to get working because it
silently rejected so many of my options and combinations of options.

title: Fix malloc-based BM bug causing reads after memory has been freed
body:
It was previously possible for an optimistic read to still be reading when the page is evicted and freed.
It was already unlikely since new reads would clear the marked state and delay eviction, but was still possible if the page being read is marked and then evicted in the second pass before the read finishes. malloc also usually doesn't immediately return memory to the OS so the read after free would rarely be a fatal error. Now a counter tracks the number of ongoing optimistic reads for the page and we skip evicting if the counter is nonzero.
Once the page state is locked, new reads are blocked, so there is no data race when evicting.

Doesn't seem to have a noticeable performance impact (I tried benchmarking some scans and a multi copy and there was no noticeable difference in runtime).

title: AggregateHashTable memory tuning
body:
1. Remove the space reservation during finalization so that the size of the hash table just grows as data is moved from the queue and destroyed (should reduce peak memory at this point by a little).
2. Resize the AggregateHashTable by a factor of 1.5 instead of a factor of 2 (we can end up with a large amount of free slots wasting space. This changes the load (after the first resize) from 33-66% to 44-66%).

This doesn't have a particularly large impact on memory usage, but also doesn't hurt performance much.

Creating an fts index for the first segment of the msmarco 2.1 segmented dataset (from [here](https://trec-rag.github.io/annoucements/2024-corpus-finalization/)) required at least 18GB buffer pool before and succeeded with a 17GB buffer pool with these changes (the results were a little inconsistent; a few times I was able to get it to succeed with a 15-16GB buffer pool even without these changes).

title: Fix usage of system gtest in CMake

# Description

There were some issues with how we were including gtest into our test builds:

- [gtest targets are prefixed with 'GTest::'](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/FindGTest.html). CMake doesn't give any errors when you `target_link_libraries` against a target that doesn't exist so I'm assuming that's why we didn't see it complain before but we're not linking our tests against the correct targets regardless.
- Imported targets do not have global visibility so even if we were using the correct target names the CMake file in `test/` we still wouldn't find the correct targets to link against `GTest::GTest`.

I'm assuming that things may have worked before because I think we use gtest as a header-only library (I don't think we use gtest_main) and the `include(GoogleTest)` was correctly resolving the include directory. However on my system `include(GoogleTest)` doesn't work. I think this is because the gtest CMake files are in a different location from the gtest headers, and thus I rely on the gtest libraries being correctly propagated to the tests as they have the correct include directories.

Regardless this PR fixes that problem.

title: Fix pk rollback rolling back keys which failed to insert
body:
Since 0.7.1, when inserting nodes fails, we attempt to delete the inserted values from the PKIndex (so that re-inserting those values in a later commit doesn't fail). This had the unfortunate side effect of temporarily removing keys which failed to insert due to them already existing (since we aren't persisting deletions, the issue can be worked around by re-loading the database).

This fixes the issue by discarding the keys from the primary key index's uncommitted local storage, instead of also adding a deletion to the local storage which would hide any value in the persistent hash index.

title: Remove materialization of partitions for batch inserting in-memory HNSW index
body:
# Description

Refactor the `RelBatchInsert` operator with abstract interfaces so that the populating of the chunked CSR node group to insert can be customized. For the vector index this allows us to avoid materializing the HNSW index as partitions; instead the batch insert can read directly from the HNSW graphs.

Additionally refactored `PartitionerSharedState`, with the main motivation being that rel batch insert doesn't always need physical partitioning buffers anymore. Thus the `BasePartitionerSharedState` is pretty bare bones, with its intended usage being to get the next `nodeGroupIdx` to insert. Child classes will also be responsible for holding any data to be passed from source operators to the `RelBatchInsert` operator.

## Quick microbenchmark

Create HNSW index on glove-200 with 16 threads:

Branch/version | Peak memory usage (total) | Index creation time
--|--|--
master|6.4GB|458.3s
new|5.0GB|457.38s

title: Bug: KuzuDB v0.10.0 (Python API, WSL2): Tables and vector indexes created and checkpointed in one process are not found by a new process opening the same database
body:
### Kuzu version

0.10.0 (Python Client and CLI)

### What operating system are you using?

WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04 on Windows 11), Python 3.11

### What happened?

**Problem Description:**

When using KuzuDB v0.10.0 in a WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.11) environment, we are encountering a cross-process schema visibility issue. 
A "writer" Python process successfully performs the following:
1. Creates a new KuzuDB database directory.
2. Copies the `vector.kuzu_extension` (for v0.10.0) to `DB_PATH/extensions/`.
3. Opens the database (`kuzu.Database(DB_PATH, read_only=False)`).
4. Gets a connection (`kuzu.Connection(db)`).
5. Executes `LOAD EXTENSION 'vector';` successfully on the connection.
6. Creates node tables (e.g., `ExtractedEntity`) and relationship tables using explicit transactions (`BEGIN TRANSACTION; ... COMMIT;`).
7. Loads data into these tables.
8. Creates an HNSW vector index (e.g., `CALL CREATE_VECTOR_INDEX('ExtractedEntity', 'idx_name', 'embedding_prop')`) in auto-transaction mode.
9. Verifies within the same writer process and connection that the tables and indexes exist using `CALL SHOW_TABLES() RETURN *;` and `CALL SHOW_INDEXES() RETURN *;`.
10. Executes `CHECKPOINT;` successfully.
11. Attempts to ensure resources are fully released using `del conn_obj`, `del db_obj`, `gc.collect()`, and `time.sleep()`.

However, after the "writer" process terminates, a new, independent "reader" Python process (or the KuzuDB CLI v0.10.0) attempting to open the *same database directory*:
1. Can successfully open the database (`kuzu.Database(DB_PATH, read_only=False)` without lock file errors after the writer process has finished and its `.lock` file might have been handled/renamed).
2. Can successfully execute `LOAD EXTENSION 'vector';` on a new connection.
3. **Crucially, when executing `CALL SHOW_TABLES() RETURN *;`, the result is an empty set, indicating that the tables created by the writer process are not visible.**
4. Consequently, any subsequent operations targeting these tables or their indexes fail, typically with a "Table does not exist" error.

**Expected Behavior:**

We expect that after the "writer" process successfully creates tables, loads data, creates indexes, executes `CHECKPOINT;`, and properly closes the database, a subsequent "reader" process (either Python API or CLI) opening the same database directory should be able to see and query these persisted schema objects and data.

**Actual Behavior:**

The "reader" process (both our Python verification scripts and the KuzuDB CLI tool) consistently fails to find the tables (e.g., `ExtractedEntity`) created by the "writer" process, even though the writer process internally confirmed their creation and executed a checkpoint. `CALL SHOW_TABLES() RETURN *;` in the reader process returns an empty result.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Yes, the issue can be reliably reproduced using two separate Python scripts operating on the same database directory.

**Environment Setup:**

*   KuzuDB Version: `0.10.0` (Python Client and a pre-compiled Linux x86_64 CLI)
*   Python Version: `3.11`
*   Operating System: WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04 on Windows 11)
*   Ensure `vector.kuzu_extension` for v0.10.0 is available. The scripts below use an environment variable `KUZU_VECTOR_EXTENSION_PATH` to locate it, or default to `~/.kuzu/extension/0.10.0/linux_amd64/vector/libvector.kuzu_extension`.

**Script 1: `create_kuzu_db.py` (Simulates the writer process)**
(Run this script first to create the database, table, and index)

```python
# /home/zhz/zhz_agent/create_kuzu_db.py
import kuzu
import os
import shutil
import time
import gc
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import logging

# Configure a simple logger for this script
script_logger = logging.getLogger("KuzuCreateScript")
script_logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
if not script_logger.hasHandlers():
    ch = logging.StreamHandler()
    formatter = logging.Formatter('%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
    ch.setFormatter(formatter)
    script_logger.addHandler(ch)
    script_logger.propagate = False

DB_PATH = "/tmp/kuzu_standalone_test_db" # Using a temporary path for clarity
MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH = os.getenv(
    "KUZU_VECTOR_EXTENSION_PATH",
    os.path.expanduser("~/.kuzu/extension/0.10.0/linux_amd64/vector/libvector.kuzu_extension")
)
EMBEDDING_DIM = 1024 # Example dimension

script_logger.info(f"--- Standalone KuzuDB Creation Script ---")
script_logger.info(f"KuzuDB Python client version: {kuzu.__version__}")
script_logger.info(f"Target DB_PATH: {DB_PATH}")
script_logger.info(f"Vector extension path: {MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH}")


if os.path.exists(DB_PATH):
    script_logger.info(f"Removing existing test DB at {DB_PATH}")
    shutil.rmtree(DB_PATH)
os.makedirs(DB_PATH, exist_ok=True)

extensions_dir_in_db = os.path.join(DB_PATH, "extensions")
os.makedirs(extensions_dir_in_db, exist_ok=True)
target_path_vector = os.path.join(extensions_dir_in_db, "vector.kuzu_extension")

if os.path.exists(MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH):
    try:
        shutil.copy2(MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH, target_path_vector)
        script_logger.info(f"Copied vector extension to '{target_path_vector}'")
    except Exception as e_copy:
        script_logger.error(f"ERROR copying extension: {e_copy}")
else:
    script_logger.error(f"ERROR: Manual vector extension source file not found at '{MANUAL_EXTENSION_FILE_PATH}'. Index creation might fail if KuzuDB cannot find the extension.")

db = None
conn = None
try:
    script_logger.info("Opening database for writing...")
    db = kuzu.Database(DB_PATH, read_only=False)
    conn = kuzu.Connection(db)
    script_logger.info("Database and connection opened.")

    script_logger.info("Loading VECTOR extension...")
    conn.execute("LOAD EXTENSION 'vector';") # Use quoted name
    script_logger.info("VECTOR extension loaded.")

    script_logger.info("Creating NODE TABLE ExtractedEntity (within explicit transaction)...")
    conn.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION;")
    conn.execute(f"""
        CREATE NODE TABLE ExtractedEntity (
            id_prop STRING PRIMARY KEY,
            text STRING,
            label STRING,
            embedding FLOAT[{EMBEDDING_DIM}])
    """)
    conn.execute("COMMIT;")
    script_logger.info("ExtractedEntity table created and transaction committed.")
    
    script_logger.info("Loading sample data into ExtractedEntity (within explicit transaction)...")
    conn.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION;")
    entities_to_load = [
        {"id_prop": "node_test_1", "text": "This is node one for test", "label": "TEST_DOC", 
         "embedding": np.random.rand(EMBEDDING_DIM).astype(np.float32).tolist()},
    ]
    for entity in entities_to_load:
        conn.execute(
            "CREATE (e:ExtractedEntity {{id_prop: $id, text: $text, label: $label, embedding: $embedding}})",
            {{"id": entity["id_prop"], "text": entity["text"], "label": entity["label"], "embedding": entity["embedding"]}}
        )
    conn.execute("COMMIT;")
    script_logger.info(f"Loaded {len(entities_to_load)} entities and transaction committed.")

    script_logger.info("Creating vector index 'entity_embedding_idx' (auto-transaction)...")
    conn.execute(f"""
        CALL CREATE_VECTOR_INDEX(
            'ExtractedEntity',
            'entity_embedding_idx',
            'embedding',
            metric := 'cosine'
        )
    """)
    script_logger.info("Vector index creation command executed (auto-committed).")

    script_logger.info("Verifying index creation in current session...")
    result_show_idx = conn.execute("CALL SHOW_INDEXES() RETURN *;") # Get all indexes
    df_show_idx = pd.DataFrame(result_show_idx.get_as_df())
    script_logger.info("Indexes visible in current session (All Tables):")
    script_logger.info(f"\n{df_show_idx.to_string()}")
    
    # Filter for the specific index
    if not df_show_idx.empty and 'table name' in df_show_idx.columns and 'index name' in df_show_idx.columns:
        condition = (df_show_idx['table name'] == 'ExtractedEntity') & (df_show_idx['index name'] == 'entity_embedding_idx')
        if not df_show_idx[condition].empty:
            script_logger.info("SUCCESS: 'entity_embedding_idx' IS VISIBLE on 'ExtractedEntity' in current session.")
        else:
            script_logger.error("FAILURE: 'entity_embedding_idx' IS NOT VISIBLE on 'ExtractedEntity' in current session.")
    else:
        script_logger.error("FAILURE: Could not verify index due to missing columns in SHOW_INDEXES output or empty result.")


    script_logger.info("Executing final CHECKPOINT...")
    conn.execute("CHECKPOINT;")
    script_logger.info("CHECKPOINT executed.")

except Exception as e:
    script_logger.error(f"An error occurred: {e}", exc_info=True)
    if conn: # Attempt to rollback if transaction was started and error occurred
        try:
            script_logger.info("Attempting to rollback due to error...")
            conn.execute("ROLLBACK;")
            script_logger.info("Rollback successful.")
        except Exception as e_rb:
            script_logger.error(f"Rollback failed: {e_rb}")
finally:
    script_logger.info("\n--- Creation Script Attempting to Close KuzuDB ---")
    if conn:
        script_logger.info("Deleting Connection reference...")
        del conn
        conn = None
    if db:
        script_logger.info("Deleting Database reference...")
        del db
        db = None
    
    script_logger.info("Forcing garbage collection...")
    gc.collect(); gc.collect()
    
    wait_seconds = 10 
    script_logger.info(f"Waiting for {wait_seconds} seconds to allow KuzuDB to fully release resources...")
    time.sleep(wait_seconds)
    
    lock_file_path = os.path.join(DB_PATH, ".lock")
    if os.path.exists(lock_file_path):
        script_logger.warning(f"WARNING: .lock file still exists at '{lock_file_path}' after script completion.")
        try:
            os.rename(lock_file_path, os.path.join(DB_PATH, ".lock_writer_closed"))
            script_logger.info("Renamed .lock file to .lock_writer_closed")
        except Exception as e_rename:
            script_logger.warning(f"Could not rename .lock file: {e_rename}")
    else:
        script_logger.info(f"SUCCESS: .lock file at '{lock_file_path}' was released/removed.")
    script_logger.info("--- Creation Script Finished ---")
```

title: HNSW finalize memory optimization
body:
# Description
In master the entire in-memory HNSW layers are materialized in the finalize operator for `CreateHNSWIndex` before being passed to the batch insert operator. This PR changes it so that each partition (node group) is only materialized right before it is needed by a batch insert thread. This reduces the memory overhead of the materialized partitions to one node group (~140MB with ml=60) per executing thread.

This is done by making introducing a `BasePartitionerSharedState` interface. The existing partitioner shared state remains as `PartitionerSharedState` and contains all materialized partition buffers. For the vector index we introduce a `HNSWLayerPartitionerSharedState` which contains the `HNSWLayer` after the create pipeline completes. Partitions are not actually materialized until `getPartitionBuffer()` is called.

**A quick sanity check on performance:**

Dataset: graph-200-angular

Creating index takes 460.1s on master and 455.5s on the new branch.

title: Java API: fix string encoding scheme mismatches
body: Kuzu always assumes the strings it is working with are encoded in standard UTF-8. title: Reduce HNSW index upper layer memory usage

# Description

For simplicity we currently statically allocate the same size for the upper/lower layers in an HNSW index. Since the upper layer has high selectivity, we can save memory by pre-selecting which nodes in the lower layer to include in the upper layer during init time and only using the selected size for the upper layer. We then store an additional mapping from table offset to graph offset for nodes in the upper layer.

title: Collect memory optimization
body:
# Description

Closes https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5395 and https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5398

Instead of storing a `FactorizedTable` in each `CollectState`, we use the shared overflow buffer to allocate the elements in the collected list. 

The elements will form a linked list, with each element pointing to the memory in the shared overflow buffer containing the next element. This implementation was chosen over a simpler one (e.g. storing a vector of pointers in each `CollectState` to ensure that `CollectState` is trivially destructable, which is desired because the lifetimes of `CollectState` are difficult to manage (as they are stored in a FactorizedTable with their type casted away, which can prevent their destructor from being called).

Also fixes a concurrency bug where an unprotected shared overflow buffer is used in the finalizing the simple hash aggregates. Now, thread-local overflow buffers are used during finalization and the memory is merged into the shared buffer at the end of each thread's finalization.

# Microbenchmarks

First, we check to see the performance impact of the fix to the concurrency bug:

These benchmarks were done on clickbench.

Query | Execution time (master) | Execution time (new) | Peak memory usage (master) | Peak memory usage (new)
----|----|----|----|----
`MATCH (h:hits) RETURN COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID);`|507ms|540ms|4458MB|4506MB
`MATCH (h:hits) RETURN COUNT(DISTINCT h.SearchPhrase);`|455ms|395ms|5270MB|5207MB
`MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.RegionID, COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID) AS u ORDER BY u DESC LIMIT 10;`|1850ms|1840ms|5388MB|5337MB

Next, we check the performance impact on collect:

These benchmarks were done on ldbc-sf01:

Dataset|Query | Execution time (master) | Execution time (new) | Peak memory usage (master) | Peak memory usage (new)
----|----|----|----|----|----
ldbc-sf01 replyOf_Comment (~77K edges) | `MATCH (a:Comment)-[e:replyOf_Comment]->(b:Comment) WITH b, collect(a) as aList RETURN b, aList;`|2.04s|0.38ms|9592MB|1261MB
twitter (~81K nodes, ~2.4M edges) | `MATCH (a:account)-[e:follows]->(b:account) return b.ID, collect(a);`|44s|1.05s|264GB|1.68GB

# Contributor agreement

title: Bug: Kuzu Python Bindings Segmentation Fault
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.10.0

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS 15.5

### What happened?

When using the Kuzu Python bindings, segmentation faults (crashes) occur if `QueryResult` objects are garbage collected after their parent `Connection` or `Database` is closed. This is due to use-after-free in the underlying C++ code.

--
## Expected Behavior
- Python bindings should ensure that child objects (like `QueryResult`) do not outlive their parents, or at least raise a Python exception if used after parent destruction, rather than causing a hard crash.

## Workaround
- Always explicitly `del` all `QueryResult` objects before closing their parent `Connection` or `Database`.
- Immediately call `gc.collect()` after deletion to force cleanup.
- All test helpers and business logic in this project follow this pattern.

## Recommendations for Upstream Fix
- The Kuzu Python bindings should manage object lifetimes so that `QueryResult` objects cannot outlive their parent `Connection`/`Database`.
- If a `QueryResult` is used after its parent is closed, a Python exception should be raised instead of a segfault.
- Consider using weak references or parent tracking in the bindings to enforce this.

## Additional Notes
- This issue is documented in our developer and Sphinx documentation for all contributors.
- See `docs/source/kuzu_developer_guide.rst` and `docs/DEVELOPER_GUIDE.md` for more details and code examples. 

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Minimal Reproducible Example

```python
import kuzu
import gc

db_path = "/tmp/kuzu_test_db"
db = kuzu.Database(db_path)
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# Create a simple schema and insert a node
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Variant(variant_id STRING, PRIMARY KEY (variant_id))")
conn.execute("CREATE (:Variant {{variant_id: 'v1'}})")

# Query for the node
result = conn.execute("MATCH (n:Variant) RETURN n")
for row in result:
    print(row)
# If you do not explicitly delete result and collect, the following close() may segfault
# del result
# gc.collect()

conn.close()
db.close()
# At this point, if 'result' is still alive, Python may segfault due to use-after-free
```

title: Remove the early checkpoint for empty primary key indices
body:
It was necessary to refactor the `DiskArrayCollection` so that it doesn't need to know its header page index until checkpointing begins. 

The way the disk array collection handles this is more complicated than is really necessary, since it's designed to store a variable number of disk arrays, when in reality we always just need 512 (256 hash indexes with one disk array for primary slots and one for overflow slots) and they are all created at once. In its current form I think it would ideally be more self-contained and do something more like what the PrimaryKeyIndex does, serializing and deserializing the location of its header page, but I think that would actually be the wrong direction to take things (unless we actually have a use for a variable number of disk arrays). Otherwise it would probably be a better idea to make it unique to the PrimaryKeyIndex, work with a fixed number of disk arrays and incorporate the HashIndexHeaders.

### Kuzu version

_No response_

### What happened?

Given the following scenario, where we install the JSON extension and add a JSON typed column to a node table, then export it, the export schema puts the extension after the tables, meaning it fails to create the table (as JSON is not yet installed). 
Manually switching the order fixes this issue.

```py
conn.execute("CREATE NODE table test(id INT PRIMARY KEY, attributes JSON)")
conn.execute("CREATE (n:test {id: 1, attributes: {a: 1, b: 2}})")

conn.execute("export database 'test'")
conn.close()

conn = kuzu.Connection(kuzu.Database())
conn.execute("import database 'test'")
conn.execute("MATCH (n:test) RETURN n.attributes")
```


This is the produced schema.cypher file:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE `test` (id INT32,attributes json, PRIMARY KEY(id));
INSTALL JSON;
LOAD EXTENSION JSON;
```
Expected would be: 
```cypher
INSTALL JSON;
LOAD EXTENSION JSON;
CREATE NODE TABLE `test` (id INT32,attributes json, PRIMARY KEY(id));
```

title: Feature: Compact how we display the results tuple/column count
body:
### API

CLI

### Description

Currently, when we display the result of a query in the CLI, we take up two lines at the bottom of the result to show how many tuples, and how many columns there are:
```
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────┬───────────┐
│ company                 │ country_name │ commodity │
│ STRING                  │ STRING       │ STRING    │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
│ Ramelius Resources      │ Australia    │ Gold      │
│ Northern Star Resources │ Australia    │ Gold      │
└─────────────────────────┴──────────────┴───────────┘
(2 tuples)
(3 columns)
```
It would be more. space efficient, as well as more intuitive, to just show it like this instead:
```
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────┬───────────┐
│ company                 │ country_name │ commodity │
│ STRING                  │ STRING       │ STRING    │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
│ Ramelius Resources      │ Australia    │ Gold      │
│ Northern Star Resources │ Australia    │ Gold      │
└─────────────────────────┴──────────────┴───────────┘
shape: (2, 3)
```
In the `shape` descriptor, the x-value would be the number of tuples and the y-value would be the number of columns. This is commonly used in other table formats too. "Tuple" isn't something people who aren't familiar with database terminology will immediately understand.

It's the same way Polars does it, see [here](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/selectors.html#polars.selectors.ends_with) for an example.

```
>>> df.select(cs.ends_with("z"))
shape: (2, 1)
┌─────┐
│ baz │
│ --- │
│ f64 │
╞═════╡
│ 2.0 │
│ 5.5 │
└─────┘
```

title: Optimization: (Recursive) join order optimization
body:
### Description

This might be a potential interesting case for join optimization / recursive queries:
Joining reduces row count by factor ~ 180634, but worsens query performance by factor ~ 7.

First query part (runs quickly; low row count; optimally first join base):
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (t1:A)-[]->(:B)-[]->(:C {name: 'Kùzu'}) RETURN count(t1);
┌──────────────┐
│ COUNT(t1._ID) │
│ INT64        │
├──────────────┤
│ 42           │
└──────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 19.41ms (compiling), 51.99ms (executing)
```

Second query part (recursive; takes much longer; more results):            
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (:A)-[:p_A_B|value_B_A * SHORTEST]-(t2:A) RETURN count(t2);
┌───────────────┐
│ COUNT(t2._ID) │
│ INT64         │
├───────────────┤
│ 7586664       │
└───────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 71.17ms (compiling), 75965.74ms (executing)
```

Joining both and reducing results, query performance is ~ 7x worse than previous one:                                                                                               
```cypher                                                                                                                                                                                   
kuzu> MATCH (t1:A)-[]->(:B)-[]->(:C {name: 'Kùzu'}),
     (t1)-[:p_A_B|value_B_A* SHORTEST]-(t2:A) RETURN count(t2);
┌───────────────┐ 
│ COUNT(t2._ID) │              
│ INT64         │                     
├───────────────┤   
│ 1670          │                      
└───────────────┘   
(1 tuple)                                
(1 column)                            
Time: 11.12ms (compiling), 517672.18ms (executing)
```                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                            
Using `WITH` clause, we currently can manually influence join order and optimization:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (t1:A)-[]->(:B)-[]->(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      WITH t1
      MATCH (t1)-[:p_A_B|value_B_A * SHORTEST]-(t2:A) RETURN count(t2);
┌───────────────┐
│ COUNT(t2._ID) │
│ INT64         │
├───────────────┤
│ 1670          │
└───────────────┘
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 25.56ms (compiling), 77257.63ms (executing)
```

- Optimally the more expensive recursive query would be only executed for those 42 rows from first query part. Judging by their similar executing time (75965.74ms vs. 77257.63ms), it currently doesn't seem to be limited.
- If non-recursive queries do receive much more optimization, perhaps it might make sense to prioritze them over recursive queries join-wise in a first step?
- Possbility for manual join sequence optimize would be awesome (e.g. via `WITH`), if query optimizer is not be able to do so automatically. Expected query time for last query would be something in the millisecond or lower seconds range.

├──────────────┤

Bug: MATCH clause returns nodes with unrelated properties resulting in null columns in query output
body: ### Kuzu version v0.10.0 ### What operating system are you using? MacOS Sonoma 14.1.2 ### What happened? When running a Cypher query with a `MATCH` clause that matches nodes without restricting by label (e.g., `MATCH (n)-[r:IsUser]->(m)`), the returned nodes contain properties that do not belong to the intended source or destination entities. In this case, IsUser is a rel that links a Employee and User table. Instead of retrieving only properties that belong to Employee and User tables, there appear columns belonging to other nodes tables (not linked to IsUser) in the response that appear as `null` values, cluttering the output. This seems to be happening because the query matches all nodes, regardless of their specific labels or entity types, leading to a merged result set with irrelevant properties populated as `null`. **Expected behavior:** The query should only return properties belonging to the source and destination node types specified by relationship so that the result columns correspond only to those relevant nodes and do not include unrelated columns with null values. **Workarounds:** - Post-process the results to remove properties with null columns (not ideal). - Use label-restricted patterns if possible (e.g., `MATCH (n:Employee)-[r:IsUser]->(m:User)`). It seems that removing unrelated properties can be done for all queries, not just ones with a reltype passed in. Thanks! ### Are there known steps to reproduce? This can be verified using the example dataset in Kuzu Explorer with the following query `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) RETURN * LIMIT 5;`

title: Rework CREATE TABLE AS as binary plan

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently, the optimizer seems to only go down the leftmost subtrees (i.e. child at index 0) for logical operators.

For https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5274 we would like to ideally construct a binary logical plan so the subtree responsible for creating the table is independent from the subtree responsible for copying. This will fix the issue demonstrated below:

```
kuzu> create node table if not exists Foo as load from "test.csv" return *;
kuzu> explain logical create node table Bar as match (a:Foo) where false return a.*;
```

Currently, since we construct a linear plan, the above will result in a logical plan with an `EmptyResult` operator, but the optimizer truncates the children, which includes the `CreateTable` operator.

code_snippets.code:
kuzu> create node table if not exists Foo as load from "test.csv" return *;
kuzu> explain logical create node table Bar as match (a:Foo) where false return a.*;

title: stringFormat: optionally use std::format for compile-time checks
body:
The current `stringFormat` implementation does runtime checks for formatting mismatch. C++20's `std::format` does compile-time checks instead.

This PR adds optional support for `std::format` behind an off-by-default CMake flag that simply replaces the implementation behind `stringFormat`.

The idea is to catch missing arguments at compile time in CI. Already found one instance of a missing argument after turning on the flag.

The reason this is not on by default is that `gcc-12` running in self-hosted CI does not support `std::format`.

Caveats:
- The first argument now always needs to be a `const char *`.
- `std::format` does **not** check if there are unused arguments, unlike in `stringFormatHelper`.
- A little inconvenient but support for `{` and `}` is different in the two implementation. `std::format` requires escaping as `{{` and `}}`, while  `stringFormatHelper` does not.
  - This means `{` and `}` cannot appear in a format string as of this PR. I've edited the one instance this currently happens in the code.
  - We could extend the `stringFormatHelper` to detect escaped braces if needed.

title: Collect aggregate function scaling
body:
The collect function currently stores a FactorizedTable for each aggregate state (i.e. each group), which allocates at least one 256KB memory buffer to store its data (and an InMemOverflowBuffer, but that was changed recently to start with small blocks and scale upwards).

The FactorizedTable uses a fixed number of tuples per block, so it would slow down access time if we were to increase the size of the blocks as the number of values increase (though it should still be constant time using the same doubling strategy; albeit a more complicated calculation than just dividing by the number of tuples per block), but we could use a smaller block size and have the blocks be backed by the AggregateHashTable's shared InMemOverflowBuffer instead of being individually allocated which should make up for the performance cost of using smaller blocks.

We also don't strictly need the FactorizedTable: this table stores a single value per tuple with no factorization, and the copyToRowData and copyFromRowData functions work on arbitrary memory addresses. We could move the implementations of `getTuple`, `appendEmptyTuple` and the tracking of the number of flat tuples into the DataBlockCollection, and just use a DataBlockCollection in CollectState (and maybe rename DataBlockCollection).
