title: Add ability to pass python dataframes as query parameters
body:
# Description

Addresses https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5139

Offers the ability to pass a dataframe as a parameter + the ability to have scan sources for `COPY/LOAD FROM` be a parameter. Compared to the existing method of giving the dataframe name directly, this has a few advantages:
1. Unnamed dataframes can be copied from (e.g. directly using the output of a function)
2. This works for the async API (where the df may not be in the scope of the thread executing the query)

Example:
```python
df = pa.Table.from_arrays(
            ...
        )
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE pyarrowtab(id INT32, A STRING, B BOOL, PRIMARY KEY(id))")
conn.execute("COPY pyarrowtab FROM $tab", {"tab": df})
```

## Summary of changes
- Parameters dict is added as an argument to `prepare()`. This is because the dataframe currently must be known during binding, so it must be passed as a parameter to `prepare()`.
- Parameters can now qualify as scan sources. Currently the parameter must resolve to a `POINTER` type otherwise an exception will be thrown
- The `POINTER` that dataframes resolve to is used by the `ScanReplacement` infrastructure to determine how to scan from the dataframe during the actual scan operation. `ScanReplacement` can now perform replacement either by name or by directly using the pointer to the underlying python object.

# Contributor agreement

- [ ] I have read and agree to the [Contributor Agreement](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/master/CLA.md).

title: More BM exception robustness fixes
body:
# Description

When we hit + catch BM exceptions storage structure may not be in a valid state (at least until rollback completes). However other threads may still do a bit of work on the structures before they are interrupted which can lead to data corruption due to working on invalid structures.

This PR fixes two of these problems:
1. We now update the capacity after the allocation in `ColumnChunkData::resize` to avoid the case where we update the capacity but the allocation fails
2. If we hit an exception during `ChunkedNodeGroup::append` we reset the `numValues` of each column chunk to match the number of rows in the chunked group.

title: Move table entry related initialization to initGlobalStateInternal for NodeBatchInsert
body: These changes are required to finish implementing the `CREATE NODE TABLE ... AS` syntax, because the catalog entry was previously required during binding time for creating a `BoundCopyFormInfo` which would be used to call `planCopyFrom`. title: Bug: Incorrect operator precedence parsing for unary minus with IS NOT NULL
body:
### Kuzu version

v0.9.0

### What operating system are you using?

Windows 11

### What happened?

While I was using kuzudb, I encountered the following issue:
```cypher
MATCH (t4:t4)-[e1:e1]->(t0:t0) WHERE (-1 IS NOT NULL) RETURN 1
```
The query threw a binder exception: Binder exception: Cannot match a built-in function for given function NEGATE(BOOL)
It seems that the condition ``-1 IS NOT NULL`` is parsed as ``-(1 IS NOT NULL)``, which negates a boolean value, causing the binder exception.


### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE t4(c0 INT8, c1 UINT32, PRIMARY KEY (c0))
CREATE NODE TABLE t0(c0 UINT32, PRIMARY KEY (c0))
CREATE REL TABLE e1(FROM t4 TO t0)
MATCH (t4:t4)-[e1:e1]->(t0:t0) WHERE (-1 IS NOT NULL) RETURN 1
```

title: extension(neo4j): inexplicable behavior when connecting to Neo4j
Take into account start row idx for node group when checking if all rows are deleted
body:
# Description

When reclaiming space from a node group we preserve the `numRows`, instead updating the `startRowIdx` of the first chunked group. Thus we cannot only check `numRows` to see how many actual rows are in a node group (used to determine if we can reclaim an entire node group), we also need to take into account the `startRowIdx`. This fixes the issue where repeatedly fully deleting + copying into a node group would still keep increasing the size of the DB.

In the Neo4J import tool we use `call db.schema.nodeTypeProperties()` to get the properties for a label, and then use the queried properties in the order of the query output to determine the order of the properties to `COPY FROM`.

For example, if the output of the properties query is 
```
+--------------------------------+
| propertyName | propertyTypes   |
+--------------------------------+
| "id"         | ["Long"]        |
| "name"       | ["String"]      |
| "pets"       | ["StringArray"] |
+--------------------------------+
```

Our `COPY FROM` query will be
```
COPY FROM (LOAD WITH HEADERS(..., id int64, name string, pets string[]))
```

However, the order of the columns actually exported by Neo4J doesn't necessarily match this queried order which can cause the import to fail.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

1. From an empty Neo4J database, run:
```sql
create (n: Node {name: 'Alice', time: datetime("2019-06-01T18:40:32.142+0100"), date: date("2019-06-01"), is
Person: true, pid: 123, eyeSight: 0.55, friends: [1, 2, 3], pets: ['dog'], score: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]});
```
2. From kuzu run:
```sql
CALL NEO4J_MIGRATE(
    "localhost",
    "",
    "",
    ["Node"],
    []
);
```
When running that above query I get the error
`Copy exception: Error in file /tmp/Node.csv on line 2: Conversion exception: Cast failed. 2019-06-01 is not in STRING[] range. Line/record containing the error: '"0",":Node","2019-06-01"...'
`

code_snippets.code: COPY FROM (LOAD WITH HEADERS(..., id int64, name string, pets string[]))

create (n: Node {name: 'Alice', time: datetime("2019-06-01T18:40:32.142+0100"), date: date("2019-06-01"), is
Person: true, pid: 123, eyeSight: 0.55, friends: [1, 2, 3], pets: ['dog'], score: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]});

CALL NEO4J_MIGRATE(
    "localhost",
    "",
    "",
    ["Node"],
    []
);

title: Bug: The SHORTEST function does not take WHERE constraints into account

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Kuzu version

_No response_

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS Sequoia 15.4.1, python kuzu==0.9.0

### What happened?

The SHORTEST function does not take WHERE constraints into account.

It seems to first find the shortest path and then apply the constraints, which often leads to no path found.

Please find below a python script to reproduce the problem.

In a graph with cities connected with routes, we first find the shortest path between Rome and Dublin. But once we had the constraint that the route should not pass by Paris, then no solution is found.


### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```python
import kuzu

db = kuzu.Database(":memory:")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# Graph connecting cities with routes
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE City(name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (name))")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE Route(FROM City TO City)")

# Create cities
cities = ["Paris", "London", "Rome", "Milan", "Berlin", "Bern", "Amsterdam", "Dublin"]
for city in cities:
    conn.execute("CREATE (:City {name: $city});", parameters={"city": city})

# Create routes
routes = [
    ("Paris", "London"),
    ("London", "Dublin"),
    ("Rome", "Bern"),
    ("Bern", "Berlin"),
    ("Bern", "Paris"),
    ("Berlin", "Amsterdam"),
    ("Amsterdam", "London"),
]
for from_city, to_city in routes:
    conn.execute(
        "MATCH (c1:City {name: $from_city}), (c2:City {name: $to_city}) "
        "CREATE (c1)-[:Route]->(c2);",
        parameters={"from_city": from_city, "to_city": to_city},
    )

# Find the shortest path from Rome to Dublin
print("Shortest path from Rome to Dublin:")
result = conn.execute(
    "MATCH p = (:City {name: 'Rome'})-[:Route* SHORTEST]-(:City {name: 'Dublin'}) "
    "RETURN nodes(p) AS path;",
)
result = result.get_next()[0]
print(" -> ".join([node["name"] for node in result]))
# Shortest path should be Rome -> Bern -> Paris -> London -> Dublin

# Find the shortest path from Rom to Dublin without passing through Paris
print("Shortest path from Rome to Dublin without passing through Paris:")
result = conn.execute(
    "MATCH p = (:City {name: 'Rome'})-[:Route* SHORTEST]-(:City {name: 'Dublin'}) "
    "WHERE ALL(city IN nodes(p) WHERE city.name <> 'Paris')"
    "RETURN nodes(p) AS path;",
)
print("Path found?", result.has_next())
# Shortest path should now be Rome -> Bern -> Berlin -> Amsterdam -> London -> Dublin, but no path is found...

```

        'Book',
        'title_vec_index',

    {"query_vector": query_vector}
)

### API

Python, Node.js, Java, Go

### Description

Currently the closing order of objects have to be guaranteed in kuzu (QueryResult & PreparedStatement -> Connection -> Database), otherwise it will result in corrupted memory due to missing the references. title: Improve test coverage for functions so that they can handle empty list/arrays

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### Kuzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

Taking observations from the following related issues:
- https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5216
- https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5307

These are segfaults that were totally preventable had there been an empty list included in the test suite for these functions.

In Python, we have the concept of empty lists `[]`. We really should be testing for empty lists passed over to C++ objects in every case where a list/array function is present. It's incredibly common to encounter mixed lists in Python, where you have a mix of empty lists interspersed with non-empty lists.

For example, the following function should work, but it doesn't. Kuzu should appropriately handle the empty/null array during concatenation because it's very common to encounter specific instances of null/empty arrays in the wild from a realistic dataset.
```cypher
// this fails
return list_cat(['7','3'], []);
Error: Binder exception: Cannot bind LIST_CONCAT with parameter type STRING[] and INT64[].
```

This works:
```
return list_cat(['7','3'], ['1']);
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LIST_CONCAT(LIST_CREATION(7,3),LIST_CREATION(1)) │
│ STRING[]                                         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [7,3,1]                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Rule of thumb
Any time we test a function that uses a list of lists (e.g. `[['a', 'b', 'c'], ['d']]`) in Python, we must also test for empty lists as one of the components of that list of lists (e.g. `[['a', 'b', 'c'], ['d'], []]`). This applies to pandas/polars dataframes as well (where each column of type list is basically a list of lists).

@acquamarin and @ray6080 I think the entire test suite for lists/arrays can be improved to help prevent such segfaults showing up in future bug reports. See [this test](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/a418cd4186c6ed779b9e375a1f67ccdc1cea0185/test/test_files/function/list.test#L462) for an example. Shouldn't we be including `[]` as one of the items in the list? If there's a better way to handle this at the Cypher layer, that's fine too, but the hope is that we prevent these kinds of cases from segfaulting.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

Error: Binder exception: Cannot match a built-in function for given function LIST_TO_STRING(STRING[]). Supported inputs are

│ STRING                                          │

Can we make the error messages for missing function parameters like this more informative?

title: Rework rel group
body:
# Description

This PR reworks how rel tables are stored within the database, especially within Catalog.

Previously we keep both RelGroupEntry and RelTableEntry in the Catalog. The former one refers to rel tables with multiple pairs of src and dst node tables, while the latter one refers to rel tables with only one pair of src and dst node table.
A RelGroupEntry internally depends on multiple RelTableEntries. This nested way of organizing rel tables makes certain things much more complicated, such as transactions, naming conflict checks, supporting adding/removing new/existing pairs, schema altering, etc.

This PR removes RelTableEntry from Catalog completely. Every rel table is created as a RelGroupEntry in the Catalog. We still store RelTable in the storage side, each of which is assigned a unique oid, which can be used to map from a pair in RelGroupEntry to a table in the storage side.

title: Optimization: CSR header space optimization
body:
### Description

For CSR headers we currently always set its capacity to the node group size (128K by default). With FSM now implemented, we can now set the capacity to the maximum non-empty node offset (or the right boundary of the region containing the node offset) as we can now reclaim used pages if the header is updated out-of-place. This way we can keep the storage footprint of the CSR header small if the number of nodes in a graph is small (e.g. a few thousand). 

Note that other parts of the system (e.g. rel scanning, checkpoint) can make assumptions about the uniform capacity of CSR headers, there will need to be changed to get this optimization working. Some changes that will need to be made include:
- `CSRRegion` should be passed a `maxNumRegions` parameter that puts a upper bound on the `rightNodeOffset` of the region.
- When scanning rels, we may now try to scan from node offsets that are out of bounds for the CSR header. We should return an empty result in this case but continue scanning.

title: Migrate Maven Central deployment from OSSRH to Central Publisher Portal
body:
OSSRH will [reach end-of-life on June 30th, 2025](https://central.sonatype.org/news/20250326_ossrh_sunset/). They are forcing everyone to migrate to the new Central Publisher Portal by that date. 

I tried to work with the Central Publisher Portal last year and it was really bad. 
- There was no official support for Gradle build system.
- Third-party tools like [JReleaser](https://jreleaser.org/) did not work properly and also tried to take on the entire release workflow, not just pushing to Maven. 
- The publishing workflow was not standard for Gradle, meaning that we had to setup completely different workflow for publishing to Maven Central (for stable) and GitHub package (for nightly).

Now they claimed that they have a [staging API](https://central.sonatype.org/publish/publish-portal-ossrh-staging-api/) which behaves like the old OSSRH API, so hopefully we can use this and simply change the publishing endpoint and get it work with Gradle. Overall they are very annoying to work with, but we have to do it before **June 30th, 2025**, or we will no longer be able to publish to Maven Central.

title: Reclaim pages for fully-deleted node groups
body:
# Description

Reclaim the occupied storage space for node groups (both normal and CSR) that have had all tuples deleted and reset the persistent chunked group.

Since we don't support deleting from the persistent hash index yet, the row offsets of the deleted tuples are still preserved for node tables. In other words, even though the persistent/first chunked group is empty, its `startRowIdx` will be the number of rows previously in the node group. This allows us to mark those deleted rows as 'not visible'. Also make changes to scanning, serializing, etc. of node groups so that it works when the `startRowIdx` of the first chunked group is not 0.

title: Replace comparisons with toLower/toUpper with caseInsensitiveEquals
body:
For #5256. This improved the single-threaded performance significantly. On my machine the same benchmark used in #5256 took 2.8s initially (in an in-memory database) and improved to 1.7s with this change.

`toLower`/`toUpper` are not very fast since they operate entirely out of place. We could probably also create versions of them that do faster in-place modifications, or which skip changes if they aren't necessary, but that wasn't needed here.
I'd actually implemented a unicode-aware version of `caseInsensitiveEquals` before realising that it doesn't make a difference in this use-case and we already have an ascii-only version (which should generally be faster on ascii strings since it can assume that strings of different lengths are not equal, but unicode upper-case and lower-case characters do not necessarily have the same number of codepoints, so my unicode-aware implementation was a little slower, but still much faster than `toLower`).

Use the FactorizedTable's InMemOverflowBuffer in MinMaxAggregateState
body:
Alternative implementation of #5246 that came from a discussion with @ray6080.

Instead of allocating its own overflow buffer, which can't be freed very easily. Should also reduce data fragmentation, but limits our ability to re-use/free space, though we weren't clearing the overflowBuffer before replacing strings as we could have before anyway.

~~The MinMaxAggregateState now also tracks the actual size allocated (instead of using the size of the string currently stored) so that it won't allocate more memory if the value is first replaced by a small, then a slightly larger value
(e.g. for MAX, if "aaaa" -> "b" -> "cc" we can avoid allocating more memory)~~ *Edit: this turned out to be a problem since short strings would overwrite the overflow pointer. I've reverted it since I think the savings from avoiding re-allocations in these cases may not be worth increasing the base size by 12 bytes (by also adding an extra pointer to the buffer).*

title: Hash Aggregate memory fix
body:
When the hash aggregate operator using the `MIN`/`MAX` functions on strings fails (and also distinct simple aggregate) we are leaking memory since the `AggregateState` objects are being stored as raw data in the FactorizedTable and don't get their destructor called automatically when the FactorizedTable is destroyed (`MinMaxAggregateState` stores a `std::unique_ptr<InMemOverflowBuffer>`).
I've added an AggregateFactorizedTable class with a custom destructor that will call the destructors on all the AggregateState objects it holds.

I had to flip the polarity of the `AggregateState::isNull` field (renaming it to `isValid`) since zeroed memory that was never initialized would have invalid vtable pointers (causing a segfault when the destructor is called), but isNull would be false, and it's easier to have `isNull` become `isValid` and default to invalid and check isValid before trying to call the destructor, than it is to check if the vtable pointer is valid (I'm not sure if there's a good way of doing that).

Also note that the values when being moved from one table to another need to be cleared so that they don't get double-freed, which I've done with a memset in `HashTableQueue::appendTuple` (since each copy of the AggregateState stores a copy of the `std::unique_ptr`; storing it as raw data removes the usual ways of guaranteeing that the unique_ptr is unique). I also renamed appendTuple to moveTuple to better indicate that it's modifying the source data.

title: Feature: Convenience methods to fetch results from Python QueryResult

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
> Couple of comments. Our Python API is more or less similar to DuckDB's.
> 
> Here's an example of using the DuckDB relational API, that's similar to Kuzu's `conn.execute()`.
> ```py
> import duckdb
> 
> conn = duckdb.connect()
> 
> conn.execute("CREATE TABLE User(person STRING PRIMARY KEY, age INT)")
> 
> conn.execute("INSERT INTO User VALUES ('Adam', 25)")
> conn.execute("INSERT INTO User VALUES ('Karissa', 23)")
> 
> result = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM User")
> print(result.fetchmany(size=1))
> 
> result = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM User")
> print(result.fetchone())
> 
> result = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM User")
> print(result.fetchall())
> ```
> This outputs:
> ```
> [('Adam', 25)]
> ('Adam', 25)
> [('Adam', 25), ('Karissa', 23)]
> ```
> As a starting point, it makes sense to implement the convenience methods that DuckDB provides so that users don't need to write the `while` loops every single time they want to retrieve a subset of their result object.
> - `fetchone`
> - `fetchmany`
> - `fetchall` 

 _Originally posted by @prrao87 in [#5240](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5240#issuecomment-2809544644)_

title: Improve scc performance
Feature: Iterator over query.execute() results

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Upon execution of a query, the `Connection.execute()` method returns a QueryResult object (or list of such objects) through which we can explicitly iterate over one or more result sets: 
```py
result = conn.execute(query)
while result.has_next():
    row = result.get_next()
    # ...
```

Unfortunately, QueryResult does not implement the standard Python iterator protocol, which makes retrieving results a bit unusual for Python developers.

A common approach shared by many libraries (such as Alchemy) is to return an object that implements the Python iterator protocol. This would be very welcome (and easy) addition to the interface of the QueryResult class:
```py
class QueryResult:
    # ...
    def __iter__(self):
        self.reset_iterator()
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        if self.has_next():
            return self.get_next()
        raise StopIteration
```
The second improvement, could be combining the `list` and `dict` semantics in the object returned from `get_next()`. Something that BigQuery library provides with their query results. Such an object would allow retrieving individual columns from a row by either their offset (as it is today) or by column name:
```py
row = result.get_next()  # assuming `row` contains 3 columns 'id', 'name', and 'email'
email = row[2]           # as it is today
email = row['email']     # not supported, but would be nice to have 
```

    # ...

row = result.get_next()  # assuming `row` contains 3 columns 'id', 'name', and 'email'

title: Fix failure limit when doing BM Evictions
body:
This was an annoyingly simple mistake, since the intention from the beginning (as the comment indicates) was to use the capacity of the eviction queue as the failure limit.

When doing lots of 256KB allocations the size of the eviction queue is significantly smaller than the capacity even when the buffer pool size has been reached, leading to the failure limit being exceeded before the eviction cursor has wrapped around to the beginning of the queue. And because of the two-stage mark/evict process we don't actually evict anything before failing in this situation.

title: FSM: Reclaim pages when dropping columns/tables
body:
# Description

When dropping a column is committed (dropping a table is just dropping a bunch of columns), pushes the page ranges for the column chunks into the FSM's `uncheckpointedFreeChunks`. After the end of the next checkpoint, these pages will become reusable.

Detecting if a column/table has been dropped is done in the storage layer. In the storage manager, any tables that don't exist in the catalog entry during checkpoint are considered to have been dropped. The same is done at the node group level for dropped columns.

# Testing

There are two types of tests in this PR:
1. Cypher tests that perform basic sanity checks (e.g. does the FSM have >0 pages when expected). These tests are easier to debug and hopefully catch simpler bugs
2. Python tests that perform more complex checks to see if the free page ranges (start page + num pages) exactly match their expected values.

title: Optimization: Add a rewrite rule for queries that use WITH clauses
body:
## Use case

In Q5 and Q6 of [this benchmark](https://github.com/prrao87/kuzudb-study/tree/main/kuzudb), Kuzu is slower than it should be (in comparison to its performance on other queries in the suite).

Q5 (aggregates the returned persons):
```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE c.city = $city AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons
```

Q6 (aggregates the returned persons grouping on other nodes and sorts them):
```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
RETURN count(p.id) AS numPersons, c.city AS city, c.country AS country
ORDER BY numPersons DESC LIMIT 5
```
The usage of the `WITH` clause seems to be slowing the queries down.

In both cases, the query plan could internally be rewritten to avoid using the `WITH` clause. The plan would execute something like the following (per @andyfengHKU's advice):

```cypher
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest),
      (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
AND c.city = $city
AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons
```

### Benefit

A lot of users coming from Neo4j who have `WITH` clauses in their queries like this example could benefit from a performance improvement in Kuzu, without having to rewrite the query.

code_snippets.code:
MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE c.city = $city AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons

MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
WITH p, i
MATCH (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
RETURN count(p.id) AS numPersons, c.city AS city, c.country AS country
ORDER BY numPersons DESC LIMIT 5

MATCH (p:Person)-[:HasInterest]->(i:Interest),
      (p)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City)
WHERE lower(i.interest) = lower($interest)
AND lower(p.gender) = lower($gender)
AND c.city = $city
AND c.country = $country
RETURN count(p) AS numPersons

title: Free space management initial PR
body:
# Description

This PR adds the main infrastructure needed to support free space management. In this PR space is only reclaimed after out-of-place updates of column chunks, reclaiming space after other operations (e.g. dropping columns) will be added in future PRs.

New classes:
- `PageChunkManager`: All data file page allocations are routed through this class. Consumers of this class will request sequential chunks of pages from this class, which will either be allocated by appending new pages to the data file or by reallocating free pages. This class is also used by consumers to free pages when they are no longer needed.
- `FreeSpaceManager`: Keeps track of chunks of pages that are freed. When page allocations are requested, this class can be used to reallocate previously freed pages. This class should not be used directly, instead calls should be made to the `PageChunkManager` which will handle accesses to this class.

Updated benchmarks [here](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/5205#issuecomment-2795154748)

title: Feature: passing object references via "parameters" mechanism for LOAD FROM
body:
### API

Python

### Description

One can use Pandas DataFrame to scan data for `COPY <table> FROM (LOAD FROM df ...)`

The way of specifying the reference to a dataframe is by providing the name of the Python variable inside the text of the query:
```
df = pd.DataFrame({...})  # --------------vv
conn.execute("COPY Person FROM (LOAD FROM df WHERE name="Alice" and age>=18 RETURN *)")
```
IMO, this is very unusual way of passing a Python object reference to a function.

Typically, when a query text is composed in the code, we'd use either literal values, e.g. `where name='Alice' and age>=18` or
placeholders, e.g. `where name=$p1 and age>=$p2` and then we would supply the associations between placeholders and
references to Python objects: `parameters={"p1": "Alice", "p2": get_min_age()}`

Accessing a local variable by its name embedded into query text also has some minor performance penalty as the implementing code has to call `locals()` and lookup for the `df` name within a dict in order to get the object reference.

Also, it seems impossible to use a function call rather than the name of a variable. The code below will fail:
```
def build_df():
    return pd.DataFrame({...})

conn.execute("COPY Person FROM (LOAD FROM build_df() WHERE age >= 18 RETURN *)")
```

Lastly, linters will complain about "not used variable df", as from their point of view `df` is defined but never used in the code.

I suggest to consider implementing an alternative approach for passing references to Python objects (e.g. dataframes) to the
`Connection.execute()` method. Most intuitive seems to be using the existing placeholder parameters mechanism, as it will be consistent with the rest of the Python API.

code_snippets.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({...})  # --------------vv
conn.execute("COPY Person FROM (LOAD FROM df WHERE name="Alice" and age>=18 RETURN *)")

title: Process potential BufferManager eviction candidates in batches
body:
To avoid CPU cache conflicts in heavily concurrent workloads (and also better vectorize the code).

Where previously each thread would seek using the shared atomic cursor to the next non-empty candidate, check if it is evictable and add it to the list of candidates it will attempt to evict and repeat until the thread has found 64 candidates (stopping after a certain point), they will now use the shared cursor to grab the next set of 64 candidates, check them all and try evicting them if any were evictable (if they are all empty or non-evictable then it will continue looping until it finds something or the stop threshold is reached, like before). The main difference is that the cursor is modified just once for each batch of candidates checked, instead of once per candidate, and threads shouldn't be trying to evict candidates from the same cache line (most CPUs I think currently have cache lines of about 64 bytes; I saw a source indicating that some apple CPUs have 128 byte cache lines, but in either case 64 8-byte eviction candidates is much larger. There could still be overlap if another thread goes through the entire eviction queue while a thread is evicting, but that's unlikely).

This reduced the time taken to produce a buffer manager exception using a simplified query I was using when looking at #5176 and #5169 (`MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.Referer, MIN(h.Referer);`) from ~40-60 seconds to about 7 seconds on the 128 thread machine with 512GB ram. I haven't tested it more generally except in some synthetic benchmarks where the performance ranged from marginally to ~10x better. The cases where it was 10x better had a lot of noise and were sometimes also worse. neither the baseline or new times were consistent on the 128 thread machine, but the results did seem generally better. Trying it on my 12-threaded personal machine the benchmarks results were more consistent, but the performance improvements were smaller (~60% faster on an EvictionQueue that's 99% non-evictable with 12 threads, and ~20% faster in the same situation single-threaded).

title: Fix windows import db path bug
body: This is a temporary workaround because our parser requires input cypher queries to escape all special characters in string literal. E.g. The user input query is: 'IMPORT DATABASE 'C:\\db\\uw''. The parser removes any escaped characters and this function accepts the path parameter as 'C:\db\uw'. Then the ImportDatabase operator gives the file path to  antlr4 parser directly without escaping any special characters in the path, which causes a parser exception. However, the parser exception is not thrown properly which leads to the undefined behavior.

title: Bug: JSON extension returns strange errors when handling nulls

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### Kuzu version

v0.9.0

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### Summary of issue

There are 2 versions of a JSON file with `null` values, and each of them behaves differently. The error messages are impossible to understand, so there is a usability concern in this common use case for JSON.

### What happened?

Here's 3 versions of a JSON file named `customer.json`. I'm trying to `LOAD FROM` a file using the JSON extension.

### Version 1

```json
{
    "accountContacts": [
        {
        "objectType": "contact",
        "schemaVersion": "135",
        "contactIdentifier": "320864",
        "contactNamespace": "56127",
        "contactDetail": {
            "fullname": "Renee Luke",
            "email": "renee.luke@datapath.com",
            "phone": "(678) 252-4828 - Direct"
            }
        }
    ]
}
```
Runs successfully and I can get the following result from the `MATCH` query:
```
shape: (1, 5)
┌────────┬─────────────┬────────────┬─────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
│ n.id   ┆ n.namespace ┆ n.fullname ┆ n.email                 ┆ n.phone                 │
│ ---    ┆ ---         ┆ ---        ┆ ---                     ┆ ---                     │
│ str    ┆ str         ┆ str        ┆ str                     ┆ str                     │
╞════════╪═════════════╪════════════╪═════════════════════════╪═════════════════════════╡
│ 320864 ┆ 56127       ┆ Renee Luke ┆ renee.luke@datapath.com ┆ (678) 252-4828 - Direct │
└────────┴─────────────┴────────────┴─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘
```

### Version 2

Sometimes, the input source can provide a `null` value in the JSON (note that the source actually returns `null` and not the string `"null"`, so this is something that's hard to fix upstream). In this example, the `"schemaVersion"` key has a `null` value.

```json
{
    "accountContacts": [
        {
        "objectType": "contact",
        "schemaVersion": null,
        "contactIdentifier": "320864",
        "contactNamespace": "56127",
        "contactDetail": {
            "fullname": "Renee Luke",
            "email": "renee.luke@datapath.com",
            "phone": "(678) 252-4828 - Direct"
            }
        }
    ]
}
```
This produces the following error during `COPY` in Kuzu:
```
RuntimeError: Runtime exception: Trying to a create a vector with ANY type. This should not happen. Data type is expected to be resolved during binding.",
```

### Version 3

Let's move the null value to another key, namely the `"contactNamespace"`.

```json
{
    "accountContacts": [
        {
        "objectType": "contact",
        "schemaVersion": "135",
        "contactIdentifier": "320864",
        "contactNamespace": null,
        "contactDetail": {
            "fullname": "Renee Luke",
            "email": "renee.luke@datapath.com",
            "phone": "(678) 252-4828 - Direct"
            }
        }
    ]
}
```
A totally different error is returned:

```
RuntimeError: Binder exception: Data type of expression namespace should not be modified.
```



### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Run the following code on each JSON version:

```python
import kuzu

db = kuzu.Database()
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

conn.execute("INSTALL json; LOAD json;")

conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Contact(id STRING PRIMARY KEY, namespace STRING, fullname STRING, email STRING, phone STRING);")

res = conn.execute(
    """
    LOAD FROM 'customer.json'
    WITH accountContacts AS account_contacts
    UNWIND account_contacts AS contact
    RETURN
        contact.contactIdentifier AS id,
        contact.contactNamespace AS namespace,
        contact.contactDetail.fullname AS name,
        contact.contactDetail.email AS email,
        contact.contactDetail.phone AS phone
    """
)
print(res.get_as_pl())
```

## Desired outcome from a usability perspective

- The JSON extension should be able to handle `null` (not the string, but the actual value itself) because this is commonly output in this form from some upstream systems. Missing keys aren't the only scenario where we need to handle nulls in JSON.
- If some unexpected value is sent to the JSON that doesn't align with Kuzu's schema expectations, we should show a helpful error to help the user know what went wrong. The current errors are too hard to interpret.

title: Fix stop threshold for BM evictions
body:
Sets the stop threshold for eviction to be exactly twice through the eviction queue

Previously we were not only skipping counting empty slots (`EvictionQueue::next` returns what is possibly the next non-empty slot), but were not taking into account other threads evicting at the same time (the eviction cursor is shared, and if there are n threads evicting at once, it's overkill to try to check the entire queue 2n times; we just need to do it twice to make sure that any pages which were unlocked when we start are marked on the first pass and evicted on the second).

This significantly improves failure time when a large number of threads are trying to evict at the same time, and partially addresses the last issue I mentioned in #5169.

title: Migrate / mirror all containers to ghcr.io

title: Old dates not parsed correctly for Node.js API
body:
# Historical dates not parsed correctly

## Description of the problem

Kuzu Explorer does not seem to correctly parse historical dates, such as date objects from the Middle Ages. Such very old dates are correctly parsed and loaded into a Kuzu database from the Python client (no problem there!). But when a database with historical dates is loaded into Kuzu Explorer, the data is corrupted. And when a historical date is created in Kuzu Explorer the same problem occurs.

## Reproduce the problem

In Kuzu Explorer, a date can be created and read, as shown in the example [here](https://docs.kuzudb.com/cypher/data-types/#date).

```
RETURN date('2025-04-01') as x;
>>> 2025-04-01
```

But when we do the same for a historical date (i.e. Middle Ages), the data is incorrectly parsed.

```
RETURN date('1400-04-01') as x;
>>> 1984-10-20
```
```
RETURN date('1300-05-01') as x;
>>> 1884-11-18
```

## Conclusion

The error I encountered when loading my Kuzu database into Kuzu Explorer seems to be related to this general issue of how Kuzu Explorer creates / interprets very old date objects. Hopefully this simpler reproducibility example gets to the root issue, without the need to generate a full reproduction of creating historical date objects in a database and loading them into Kuzu Explorer.

title: Fix click benchmark query 29
body:
There were two issues here, one was that I mistyped the regex, leading to it aggregating on 19 million groups instead of ~75 (I think it was failing to match anything, so it produced the original URL instead of replacing it with the domain name), and the second being that the min function (as well as max and presumably other similar aggregate functions) allocates through `MemoryManager::allocateBuffer` which was always increasing the buffermanager's used memory by at least 256KB (19M * 256KB = ~4.6TB).

It might be worthwhile to look at the comparative performance and introduce other size classes (at the moment it would be easy to add 4KB) to the BM-backed allocations supported by the MemoryManager.
And while are other limits on how `BufferManager::pin` works (such as the size of the eviction queue being computed based on the assumption that we cannot ever fill it if all allocations have the smallest page size class (4KB)), it might be possible to have the buffer manager record the actual amount of memory used within the page's region in the PageState so that we can avoid this issue with most sizes that go through the memory manager (to avoid exhausting space in the eviction queue we could use malloc for sizes below 4KB and above 256KB and use this for sizes in-between).

For some reason though, on our 128 thread 512GB machine the query was hanging instead of throwing a BufferManagerException when it ran out of space. It seems like it's just getting stuck just below the buffer manager memory limit and spending a lot of time trying to evict pages to make space for new allocations, and it might just be that it's taking a disproportionately long time to evict the few actually evictable pages in the queue (after which it will throw a BufferManagerException), while the rest are unevictable pages pinned by the MemoryManager (and maybe it's also adding new evictable pages at the same time). I'm not really sure what can be done to improve responsiveness in this case, as I think the issue might be made worse by many threads trying to evict simultaneously and the eviction queue being particularly large due to the default buffer pool size of 410GB, so it might just be an issue with the BufferManager not being very efficient at this scale (using malloc instead of the BM should help with that though, as pages from the MemoryManager that are pinned for long periods of time are a big part of the problem).

For the moment I've just made allocateBuffer use malloc internally for all sizes except 256KB, and merged mallocBuffer with allocateBuffer since there is no reason to distinguish between them any more.

title: Recursive query takes long time, none-recursive query returns immediately (same output row count and query structure)
body:
### Description

I am currently using a query looking similar to this one:
```cypher
MATCH (b:A)-[]->(:Attribute)-[]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);
```
Above query returns ~ 1k rows immediately.

In order to make statement a bit more concise, I changed it to:
```cypher
MATCH (b:A)-[* 2..2]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);
```
This query works hard - I skipped at "Current Pipeline Progress: 10%" after a minute or so.

Conceptually type `A` or `C` - there are more, but let's limit to these - is always followed by `Attribute`, which then is followed by `A` or `C` again, and cycle may repeat multiple times. There is a single relation type for `(A|C) --> (Attribute)` and another for `(Attribute) --> (A|C)`. `Attribute` is a reified node, hence this pairwise hopping sequence.
```
(A|C) --> (Attribute) --> (A|C) --> (Attribute) -> ...
```

In summary, given same output rows and otherwise equal query structure, there is a big performance difference between recursive and non-recursive searching. Here is the row count from splitting query parts:
```cypher
MATCH (c:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'}) RETURN count(c);
// 33
MATCH (b:A)-[]->(:Attribute)-[]->(:C) RETURN count(b);
// 41206
MATCH (b:A)-[* 2..2]->(:C) RETURN count(b);
// 41206
```

Is this expected behavior? 
For now I marked issue as performance optimization, not sure about a bug. Hopefully you got a hint from description, otherwise let me try to re-create a graph with dummy data.

code_snippets.code:
MATCH (b:A)-[]->(:Attribute)-[]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);

MATCH (b:A)-[* 2..2]->(:C)<-[* SHORTEST 1..6]-(:C {name: 'Kùzu'})
      RETURN count(b);
(A|C) --> (Attribute) --> (A|C) --> (Attribute) -> ...

title: WAL replaying optimization for incomplete transactions
body:
### Description

Our WAL replaying can be quite slow. This can lead to cases like in https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5016 where upon killing a long-lasting query and then reloading the DB it can appear like the DB is hanging (when in reality we are just replaying the query).

In the above case uncommitted records actually don't need to be replayed. Thus one possible optimization would be to deserialize records in batches and only replay the records if they are followed by a commit. In the above case this would mean that we only pay the cost of deserializing records and not the cost of replaying them.

title: Fix size of chunks in RelBatchInsert

In RelBatchInsert, the size of the in-memory local chunked group is being set before the end offset is adjusted in     `csrHeader.finalizeCSRRegionEndOffsets(rightCSROffsetOfRegions);`, leading to the chunk being larger than necessary (with memory that prior to #5082 was uninitialised).

As far as I can tell this isn't affecting what gets written to disk, just what's in-memory (at least in the examples I was looking at).

title: Allow WAL replaying on some corrupted WAL files (e.g. after DB was killed)

# Description

After a kuzu process is killed, the WAL may be in an incomplete state. This PR stops an error from being reported if we are replaying an incomplete WAL. Instead the replaying logic will be:
```
for each WAL record:
  record = WAL::deserializeRecord() // if this throws stop replaying
  WAL::replayRecord(record) // if this throws we continue replaying as the next record should be a rollback
```

Fixes https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5016

title: Avoid project constant expression in WITH
body:
# Description

Avoid projecting constant expression in WITH clause. We will explicitly project constant and write to schema/resultSet if user writes it in projection list. However, consider the following case

```
WITH constant
MATCH (a) WHERE a.prop =  constant.
```

The planner will treat this as a cross product between `Scan(constant)` and `Scan(a)`. It cannot even resolve the join condition properly because `a.prop = constant` is considered as a simple predicate that should be pushed into scan.

I think the right solution is to rewrite the projection list to not contain any constant.

Fixes #5040 

# Contributor agreement

title: Make Python API queries interruptable
body:
# Description

Add `interrupt()` to Python API which will interrupt the currently executing query for a connection. I also modified the async API so that `interrupt()` is called when an async execution is cancelled.

I was originally going to add some functionality to the synchronous connection so that it will automatically interrupt if a SIGINT/KeyboardInterrupt is received but due to how signal handling works in Python + our implementation I don't think it is a good idea to do this. I'll elaborate more on this below:

1. Only the main Python thread can raise/handle signals. This immediately prevents us from checking for signals from worker threads. There is also a chance that the user is calling kuzu functions from other python threads as well in which case no threads running our code will be able to raise signals.
2. Assuming that we decide to handle SIGINTs only if `execute()` is called from the main python thread, we will need to execute the query in a separate thread (similarly to what the async API does) so that the calling thread can busy-loop and poll for any signals. However this runs into the same issues as the async API [like this](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu-docs/issues/414#issuecomment-2744264216). 

So I think it's best for us not to do any special handling of SIGINTs for now and leave it up to the user.

Partially addresses https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/5016

title: Feature: Add naive hybrid search (FTS + vector search)

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

With the upcoming vector index, we should consider adding support for hybrid search, where the user may want to combine FTS (keyword-based) and vector search results to improve the relevance of results.

A naive, simple implementation is shown in [this blog post](https://isaacflath.com/blog/blog_post?fpath=posts%2F2025-03-17-Retrieval101.ipynb) and would be a good starting point.

Here's how it would look in Python:

```py
def hybrid_search(query, top_k=5, vector_weight=0.7):
    """Perform hybrid search using both vector similarity and BM25 keyword matching."""
    # Vector search
    query_embedding = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)
    vector_results = chunk_table.search(query_embedding).metric('cosine').limit(top_k*2).to_pandas()
    vector_results['vector_score'] = 1 - vector_results['_distance']
    
    # Keyword search with BM25s
    # Create corpus from our chunks
    corpus = chunks_df['content'].tolist()
    
    # Tokenize the corpus and index it
    corpus_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(corpus)
    retriever = bm25s.BM25(corpus=corpus)
    retriever.index(corpus_tokens)
    
    # Tokenize the query and retrieve results
    query_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(query)
    docs, scores = retriever.retrieve(query_tokens, k=len(corpus))  # Get scores for all documents
    
    # Map BM25 scores to our dataframe indices
    bm25_scores = {i: scores[0, idx] for idx, i in enumerate(docs[0])}
    vector_results['bm25_score'] = vector_results.index.map(
        lambda x: bm25_scores.get(x, 0) if x in bm25_scores else 0)
    
    # Normalize BM25 scores
    if vector_results['bm25_score'].max() > 0:
        vector_results['bm25_score'] = vector_results['bm25_score'] / vector_results['bm25_score'].max()
    
    # Combine scores with weighting
    vector_results['combined_score'] = (
        vector_weight * vector_results['vector_score'] + 
        (1 - vector_weight) * vector_results['bm25_score'])
    
    return vector_results.sort_values('combined_score', ascending=False).head(top_k)
```

This maps the retrieved results from BM25 to the vector search indices, normalizes the BM25 scores to align with the vector search results, and then applies the user-specified `vector_weight`, which instructs the algorithm how much to weight the vector search results over the FTS results. 0.7 is a sensible default (because too high a weight given to FTS can result in fewer matches overall - vector search is more forgiving).

I think this would be a decent base implementation to do at the C++ level, that can then be exposed to the higher level clients with the specified arguments without too much work. Alternatively, we could only implement this in Python for an initial release, so that users at least have an option to get relevant keyword-based results alongside vector search results from their graphs.

title: Add AsyncConnection for asynchronous query execution on Python API
body:
# Description

This PR adds an async connection for executing queries asynchronously in Python. It is backed by a thread pool.

## Examples
```py
import asyncio
import shutil

import kuzu

shutil.rmtree("test_db")
db = kuzu.Database("test_db")

# create the async connection, the underlying connection pool will be automatically created and managed by the async connection
conn = kuzu.AsyncConnection(db, max_concurrent_queries=4, max_threads_per_query=4)


async def main():
    # create a table
    await conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE person(ID INT64 PRIMARY KEY, age INT64)")
    await conn.execute("MERGE (p:person {ID: 0, age: 20})")
    await conn.execute("MERGE (p:person {ID: 1, age: 25})")
    await conn.execute("MERGE (p:person {ID: 2, age: 30})")
    # run one query
    query = "MATCH (a:person) RETURN a.*;"
    result = await conn.execute(query)
    while result.has_next():  # type: ignore
        print(result.get_next())  # type: ignore

    # run concurrent queries
    num_queries = 10
    queries = [f"MATCH (a:person {{ID: {i}}}) RETURN a.*;" for i in range(num_queries)]
    result = await asyncio.gather(*[conn.execute(query) for query in queries])
    for r in result:
        while r.has_next():  # type: ignore
            print(r.get_next())  # type: ignore

    # use prepared statement
    query = "MATCH (a:person) WHERE a.ID = $1 RETURN a.*;"
    prepared = await conn.prepare(query)
    result = await conn.execute(prepared, {"1": 0})
    while result.has_next():  # type: ignore
        print(result.get_next())  # type: ignore


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
``` 

## Full example

Here's a more complete example.

```py
import asyncio
import shutil

import kuzu

shutil.rmtree("test_db")
db = kuzu.Database("test_db")
# Create the async connection
# The underlying connection pool will be automatically created and managed by the async connection
conn = kuzu.AsyncConnection(db, max_concurrent_queries=4)

async def create_tables(conn: kuzu.AsyncConnection) -> None:
    """Create the node and relationship tables"""
    await conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE User(name STRING PRIMARY KEY, age INT64)")
    await conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE City(name STRING PRIMARY KEY, population INT64)")
    await conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE Follows(FROM User TO User, since INT64)")
    await conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE LivesIn(FROM User TO City)")


async def copy_data(conn: kuzu.AsyncConnection) -> None:
    """Copy the data from the CSV files to the node and relationship tables"""
    await conn.execute("COPY User FROM 'example_data/user.csv' (header=true)")
    await conn.execute("COPY City FROM 'example_data/city.csv'")
    await conn.execute("COPY Follows FROM 'example_data/follows.csv'")
    await conn.execute("COPY LivesIn FROM 'example_data/lives-in.csv'")


async def query_1(conn: kuzu.AsyncConnection) -> None:
    result = await conn.execute("MATCH (u:User)-[:LivesIn]->(c:City) RETURN u.*")
    print(result.get_as_pl())  # type: ignore


async def query_2(conn: kuzu.AsyncConnection) -> None:
    result = await conn.execute(
        """
        MATCH (u:User {name: $name})-[:Follows]->(u2:User) RETURN u.name, u2.name
        """,
        parameters={"name": "Karissa"},
    )
    print(result.get_as_pl())  # type: ignore


async def main():
    await create_tables(conn)
    await copy_data(conn)
    # Run queries
    await query_1(conn)
    await query_2(conn)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

title: Compress neighbour offsets for in-mem HNSW graph
body:
# Description

Depending on the number of nodes in the graph we may not need to use 8 bytes to store each node offset. This PR determines the smallest type that can fit in every node offset in a graph and uses it to store the offsets, reducing memory usage of the `dstNodesBuffer` in `InMemHNSWGraph` from `num_nodes * max_degree * 8` to `num_nodes * max_degree * compressed_offset_size`.

**Some quick microbenchmarks for index creation:**
Dataset: `mnist-784`
Ran with 8 threads
Branch|Peak RSS usage|index building time
----|----|----
master|937.6MB|12.58s
new|896.2MB|12.80s

title: Feature: Support for Atomic Backup API (Similar to SQLite Backup API)

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Node.js

### Description

Kuzu currently lacks an atomic export operation to create a full database backup while allowing writes to continue. This feature would be useful for use cases such as event-sourced architectures, where backups need to be taken at a specific event index to enable point-in-time recovery.

### Use Case:

- In an event-sourced system, all writes to Kuzu are synchronized through an event log.
- During a backup, it's crucial to capture the exact event index to enable deterministic recovery.
- A feature similar to [SQLite's Backup API](https://www.sqlite.org/backup.html) would allow creating a consistent database snapshot without stopping writes.

### Proposed Solution:

- Implement a mechanism to clone or export the entire database atomically.
- Ensure that the snapshot remains consistent even if writes occur during the operation. Or automatically pause all writes on the SDK layer so the client code doesn't need to worry about locking.
- Provide an API to initiate and manage such a backup process.

title: Distinct Aggregate vectorization
body:
This involved refactoring the AggregateHashTable a bit, since the distinct tables end up having mixed flat/unflat vectors when you add the distinct key (since it always is the last column, but may be flat when there are unflat vectors, so the existing split of flat vectors first, then unflat vectors didn't really work).

The performance difference isn't huge for most queries, but it makes a much bigger difference for aggregation over complex data types where there is more overhead when calculating the hashes (the list and struct hashing functions allocate a temporary ValueVector, which is probably the main difference in the performance).

Performance (first is from Clickbench, the others were just constructed to see how similar queries perform with lists/structs as the keys):
| Query | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.RegionID, COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID) AS u ORDER BY u DESC LIMIT 10;` | 2.25s | 2.1s |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.RegionID, COUNT(DISTINCT [h.UserID]) AS u ORDER BY u DESC LIMIT 10;` | 17.5s | 2.7s |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.RegionID, COUNT(DISTINCT {"id": h.UserID}) AS u ORDER BY u DESC LIMIT 10;` | 3.7s | 2.3s |

# Description

In a multi-label graph like SF100, when running page_rank, ther memory error occurs mainly because Degrees & pValues are not correctly pinned with the pinTable operation:

1. The calculation of degrees uses EmptyGDSAuxiliaryState, which does not have pinTable.
2. In the PageRankAuxiliaryState, pNext should use pinTable(fromTableID) because pNext updates with boundNodeID.
3. It is necessary to inherit from FrontierPair to implement PageRankFrontierPair, because the activesNode added to nextDenseFrontier is boundNodeID.

title: Feature: Convenience function to return a table of database statistics

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Feature

Return a single table containing statistics of the number of nodes and relationships (grouped by table name).

### Description

As of v0.8.2, it's quite tedious to display the summary of the number of nodes and relationships, grouped by the table name. It takes the following two queries run sequentially:

#### Query 1

```cypher
MATCH (n) 
RETURN label(n), COUNT(label(n));
```
```
┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
│ LABEL(n._ID,[User,City]) │ COUNT(LABEL(n._ID,[User,City])) │
│ STRING                   │ INT64                           │
├──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
│ User                     │ 4                               │
│ City                     │ 3                               │
└──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Query 2
```cypher
MATCH ()-[r]->() 
RETURN label(r), COUNT(label(r));
```
```
┌──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LABEL(r._ID,[,,Follows,LivesIn]) │ COUNT(LABEL(r._ID,[,,Follows,LivesIn])) │
│ STRING                           │ INT64                                   │
├──────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LivesIn                          │ 4                                       │
│ Follows                          │ 4                                       │
└──────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
It takes a lot of manual typing and remembering the Cypher syntax for `label(x)` to get the results in two separate statements.

## Suggested syntax

It would be great to expose a function that does this in one single command.

```cypher
CALL get_db_stats() RETURN *;
```

Or something along those lines, to return a combined table that shows the number of nodes and relationships, grouped by the table name. Neo4j's APOC does this via [apoc.meta.stats](https://neo4j.com/labs/apoc/4.4/overview/apoc.meta/apoc.meta.stats/).

## Why is this useful?

After a large data ingestion job, it can be very useful to run a single command to check that the right number of nodes and relationships exist in the database. Many visualization tools do this by default. Examples of G.V() and Neo4j browser below.

#### G.V()

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cc0be4ca-0b24-4611-8148-f8246673b801)

#### Neo4j browser

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c038475e-57b4-41a1-8046-25f1c4058044)


## Downstream benefit

If this is implemented, we can pass the results to the Kuzu Explorer UI so that we can display the statistics when the user opens the UI, similar to how other visualization tools do it.

code_snippets.code:
MATCH (n) 
RETURN label(n), COUNT(label(n));

MATCH ()-[r]->() 
RETURN label(r), COUNT(label(r));
CALL get_db_stats() RETURN *;

title: Filtered HNSW search
body:
# Description

Implement the global adaptive filtered search.
The idea is to make use of semi mask to pass the filtering information on node table to the QueryHNSWIndex function.
Inside the function, we follow a heuristic rule based on the selectivity of semi mask:
- If the selectivity is pretty low (<=0.08), we would perform `blindTwoHopFilteredSearch`, which blindly explores the first and second hop neighbours to find those that are selected.
- If the selectivity is somewhat low (<=0.4), we would perform `directedTwoHopFilteredSearch`, which explores the first hop neighbours first to gat a candidate set, and then explore the second hop neighbours in a more directed way that prioritizes nodes in the candidate set that is closest to the query vector. This will hopefully leads to faster converge to the area with closeted nodes.
- If the selectivity is high (>0.4), we would perform `oneHopFilteredSearch`, which finds all selected nodes in the first hop neighbours.

There is a more advanced way, which is based on each node's selectivity to perform adaptive searches. We can move to that in a later PR.
Also, there are two left TODOs:
- add the brute force computation into the adaptive strategy.
- provide options for configuration of the threshold for each method.

body:
The performance improvement isn't as good as I was first expecting, I think it was somewhat over-represented in the profiling.

Copying 100000000 edges from datagen-9_0-fb (as nodes in a parquet file) took ~12.8s before and ~12.2s after (~5% speedup).

I also noticed that the way we are calculating the statistics for nulls/bools was bugged in certain cases since for bools we weren't taking into account the offset of the input data in `getMinMaxStorageValue` (which required rewriting NullMask::getMinMax). That deficiency was being offset by `copyFromBuffer` just assuming that there are always both `false` and `true` values (but only if there are at least some true values, so it wasn't hiding the issue always). 
So this might improve read performance and compression of nulls in some cases where it was previously miscalculating/over-estimating the statistics, but I think in the trivial case where we're just appending full vectors at a time without any nulls it won't make a difference.

title: Make QueryResult::toString const
body:
Having toString mutate the query result means that in rust we can't use the Display trait (safely anyway). I think it's also somewhat unintuitive for it to mutate itself in this case.

I'd actually looked at this a while ago but had been attempting to separate the iterator from the QueryResult entirely (e.g. have a `QueryResult::iter` method that produces an iterator which has getNext/hasNext functions instead of having that be directly on the QueryResult, but that affected a lot of stuff so I never finished it. 
Instead, I've made it so that QueryResult::toString uses its own FlatTupleIterator/FlatTuple and avoids mutating the one from the QueryResult. 

There will be a subtle difference in behaviour, as you can no longer start consuming the results and then use `toString` to print the remaining results, but [hopefully](https://xkcd.com/1172/) that's not behaviour anyone was relying on.

title: Implement SQL_QUERY function
body:
This PR introduces an utility function `SQL_QUERY` which allows users to execute any read sql queries in postgres and retrieve the result in kuzu.

Currently, the query to be executed in postgres must be a read-only query. 

## Grammar:
```sql
SQL_QUERY(ATTACHED_PG_DB, PG_QUERY)
```
### Parameters: 
`ATTCHED_PG_DB`: is the postgres database name attached previously.
`SQL_QUERY`: is the query to be executed in the attached postgres instance.

### Result:
The queryResult in kuzu format.

## Example:
The remote postgres database must be attached first by the attach command:
```sql
ATTACH 'dbname=university user=postgres host=localhost password=testpassword port=5432' AS uw (dbtype postgres);
```

## Features supported in this PR:
Use `CALL` statement to execute the PG_QUERY function and retrieve the result.
```
CALL SQL_QUERY(uw, 'select * from person')
```

## Features to support in the next PRs.
After attaching the postgres database, users can utilize the `LOAD FROM` statement to scan from any postgres query result:
```
LOAD FROM SQL_QUERY(uw, "select name, award from professor INNER JOIN scientist  ON professor.ID = scientist.ID;")
RETURN name, grade;
```

Or use the `COPY FROM` clause to do data ingestion from a complicated PG join query (which is request by the user: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4970):
```
COPY city FROM SQL_QUERY(uw, "select city.name, country.name
from city JOIN country 
ON country.id = city.country_id
WHERE country.name in ('Germany', 'France')
```

The optional arguments to the GDS functions should either be:
1. Literal expression,
2. Paramater expression and should be evaluated as a literal at execution time.

title: Selection vector slicing with lightweight SelectionView
body:
The goal was to remove the selection vector copy in `ChunkedNodeGroup::append`, since the partitioner used in rel table copies appends values one at a time and the allocation is relatively expensive.

I ended up creating a parent class for the SelectionVector called SelectionView which is a read-only version of the SelectionVector, and then `SelectionVector::slice` produces a SelectionView over a subsequence of the original selection vector (you can also create SelectionViews over the static `INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS` array which don't do any heap allocations using its constructor). I had considered just a variant of the SelectionVector which doesn't allocate anything, but I think this works out to be a cleaner interface, and it wouldn't have been possible to easily guarantee that a sliced SelectionVector wouldn't be able to modify the original data using `SelectionVector::operator[]`.

Copying 100 000 000 edges from the datagen-9_0-fb dataset took ~17s before this change and ~15s after.

title: Add projected graph node filter
body:
# Description

This PR adds node filter to projected graph. 

For node filter, we do lazy evaluation to make sure data is always up to date, i.e. the node filter is evaluated on each GDS call. Prior to GDS evaluation, node filters are converted to semi masks and pass to GDS shared state & on disk graph.

With node filter, on-disk-graph edge scan will filtered out nbr nodes that doesn't pass the mask. I didn't implement the same logic for vertex scan because it is used for full text search only. Instead, GDS does not scan anything from on-disk-graph so the logic to check mask is implemented in vertex compute. This design is still debatable and may change in the future.

An immediate problem revealed from this PR is that we should separate recursive join from GDS into different operators. 

Btw I skipped SCC in this PR.

title: Fix deserialization of empty node groups
body:
# Description

When we deserialize an empty node group, we don't correctly copy the data types over to the new node group which causes the DB to crash when serializing + deserializing a second time (and probably many other problems).

For node tables this isn't an issue because we should never have empty node groups, but this becomes an issue for rel tables because the node group idx of a rel is determined by the node group idx of the bound node. This can create gaps between populated csr node groups that are filled with empty node groups.

Fixes https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4953

title: Bug: Inconsistent behaviour of `to_json` function
body:
### Kùzu version

v0.8.2

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS Sequoia 15.3.1

### What happened?

First off, I'm loving kuzu -- great job everyone!

I'm attempting to write a query returning nodes for which a particular JSON property matches a user-provided query in the form of a path and expected value. In python:

```python
conn.execute(
    """\
    MATCH (n)
    WHERE json_extract(n.property, $p) = $v
    RETURN n
    """,
    parameters={
        "p": "path/into/json",
        "v": "value",
    },
)
```
This results in an exception:
```
RuntimeError: Binder exception: Data type of expression json_extract(n.property,$p) should not be modified.
```

This seems a little odd, but not the end of the world. Modifying the query slightly, wrapping the right-hand side of the comparison in `to_json` allows the query to run, but this is where I start seeing strange behaviour -- certain values yield strange results. Rather than worry about creating and populating a table to test, It's easier to illustrate with a simpler example:

```cypher
RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", XXX), "foo") = to_json(XXX);
```
Aside from `NULL`, I'd expect the above to return `true` for any valid JSON, but it doesn't.

## Works as expected

✅ String value (`"bar"`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", "bar"), "foo") = to_json("bar");
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,bar),foo),to_json(bar)) │
│ BOOL                                                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ True                                                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

✅ Integer value (`5`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", 5), "foo") = to_json(5);
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,5),foo),to_json(5)) │
│ BOOL                                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ True                                                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

✅ Boolean value (`true`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", true), "foo") = to_json(true);
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,True),foo),to_json(True)) │
│ BOOL                                                          │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ True                                                          │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Unexpected results

❌ String containing integer (`"5"`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", "5"), "foo") = to_json("5");
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,5),foo),to_json(5)) │
│ BOOL                                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ False                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

❌ String containing boolean (`"true"`)
```
kuzu> RETURN json_extract(json_object("foo", "true"), "foo") = to_json("true");
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EQUALS(json_extract(json_object(foo,true),foo),to_json(true)) │
│ BOOL                                                          │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ False                                                         │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The left-hand side (`json_extract`) is always returning what I'd expect -- a JSON-encoded string. The right-hand side (`to_json`) appears to sometimes interpret its input as a literal and sometimes interpret as a JSON document. Since, in my use case, both the path and value are provided by the user, I appear to have no choice but to make use of `to_json` (else hit a binder exception) but that has gives unexpected results.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Prerequisite:
```
INSTALL JSON;
LOAD EXTENSION JSON;
```

Minimal examples highlighting inconsistent behaviour of `to_json`:
```
kuzu> RETURN to_json(5);
┌────────────┐
│ to_json(5) │
│ json       │
├────────────┤
│ 5          │
└────────────┘
kuzu> RETURN to_json("5");
┌────────────┐
│ to_json(5) │
│ json       │
├────────────┤
│ 5          │
└────────────┘
kuzu> RETURN to_json(true);
┌───────────────┐
│ to_json(True) │
│ json          │
├───────────────┤
│ true          │
└───────────────┘
kuzu> RETURN to_json("true");
┌───────────────┐
│ to_json(true) │
│ json          │
├───────────────┤
│ true          │
└───────────────┘

title: Statistics update optimization
body:
As far as I can tell, the issue in #4936 (where speed is concerned; I still need to look into memory usage) is that it's hitting a particularly slow way of updating our statistics. Copying from CSV is significantly better, but was still slower than it could be.

I've optimized this particular part of the code by removing the repeated calls to the single-input `ColumnChunkStats::update` and replacing it with code that calculates the min/max of the vector and passing those to the ColumnChunkStats just once (I also inlined the single-input update to remove the unnecessary optionals).

~~I'm still a little concerned by how much time is spent updating statistics when copying relationship data (even after the optimization, \~86% of the time spent in `ChunkedNodeGroup::append` is spent in `ColumnChunkData::updateStats` (and `ChunkedNodeGroup::append` itself is 76% of the runtime of the copies). I'll try and look further into that to see if it's actually reasonable, but this is a significant improvement by itself.~~ *Update: Figured this out: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4980#issuecomment-2694911770. Due to the partitioner selecting just one value from a vector at a time, and that the SelVector passed in is not the same as the one on the vector (which I think usually has the full vector selected), we end up doing vastly more work than necessary. Of course, optimising the update still will help.*

Copying the first 10000000 edges from the datagen-9.0-fb dataset:

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Edges from CSV | 13s | 2.3s |
| Edges from Parquet | 70s | 1.8s |
| Edges from Pandas Dataframe (created from parquet in python) | 70s | 1.8s |

title: Support lambdas on lists with size > DEFAULT_VECTOR_CAPACITY
body:
# Description

Fixes https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4811

Pass slices of the list data vector to the evaluator to ensure that each slice size doesn't exceed `DEFAULT_VECTOR_CAPACITY`.

Introduces the class `ListSliceInfo` to facilitate this, see the comment in `list_slice_info.h` for how to use this. The summary is that the `ListSliceInfo` instance will contain two sel vectors, one that contains the data offsets in the current slice and another that points to the list entries corresponding to each data offset.

I also needed to rework how each lambda's `execFunc` works to get this working (the main challenge was getting list reduce to work since data for a single list could be broken up into multiple slices). Now the way each `execFunc` works is:
- Loop through each data offset in the slice:
  - Get the list entry for the current data offset
  - Do some processing on the data at the offset
  - Update the list entry if needed

title: Reuse scan state for multiple table scans
body:
# Description

This should be able to fix #4943.

This optimization greatly reduces the overheads of scan state allocation when scanning of multi-labelled rel tables. A simple case is referred here (https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4943). Now the queries can run with ~**24MB** bm, which were previously reported to OOM with **12.8GB** bm.

The idea is to decouple table specific info from the scan state by introducing a new interface `setToTable`, which needs to be called before `initScanState` and actual reads.
To make the PR minimal, a new constructor of `TableScanState` is introduced to keep previous ones as they were, so they can be refactored in following PRs.
