title: Only merge distinct aggregate hash tables into the global queues when full
body:
Instead of whenever their parent hash table is full. This improves performance when the distinct hash tables fill up significantly more quickly than their parents.

| Query | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.RegionID, COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID) AS u ORDER BY u DESC LIMIT 10;` | 2.5s | 2.2s |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.RegionID, SUM(h.AdvEngineID), COUNT(*) AS c, AVG(h.ResolutionWidth), COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID) ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10;` | 2.7s | 2.3s |

In more extreme cases the difference would probably be larger.

title: Feature: Add utility `transform` function for `RECURSIVE_REL` (named paths; recursive patterns)

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

We get `RECURSIVE_REL`, when dealing with recursive queries or named paths, like `p` or `e`:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[e*]->(u2:User) RETURN p, e;
```
and its output is quite verbose:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User) RETURN p;
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ p                                                                                                                                                                                        │
│ RECURSIVE_REL                                                                                                                                                                            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name: Noura, age: 25}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Follow... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Foll... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:1, since: 2020}->(0:2)]}                 │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: User, name: Adam, age: 30},{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40}], _RELS: [(0:0)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:0, since: 2020}->(0:1)]}               │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name: Noura, age: 25}], _RELS: [(0:1)-{_LABEL: Fol... │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: User, name: Karissa, age: 40},{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50}], _RELS: [(0:1)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:2, since: 2021}->(0:2)]}              │
│ {_NODES: [{_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: User, name: Zhang, age: 50},{_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: User, name: Noura, age: 25}], _RELS: [(0:2)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:3, since: 2022}->(0:3)]}                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
There might be need for a custom and/or more concise output format like
```
[Karissa-:Follows->Zhang]
```
instead of 
```
[(0:1)-{_LABEL: Follows, _ID: 2:2, since: 2021}->(0:2)]
```
With current functions, custom `RECURSIVE_REL` is hard to implement (can it?), as nodes / `_NODES` and relations / `_RELS` are separated in `STRUCT`, `REL` instances only contain internal id of node and one might be interested in domain ID or other node descriptor like `name`.

Here is a pseudo-code implementation using fictive `list_find(["a","b","c"], "b")` function using predicates dealing with internal node ids of `_src` and `_dest` of rel. Desired rel record output here would be `SRC_NAME-:REL_LABEL->DST_NAME`, e.g. `Karissa-:Follows->Zhang`:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User) 
RETURN list_transform(
  rels(p), 
  r -> list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._src).name +
  "-:" + label(r) + "->" + 
  list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._dst).name);
```


### Suggestion 
Provide `rel_transform`/`rel_map` utility function to create a custom output for `RECURSIVE_REL`.
This function receives `p` (`RECURSIVE_REL`) and a mapper lambda with parameters `src_node`, `dst_node`, `rel`.

Example 1: Format `RECURSIVE_REL` as string:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> src_node.name + "-:" + label(rel) + "->" + dst_node.name)
```

Example 2: Output `RECURSIVE_REL` as mapped tuple:
```cypher
MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> [src_node.name, label(rel), dst_node.name]
```

In summary, this function can provide custom processing of `RECURSIVE_REL` data type directly within Kuzu. Currently a post-processing step is needed via client API/programming language.

### Alternative
Provide `LIST` and `ARRAY` `reduce` function in combination with `STRUCT`enhancement functions like `keys()`, `values()`, `add()`/`append()` to process `RECURSIVE_REL` (similar to Python `functools.reduce`). As described, this also would need some kind of `list_find` to map between  `_RELS` and `_NODES`.

[Karissa-:Follows->Zhang]

MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User) 
RETURN list_transform(
  rels(p), 
  r -> list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._src).name +
  "-:" + label(r) + "->" + 
  list_find(nodes(p),n -> id(n) = r._dst).name);

MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> src_node.name + "-:" + label(rel) + "->" + dst_node.name)

MATCH p = (u:User)-[*]->(u2:User)
RETURN rel_transform(
  p, 
  (src_node, dst_node, rel) -> [src_node.name, label(rel), dst_node.name]

title: Feature: Possibility to use JOIN with LOAD FROM when importing data from a SQL database

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Hi everyone,

As previously discussed here: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/discussions/4944, it would be very useful to have the capability to LOAD FROM a SQL database using JOIN operations.

My usecase is the following:

I have a complex Postgres database with a lot of tables. A part of the database corresponds to "cities" with objects "stations" connected to other stations via the object called "railroad". 

I want to leverage the power of kuzu to find paths and do analytics in this graph of cities subpart of the global database.

I would like to copy cities and the railroad connections between from my Postgres DB into kuzu using the `COPY FROM` feature.

The connections between cities can only be retrieved with JOIN operations. And in addition, some attributes of the cities are foreign keys to an attribute table.

Here is an example : 

**city table**
| id | city       | country_id |
| -- | --------- | ------- |
| 1   | Berlin  |  1   |
| 2   | Paris |  2   |
| 3   | Munich  |  1  |
| 4   | Rome  |  3  |

**country table**
| id | name       |
| -- | --------- | 
| 1   | Germany  |
| 2   | France | 
| 3   | Italy | 

**station table**
| id | name   | city_id |
| -- | ------ | ------- |
| 1   |  Gare Austerlitz  |  2  | 
| 2   |  Gare Montparnasse  |  2  | 
| 3   | Berlin Hauptbahnhof |   1  | 
| 4   | München Hauptbahnhof  |  3  | 
| 5   | Rome Termini     |  4   | 

**railroad table**
| id | name       | station_start_id | station_dest_id | travel_duration_h |
| -- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- | ------- |
| 1   |  Paris-Berlin-1  |  1  |  3  | 10  |
| 2   | Paris-Munich-SNCF  |  2  |  4  |  9  |

What I am to get into Kuzu is the following:
* Nodes of type `City` with the following attributes: `id`, `name` and `country` (field `name` from the table `country`)
* Relations of type `ConnectedTo` with the following attribute `travel_duration_h`

The connections are then:
1. `Paris - [Paris-Berlin-1 (10)] -> Berlin`
2. `Paris - [Paris-Munich-SNCF (9)] -> Munich`

It would be awesome to be able to do something like:
```
COPY City FROM pg.city
JOIN pg.country ON pg.country.id = pg.city.country_id
WHERE pg.country.name in ('Germany', 'France')
RETURN pg.city.name, pg.country.name
```

```
COPY ConnectedTo FROM pg.railroad
JOIN pg.station AS station_start ON station_start.id = pg.railroad.station_start_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_start ON city_start.id = station_start.city_id
JOIN pg.station AS station_dest ON station_dest.id = pg.railroad.station_dest_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_dest ON city_dest.id = station_dest.city_id
RETURN city_start.name, city_dest.name, pg.railroad.travel_duration_h
```

code_snippets.code:
COPY City FROM pg.city
JOIN pg.country ON pg.country.id = pg.city.country_id
WHERE pg.country.name in ('Germany', 'France')
RETURN pg.city.name, pg.country.name

COPY ConnectedTo FROM pg.railroad
JOIN pg.station AS station_start ON station_start.id = pg.railroad.station_start_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_start ON city_start.id = station_start.city_id
JOIN pg.station AS station_dest ON station_dest.id = pg.railroad.station_dest_id
JOIN pg.city AS city_dest ON city_dest.id = station_dest.city_id
RETURN city_start.name, city_dest.name, pg.railroad.travel_duration_h

title: Fix label predicate in recursive pattern
body:
# Description

If a node is single labeled, we rewrite its label function as string literal. This however, should be applied to recursive pattern predicate because if path is of length <= 1, there is no intermediate node and thus the predicate should be a noop. If we try to evaluate, it may lead to empty result. e.g.
```
 [* (r, n | WHERE label(n)='dummy') ]
```

Fixes #4918

macOS Sequoia 15.3.1

### What happened?

I have an application where adding edges to the database will randomly cause kuzu to crash and the edge table needs to be deleted. The failure happens sporadically because the program will crash at different times throughout my data ingestion process and I will rerun the step where it failed and then the data ingestion process will work for that step only to fail at a later step or at a step that worked before. I have ruled out this being do to size or data types used because I have randomly generated nodes and edges of the same size and the database creation process has worked fine. I also ruled out this being due to parallelization. I added steps to reproduce below and if there is an error on schema definition or something like that, I think one improvement would be failing more gracefully than the current process which simply fails and seems to corrupt the database until the "ComponentOf" table is deleted.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

I was not able to upload the parquet files that lead to this issue (probably because they are large) but am happy to provide them. They are quite large; about 340M records in total:


title: Temporarily disable daily build until 0.8.2 release
Skip inserting null keys into distinct hash tables
body:
We always skip them when updating the aggregate state, so there's no point including them in the table at all.

There was a small regression introduced in #4881, which led to null values being included in the distinct output.

title: Refactor scalar_func_exec_t to take in separate selection vectors
body:
# Description

Introduce the struct `SelectedVector` which contains pointers/references to a vector and a selection vector. This struct is now passed to instances of `scalar_func_exec_t`, allowing us to pass a selection vector that is separate from the selection vector that is in a vector's state.

This brings us closer to decoupling `ValueVectors` from their states, and also gives us the flexibility to do things such as using the separate selection vectors to allow us to slice resized list data vectors (which is needed to support list lambdas on lists larger than vector size)

# Contributor agreement

According to the neo4j grammar: https://neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/5/functions/predicate/#functions-all
A where clause must be provided in the where predicate function. This PR throws an exception instead of seg fault in such case.

Implement `select` function for list_predicate functions

This PR bundles the `httpfs`, `delta` extensions in duckdb library. So we don't have to call  `install` and `load` on `httpfs` and `delta` extensions in our extensions. This should significantly improves the loading time of our extensions.

@mewim Can you rebuild duckdb on our CI?  We have to add these two lines to `extension_config.cmake` @line 12:

```
duckdb_extension_load(delta)
duckdb_extension_load(httpfs)
```

title: Parallel Distinct SimpleAggregate
body:
Extends the same method used to parallelize the hash aggregate and distinct hash aggregate to the simple, non-grouped aggregates.

~~There is still a reasonable amount of work being done single-threaded since after doing the parallel build + finalize of the distinct hash table we have to then scan it to actually compute the function result and that's currently being done in the single-threaded finalize since it can't be started until the parallel finalization is complete.
It would be possible to add another operator which does that in parallel, which I think could yield up to another 2x improvement to the runtime (skipping this step dropped both of the below benchmarks to \~0.9s, so this single-threaded part is clearly a significant part of the total runtime). But I think that's best left for a different PR.~~
 (*Edit: this can actually be done in the current operator fairly easily, we just need to store a state for each partition and combine them in finalize instead*).

| Query | master | 1 thread | 128 threads |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID);` | 20.5s | 18.6s | 0.77s |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN COUNT(DISTINCT h.SearchPhrase);` | 16.6s | 15.9s | 0.85s |

~Probably needs a bit more cleanup so I'm opening as a draft for now.~ (Should be good now; I updated the benchmarks twice between what was mentioned above as well as a small optimization to make it use fixed-sized hash tables prior to partitioning like in the hash aggregate).

title: Add tests with different node group sizes + fix bugs
body:
# Description

The smallest node group size test I added to CI was 16 since testing with node group size 2 causes the tests to run too slow (since we write metadata for each node group). For the test failures I caught when running with node group size 2 I added separate tests to check for regression.

Bug Fixes:
- Reset `nextCachedRowToScan` when initializing CSR node group scan state (I think this was only an issue if node group size was less than the number of adjacent nodes for a single bound node)
- Reserve rel offsets all at once in `RelTable::updateRelOffsets()` instead of separately per chunked group (If the local table is larger than the chunked group size this avoids adding extra offsets to the local offset)
- Use correct node offset for committing local table delete in `NodeTable::commit()`
- Fix startNodeOffset passed to semi mask when scanning for rollback hash index insert (if a COPY was interrupted you might have empty node groups and previous we added up the number of rows in the previous node groups).
- Correctly account for a node group potentially being deleted earlier when rolling back a node table insert

Other Changes:
- Update testing framework so that `BUFFER_POOL_SIZE` environment variable is respected

title: Enable spilling during finalization of CreateHNSWIndex
body:
# Description

Adding spilling support during CreateHNSWIndex finalization, which utilizes the same mechanism as `Partitioner` in COPY REL pipeline.

Also release embedding caching earlier to reduce peak memory usage.

With spilling, deep-1M can be indexed with 6 threads given 2GB bm size, compared to ~4GB without spilling.

title: Optimize embedding caching in vector index construction
body:
# Description

Pre-resize data chunk for the cached embeddings. Also parallel the scan of embedding column.
This can greatly reduce cache initialization time.

On a dataset of 1M vectors with 96 dimension extracted from Yandex DEEP (https://big-ann-benchmarks.com/neurips21.html), the index building time can be reduced from 95.7s to 80.9s on a Mac Studio (M1 Max chip, 64GB RAM).

Note that this PR introduces a framework for transaction local object caching.
`CREATE_HNSW_INDEX` makes use of this mechanism to fetch cached column populated with `_TRANSACTION_LOCAL_CACHE_COLUMN()`.

title: Bug: Clarify `r, n` in recursive relation filter `(r,n | WHERE ...)`
body:
### Kùzu version

nightly

### What operating system are you using?

_No response_

### What happened?

Consider following graph:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE V (id int PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE REL TABLE E (FROM V TO V, val STRING);
CREATE (:V {id: 1})-[:E {val: "foo"}]->(:V {id: 2});
```
and a recursive query with predicate:
```cypher
MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE n.id = 1)]->(b) RETURN *;
```
I'd assume `r` is set to `:E` relation above, and `n` is NOOP/unset variable, as there is just 1 intermediate hop. Endpoint nodes are covered by `a` and `b` variables and no `n` node in-between exists with current data.

At least below queries reflect this assumption (it doesn't matter what value `x` is typed for `WHERE n.id = x`):
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE n.id = 1)]->(b) RETURN *;
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ a                            │ b                            │
│ NODE                         │ NODE                         │
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │                                                                                                                                
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                               
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE n.id = 100000)]->(b) RETURN *;                                                                                                                              
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐                                                                                                                                
│ a                            │ b                            │                                                                                                                                
│ NODE                         │ NODE                         │                                                                                                                                
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤                                                                                                                                
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │                                                                                                                                
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘                                                                                                                                
```                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                               
On the other side, `label(n)` is evaluated (to false in last case) and not ignored:                                                                                                            
```cypher                                                                                                                                                                                      
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE label(n) = "V")]->(b) RETURN *;                                                                                                                             
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐                                                                                                                                
│ a                            │ b                            │                                                                                                                                
│ NODE                         │ NODE                         │                                                                                                                                
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤                                                                                                                                
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │                                                                                                                                
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                               
kuzu> MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE label(n) = "Foo")]->(b) RETURN *;                                                                                                                           
┌──────┬──────┐                                                                                                                                                                                
│ a    │ b    │                                                                                                                                                                                
│ NODE │ NODE │                                                                                                                                                                                
├──────┼──────┤                                                                                                                                                                                
└──────┴──────┘                                                                                                                                                                                
```                                                                                                                                                                                            
Hence I am not sure about current behavior of `r` and `n`: Shouldn't Kuzu raise an error, if `n` in a recursive filter predicate is used, given there are not intermediate nodes and this variable cannot be set to any node? Alternatively every expression involving `n` might be made NOOP.                           

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

code_snippets.code: MATCH (a)-[:E * (r,n | WHERE n.id = 1)]->(b) RETURN *;

title: Bug: [Filter recursive relationships] Error: Binder exception: Cannot evaluate OR/CASE (...)  in recursive pattern .
body:
### Kùzu version

nightly

### What operating system are you using?

Debian 12

### What happened?

I'd like to use `OR` operator within a recursive relationship filter predicate. 
https://docs.kuzudb.com/cypher/query-clauses/match/#filter-recursive-relationships shows an example with `AND`. But if replacing it by `OR`, I get following error:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH p = (a:User)-[:Follows*1..2 (r, n | WHERE r.since < 2022 OR n.age > 45) ]->(b:User)
      WHERE a.name = 'Adam'
      RETURN b.name, COUNT(*);
Error: Binder exception: Cannot evaluate OR(LESS_THAN(r.since,2022),GREATER_THAN(n.age,45)) in recursive pattern .
```

Here is another one with `CASE`:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH p = (a:User)-[:Follows*1..2 (r, n | WHERE CASE WHEN r.since < 2022 THEN true ELSE n.age > 45 END) ]->(b:User)
      WHERE a.name = 'Adam'
      RETURN b.name, COUNT(*);
Error: Binder exception: Cannot evaluate CASE WHEN LESS_THAN(r.since,2022) THEN True ELSE GREATER_THAN(n.age,45) in recursive pattern .
```

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Setup Kuzu demo database and use above query.

code_snippets.code:
kuzu> MATCH p = (a:User)-[:Follows*1..2 (r, n | WHERE r.since < 2022 OR n.age > 45) ]->(b:User)
      WHERE a.name = 'Adam'
      RETURN b.name, COUNT(*);
Error: Binder exception: Cannot evaluate OR(LESS_THAN(r.since,2022),GREATER_THAN(n.age,45)) in recursive pattern .

kuzu> MATCH p = (a:User)-[:Follows*1..2 (r, n | WHERE CASE WHEN r.since < 2022 THEN true ELSE n.age > 45 END) ]->(b:User)
      WHERE a.name = 'Adam'
      RETURN b.name, COUNT(*);
Error: Binder exception: Cannot evaluate CASE WHEN LESS_THAN(r.since,2022) THEN True ELSE GREATER_THAN(n.age,45) in recursive pattern .

title: Fix timing in the final QueryResult for create fts/hnsw index
body:
# Description

Create fts/hnsw index invokes the rewrite mechanism, thus a single query expands into multiple statements, but only the last statement's execution result is visible to users (others are internal and their execution results are indivisible to users unless there are errors encountered). This causes a gap between the execution/compiling time of the last statement and the actual one for the whole query.
To fix the gap, this PR collects compiling/execution time for all internal statements and aggregate them into the final query result, which is visible to users.

title: Break when error in the middle of multi statements
body:
# Description

This fixes the behaviour for execution of multiple statements in a single query. When there is an error with a statement in the middle of the query, we should error and break the execution.

Also changed how shell collects query results. Previously shell manually splits a query by ";" into multiple statements, however, I don't think this is safe in the first place, it also is not consistent with the behaviour of executing a single query with multiple statements through API.

title: Separate hash aggregate finalization into its own operator
body:
This fixes the data race I mentioned in #4906. It's a little difficult to rigorously test since I was having a hard time reproducing it, but moving the finalization into a separate operator should guarantee that all threads running HashAggregate operator tasks finish before finalization starts.

I think this may fix the issue in #4903, but I'm not positive that it's the same issue.

body:
There was also a bug where a few bytes at the end of the list (just for factorized table to factorized table comparisons) wouldn't be checked since we were omitting to take into account the null mask at the beginning.

E.g. https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/actions/runs/13324561162/job/37215093604?pr=4908. Lists containing null entries sometimes compare as non-equal when they should be equal, presumably since we don't guarantee that the data part of the entry is a consistent value if the entry is null.

title: Try to mitigate data race in the HashAggregate
body:
There's a test that has occasionally been failing in CI (e.g. https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/commit/afd089b62b2d02d919a8e0b56990bed8e71af3ec), it's happening very infrequently and I've narrowed down the issue to a data race in the HashAggregate operator.

We're tracking the number of threads running the hash aggregate so that we can wait to do the parallel finalization until all threads have finished However it's possible for threads to finish before other threads have started, leading the remaining threads to start finalization early. This tries to mitigate that by registering the thread as soon as possible (not that it's skipping a lot of work, but this might improve things slightly), however to truly fix it the finalization should be moved into a separate operator so we can guarantee that all data is partitioned before starting the parallel finalization.

There's probably a similar issue in the IndexBuilder, it's just that the IndexBuilder doesn't have a multithreaded finalization stage, and the thread tracking is just to determine if a thread should continue working on the global queues after its finished processing its local data.

title: Feature: Support querying on Internal ID

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Java

### Description

Arthur from gdotv is looking to be able to query by a node's internal Id

Currently on the Java API, we can't use parameters that reference an internal ID, e.g.:
```cypher
MATCH (s)
WHERE ID(s) = $id
RETURN s
```
The above query doesn't work.

Currently this is the workaround. There seem to be other cases to gdotv's use case where allowing the user to query on a node's internal ID passed as a parameter is useful.

```cypher
MATCH (p)
WHERE OFFSET(ID(p)) = x AND label(p) = 'y'
RETURN *
```

code_snippets.code:
MATCH (s)
WHERE ID(s) = $id
RETURN s

MATCH (p)
WHERE OFFSET(ID(p)) = x AND label(p) = 'y'
RETURN *

title: Fixes the `alias` issue of `struct_pack` function
body:
We used to set the `alias` of `struct-pack` function parameters as their field names.
E.g. `{'x': y}` => We set the alias of `y` as x
This causes a bug in nested aggregation:
```
with count(5) as x return count({y: x});
```

This PR fixes it by introducing the optionalParams field in the functionExpression

title: Add GCS support
body:
# Description

GCS's interoperability mode supports [using S3-style requests](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/aws-simple-migration), so we reuse the S3 filesystem while making a few changes to support scans (COPY/LOAD FROM, attach read-only DB) with GCS. In this case, we create a new S3 filesystem instance for communicating with GCS, with some different init-time configurations to signal that it's communicating with GCS. 

Any URLs with prefixes `gs://` or `gcs://` will have their requests directed to GCS. The path formats will be the same as S3: `${PREFIX}/${BUCKET_NAME}/${PATH_TO_FILE_IN_BUCKET}`.

Additionally, I added separate settings for configuring authentication parameters for GCS (they refer to the same parameters as S3):

```
call gcs_access_key_id=...
call gcs_secret_access_key=...
```

# Contributor agreement

- [ ] I have read and agree to the [Contributor Agreement](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/master/CLA.md).

title: Avoid recording confidential information in shell history
body:
We currently cache all executed commands in shell history.

However, there are some commands (such as when setting API secrets `call s3_secret_access_key=...`) that contain confidential information that we should not cache in shell history for security reasons.

title: Implement unity catalog extension
body:
This PR allows kuzu to scan from unity catalog.
To scan from unity catalog, users have to attach to the unity catalog first:
```
attach "catalog_name" as alias (dbtype uc_catalog)
```
Then users can query unity catalog tables as other relational tables.
```
LOAD FROM unity.person RETURN *;
```

The duckdb's implementation of unity catalog is buggy right now, so our unity-catalog extension is also an experimental feature.

title: Optimization: Hardcoded regular expressions are being compiled many times
body:
### Description

This query from ClickBench is heavily bottlenecked by our regex performance: `MATCH (h:hits) WHERE h.Title =~ '.*Google.*' AND NOT h.URL =~ '.*\\.google\\..*' AND h.SearchPhrase <> '' RETURN h.SearchPhrase, MIN(h.URL), MIN(h.Title), COUNT(*) AS c, COUNT(DISTINCT h.UserID) ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10;` (not that the original query uses a regex match, but we don't have a `LIKE` operator [original sql query for reference](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/blob/3255f83b92b9d1ae3cb56e1166c06026dcadb246/clickhouse/queries.sql#L23)).

See https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4881#issuecomment-2651119621: it takes 17s with the regex match compared to ~2.5s using `contains` instead.

Performance profiling shows that about 67% of the runtime is spent repeatedly compiling the regex (and a further 4% destroying the regex afterwards), despite it being the same each time.
Being able to compile the regex once and re-use it would speed things up significantly.
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a343c7e5-7a14-4e2f-929e-201a29a1c84d)

title: Add empty columns to chunked node group if needed during COPY
body:
# Description

Follow-up to https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4786

After dropping a column (and before checkpointing), if we are directly appending newly-flushed chunked groups to a node group (during copy) the newly inserted node group may not have as many columns as the parent node group, which would cause the next checkpoint to fail. 

This PR adds empty columns to the newly inserted node group so that its number of columns is as expected

Also fixes another bug where warning data was being flushed to disk for rel batch insert.

# Contributor agreement

- [ ] I have read and agree to the [Contributor Agreement](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/master/CLA.md).

title: Parallel distinct hash aggregate
body:
Extends the partitioning done in the hash aggregate operator to apply to distinct hash tables as well as the main hash table. The aggregation is then disabled in the thread-local hash tables for distinct keys, and computed from scratch when combining the data into the global tables.

This still doesn't parallelize the simple distinct aggregate, which I'll do in a later PR.

This also fixes support for nested types in the hash aggregate generally (I realised that I had missed implementing the row data versions of the comparison functions for structs and lists).

# Description

title: Rework rewriteFunc of table functions
body:
# Description

Table functions that create/drop FTS and HNSW indexes make use of `rewriteFunc` to prepare tables and macros, etc.
Current implementation of `rewriteFunc` is convoluted that it pre-appends rewritten query to be executed first before the table function itself (e..g, CREATE_FTS_INDEX), instead of generating a rewritten query and directs the execution to the rewritten one.

This PR reworks Create/Drop FTS/HNSW Index functions in that:
1. `CreateFTSIndex`, `DropFTSIndex`, `CreateHNSWIndex`, `DropHNSWIndex` will only be responsible for generating rewritten query.
2. Internal functions `_CreateFTSIndex`, `_DropFTSIndex`, `_CreateHNSWIndex`, `_DropHNSWIndex` are responsible for the actual create/drop logic.

title: Support customization of stopwords in full text search
body:
We are going to extend our `CREATE_FTS_INDEX` function with an additional parameter:
```
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX(TABLE_NAME, INDEX_NAME, PROPERTY_LIST, STOP_WORDS := STOP_WORD)
```
The `STOP_WORD` is an optional parameter and it can be:
1. A file path: contains a single column of stopwords.  (The path can be a S3/local/http path path)
2. A table name in kuzu: contains a single string column of stopwords.

For example:
```
# Create a full text search index and uses the stopwords list which stores at s3.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 's3://kuzu-stopwords/english.txt')

# Create a full text search index and uses a kuzu table which stores all stopwords.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 'doc_stopwords')
```

Rules:
1. Customized stopwords must be provided at the time when the full text search index is created. If not provided, the default english stopwords will be used.
2. Once the fts index is created, users are not allowed to modify the stopwords list of the index and the same stopwords list will be used when querying the fts index.
3.  Each full text search index can use its own stopwords list, meaning that different full text search indexes can have different sets of stopwords.


Closes #4854

title: Optimize recompile times
body:
# Description

Follow up to https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4850

Reorganize includes, move stuff from header to cpp files, add forward declares to optimize recompile when system config changes. 

The main changes are:
- Remove the need to include `system_config.h` from headers, especially ones that are included everywhere such as `value_vector.h`, `sel_vector.h`, and `data_chunk_state.h`
- If the need for the constants in the headers are less simple to remove (e.g. needing a system config constant to define an member array size), try to forward-declare those classes so that the headers don't need to be included

This reduces the number of recompile steps to about 220 from 570:

title: Feature: Support customized stopword list in full text search

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

# Motivation
Kùzu currently uses a predefined english stopwords when building a full text search index. However, it is common for users to define their own list of stopwords in a practical use case.

For example:
The predefined english stopwords covers all english numbers: `six`, `five` ....
Users may not want to skip those keywords in their use case.

# Proposal
We are going to extend our `CREATE_FTS_INDEX` function with an additional parameter:
```
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX(TABLE_NAME, INDEX_NAME, PROPERTY_LIST, STOP_WORDS := STOP_WORD)
```
The `STOP_WORD` is an optional parameter and it can be:
1. A file path: contains a single column of stopwords.  (The path can be a S3/local/http path path)
2. A table name in kuzu: contains a single string column of stopwords.

For example:
```
# Create a full text search index and uses the stopwords list which stores at s3.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 's3://kuzu-stopwords/english.txt')

# Create a full text search index and uses a kuzu table which stores all stopwords.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 'doc_stopwords')
```

Rules:
1. Customized stopwords must be provided at the time when the full text search index is created. If not provided, the default english stopwords will be used.
2. Once the fts index is created, users are not allowed to modify the stopwords list of the index and the same stopwords list will be used when querying the fts index.
3.  Each full text search index can use its own stopwords list, meaning that different full text search indexes can have different sets of stopwords.

# Implementation:
When the user creates a fts index with:
1. Customized stopwords list: an internal table named `[table_id]_[index_name]_stopwords`, which stores the user given stopwords list, will be created and used for tokenizing words.
2. Default stopwords list: we will reuse the internal default englsish stopwords table for tokenizing words.
 
# Testing:
1. Test invalid s3 url stopwords.
2. Test s3 url stopwords without auth.
3. Test given stopwords path is a directory.
4. Test stopwords file with wrong format (e.g. more than one column)
5. Test given stopwords list is empty. (meaning no stopwords)
6. Test UTF8 stopwords list
7. Test INVALID-UTF8 stopwords list (we should error). 
8. Test stopwords list containing special characters (e.g. `\`, `/`)
9. Test the given stopwords file is deleted after the index is created.
10. Test the given stopwords table is dropped/altered after the index is created.

code_snippets.code: CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX(TABLE_NAME, INDEX_NAME, PROPERTY_LIST, STOP_WORDS := STOP_WORD)

# Create a full text search index and uses the stopwords list which stores at s3.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 's3://kuzu-stopwords/english.txt')

# Create a full text search index and uses a kuzu table which stores all stopwords.
CALL CREATE_FTS_INDEX('doc', 'doc_idx', ['author', 'title'], STOP_WORDS := 'doc_stopwords')

# Description

### Description

The lock is introduced in https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4827 to address race conditions, however, it creates bottleneck in the pipeline.

This requires rework of the interface and implementation of `ScalarFunction` and `ExpressionEvaluator`.

body:
### Example
`user.csv`
```
id,name
```


`likes.csv`
```
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,055f6041-8bab-4ce6-a201-b85dab43442a
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,8082bb02-7c30-4a06-8600-885df4fc0eab
```

```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE User (id UUID PRIMARY KEY, name STRING);
CREATE NODE TABLE Post (id UUID PRIMARY KEY, content STRING);
CREATE REL TABLE GROUP likes(FROM User TO User, FROM User TO Post);

COPY User FROM "user.csv" (header=true);
COPY Post FROM "post.csv" (header=true);

COPY likes FROM "likes.csv";
// Error: Binder exception: Cannot copy into likes table with type REL_GROUP.
```

### Question

Is there a solution planned to allow REL GROUP (or more in general rel unions, as REL GROUP is deprecated) + COPY FROM imports?

### Proposal

Two ideas:
- The actual rel union type can be derived by following FROM/TO id constituents, assuming node IDs are unambiguous amongst rel unions (e.g. with `UUID`).
- Allow a discriminator column for rel unions. `likes.csv` example, with discriminators for FROM/TO appended:
```
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,055f6041-8bab-4ce6-a201-b85dab43442a,User,Post
ef2b4363-66ab-4a2f-af59-f7f6cd80f250,8082bb02-7c30-4a06-8600-885df4fc0eab,User,User
```

Related: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/3627

title: Update API docs: QueryResult getNext() reuses the same underlying flat tuple
body:
# Description

In the C, C++, and Java APIs, `QueryResult::getNext()` returns references to the output flat tuple. Additionally, the same flat tuple object is reused for each call to `getNext()` meaning that each call to `getNext()` will overwrite the return result of the previous call to `getNext()`. This PR updates the API docs to document this behaviour.

Fixes https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4814

title: Use the most significant bits for partitioning in the HashAggregate
body:
Instead of the least significant

A small but fairly important thing I missed in #4655; I ran a few quick benchmarks and it gave a speedup of up to 20% (128 thread 2x EPYC 7551)

Using the least significant bits meant that only a fraction of the slots in a given partition would match the hashes. Because we're using linear probing the performance wasn't previously too terrible as the hash table would still get filled, however it would have been increasing the average number of probes needed when inserting or looking up values in the table.

| Query | master | new |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MATCH (h:hits) WHERE h.SearchPhrase <> '' RETURN h.SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) AS c ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10;` | 0.89s | 0.84s |
| `MATCH (h:hits) WHERE h.SearchPhrase <> '' RETURN h.SearchEngineID, h.SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) AS c ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10;` | 0.5s | 0.45s |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.UserID, COUNT(*) ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 10;` | 0.93s | 0.73s |
| `MATCH (h:hits) RETURN h.UserID, h.SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 10;` | 1.17s | 0.98s |

### Kùzu version

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS & Windows

### What happened?

The Java API appears to be returning duplicated records for every query being ran.
For instance, `MATCH (s:Comment) RETURN s LIMIT 50` will return the same comment node 50 times. Each time a new query is run, that behaviour persists but with a different node.
The `FlatTuples` extracted from the `QueryResult` all point to the exact same node when using the `hasNext()`/`getNext()` pattern, so it looks like either `getNext()` is not moving the cursor on the query result or the query result itself contains duplicated information.
Variations of queries with `DISTINCT` lead to the same result, but `COUNT` queries accurately return node counts.

This can be reproduced on the Java API using the LDBC test sample from Kuzu Explorer. To reproduce this, you need to create a Database instance in the Java API pointing to a dataset, then run one of the queries suggested above. This appears to happen consistently for all datasets.

title: Bug: List lambda functions don't work if lists are longer than vector size
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22

### What happened?

In `ListLambdaEvaluator`, the result vector is stored as value vector of the list's data type (instead of as the list type itself). If `evaluate()` is called on the lambda evaluator with an input vector larger than the value vector capacity, we will get an assertion error due to attempting to write a larger vector than will fit in the result vector. 

This bug can be reproduced with the following python script (the last line/query triggers the assertion failure):
```py
import kuzu
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
    db = kuzu.Database(temp_dir)
    conn = kuzu.Connection(db)
    conn.execute("create node table tab(id int64, vals int64[], primary key (id))")
    conn.execute("create (:tab {id: 0, vals: list_creation()})")
    # for some reason using the below query only generates a list of size 2, not sure if this is also a bug
    # conn.execute(
    #     "unwind range(1, 5000) as i match (t:tab) set t.vals = list_append(t.vals, i)"
    # )
    for i in range(5000):
        conn.execute(f"match (t:tab) set t.vals = list_append(t.vals, {i})")
    print(
        conn.execute(
            "match (t:tab) return list_transform(t.vals, x -> x + 2)"
        ).get_as_df()
    )
```

A proposed solution would be the store the result vector in `ListLambdaEvaluator` as a vector of lists (which can then be resized as needed).

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Bug: Default values when adding new columns doesn't work if casting of a literal is required
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22

### What happened?

Idea is similar to https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/4389. Consider the queries:
```
create node table Person(id INT64, PRIMARY KEY (id))
create rel table likes (from person to person);
alter table likes add years int32 default 0
```

The query `alter table likes add years int32 default 0` will fail with the message 
```
Runtime exception: Cannot set a non-constant default value when adding columns on REL tables.
```
This is because the literal `0` needs to be casted from int64 to int32, and we don't consider the casted value a constant.

Similarly, the statement `alter table likes add years float default 5.4` will also fail.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Feature: Better error messages when forgetting to load extension

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Currently, the error message displayed when I try to query the FTS index (which requires me to first load the FTS extension) isn't very informative when I actually forget to load the extension beforehand.

Here is the sequence of steps:

- I create the FTS index using a Python script
- The script runs, index finishes building, and the script exits
- I open a CLI window
- But I very commonly forget to run INSTALL FTS; LOAD EXTENSION FTS;  in the beginning to load the FTS extension
- I try to run the CALL QUERY_FTS_INDEX() command and then I get this error message:

```
Error: Catalog exception: function QUERY_FTS_INDEX does not exist.
```

Can we improve this error message a bit? Ideally, it would inform the user that this function is only accessible once the FTS extension package is loaded. At the very least, it should inform the user about something generic, like "This command requires an extension to be loaded beforehand", so that the user immediately knows what to do next.

#### Motivation for better error messages

Users coming from other systems that have these indexes inbuilt, rather than requiring an extension, may not remember or know that one needs to install and load the extension each time a new CLI or client session to the Kùzu database is opened. Having a more helpful error message that immediately tells the user what's wrong and how they can fix it is beneficial for newcomers to Kùzu, and to make it more usable.

title: Deprecate rel group
body:
# Description

Address issue #3627.

We now support the syntax CREATE REL TABLE (FROM nodeA TO nodeB, FROM nodeA TO nodeC, ...) and should update the documentation to deprecate the rel group syntax, although we will continue to support it for compatibility reasons.

Internally, we maintain the distinction between RelTable and RelTableGroup. A relationship table defined with a single pair of FROM and TO node labels is categorized as a RelTable, while one defined with multiple pairs is categorized as a RelTableGroup.

Note that the internal rel table can still be referenced by the name along the pattern `groupnane_from_to`. This is needed for now to maintain compatibility for exported database from previous versions. Eventually we should disable these accesses.

Left TODO:
- [ ] Rework export database COPY statements to use the new syntax with FROM and TO options.

title: Implement show-indexes function
body:
This PR implements the `show_indexes` call function.
Usage:
```
CALL SHOW_INDEXES() RETURN *
```
This function returns all indexes currently available in the system, including those fields:
| **Field Name**        | **Description**                                                                 |
|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **table name**         | The table name on which the index is built.                                    |
| **index name**         | The name of the index.                                                         |
| **index type**         | The type of the index (e.g., `hnsw`, `fts`).                                   |
| **property names**     | The properties of the table on which the index is built.                       |
| **dependency loaded**  | Indicates whether the depended extension is loaded (`true` or `false`).          |
| **index description**  | The Cypher query used to create the index.                                     |

For indexes which depends on an extension:
1. The extension is loaded:
The `dependency loaded` column will be true, and the index description will also be shown.
2. The extension is unloaded:
The `dependency loaded` column will be false, and the index description is not available.

title: Fix query graph merge
body:
# Description

There is a bug in `QueryGraphCollection::addAndMergeQueryGraphIfConnected`, which doesn't consider the case when the `queryGraphToAdd` connects multiple existing query graphs.

An example query is 
```
MATCH (n0)-[r0]-(n1{k20:true}), (n2)-[r1]-(n3{k20:true}), (n4)<-[r2]-(n5), (n5{k39:false})-[r3]->(n2{k41:false}) WHERE (((r2.id) <> (r3.id)) AND true) RETURN n2.id as a0, r1.id as a1, n3.id as a2;
```
where we have four patterns, `n0-n1, n2-n3, n4<-n5, n5->n2`. When we loop over each pattern and try to merge it, the pattern `n5n2` connects with both `n2n3` and `n4n5`, leading to `n0n1, n5n2n3, n4n5n2`, while the correct merged query graphs are `n0n1, n2n3n4n5`.

Fix #4189.

title: Distinct optimizations
body:
Some of the distinct aggregate queries I've tried have had very poor performance due to them processing a single tuple at a time (which the AggregateHashTable is not really designed for). These two small changes mitigate a significant part of the cost of doing so, without having any adverse effects when processing larger batches of tuples.

- Re-use the temporary ValueVectors in `BaseHashTable::computeAndCombineVecHash`
- Don't copy the entire vector when updating `tmpValueIdxes` in `AggregateHashTable::findHashSlots` (this should be universally better. Even if there is some optimization that can be done by passing a constant to memcpy, any time the loop runs multiple times we'd be better off copying less than the full vector).

title: Refactor on disk graph interface
body:
# Description

This PR contains the following refactor

1. Remove unnecessary tableID in frontier morsel. Given we first pin to a specific table, frontier morsel should contain pure offset.
2. Pass TableCatalogEntry instead of tableID in many interfaces. Practically speaking they don't make a difference, using TableCatalogEntry will let us access catalog for fewer times. And code looks cleaner.
3. Pass edge property name instead of edge property idx. This is to align with vertex scan which takes vertex property names. Also using string based name is easier to interpret for new users.
4. Rename prepareScan to prepareRelScan because we also have a prepareVertexScan.
5. Remove `std::vector<std::pair<common::table_id_t, OnDiskGraphNbrScanState>> scanStates;` because we no longer need to scan multiple rel table in one `scanFwd/scanBwd`. The infrastructure force scan always happens on exactly one rel table. The design can be further simplified but I would do it in a followed up PR.

@benjaminwinger please review for changes 3, 4 & 5

Fixes # (issue)

# Contributor agreement

- [ ] I have read and agree to the [Contributor Agreement](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/master/CLA.md).

title: Optimization: Enable SIP based on cardinality information without a filter
body:
### Description

When we're trying to apply SIP from the build side to the probe side, or from the probe side to the build side, we only choose to apply SIP when there is filter on the build or probe side. This is to avoid worst cases that cardinality estimation can be very wrong. However, this also limits the use of SIP in scenarios where output distinct values is small and serve as "filters": 
1. Num of distinct Dst nodes scanned from the rel table can be small. E.g., `MATCH (a)-[e]->(b) RETURN b.id`. For plan `JOIN(SCAN(b))(Scan(a)Extend(e))`, `Scan(a)Extend(e)` can be selective if `e` contains few distinct `b` nodes as dst.
2. Table function can output few distinct nodes. Vector index search can serve as an example as it usually outputs only top `k` tuples, which is usually much smaller compared to the base node table.  Note that `SIPDirection::FORCE_BUILD_TO_PROBE` is now used in vector index search to force SIP, which should be refactored away along with addressing this issue.

This PR contains a refactor that removes DestinationOutput(Writer) and let SingleShortestPath & AllShortestPath creating their own ones. I'll add more PRs to get rid of this Output & OutputWriter design.

There will be following PRs that supports

title: Hash join flatten fix
body:
# Description

This PR fixes a bug in hash join planning exposed in PR #4625. Below is a description of the bug.

We append flatten to probe side if and only if join key is an internal ID and this ID is guaranteed to be unique on the build side. The check was done based on number of factorization group. This is not true if an aggregation happens, which will always reduce the number of factorization group to 1.

This PR checks by looking at operators along the build side subplan. 

### Testing

The bug cannot be revealed easily on master because we don't reorder multi-part queries. So aggregation does not happen on build side. I have tested by cherry-picking to #4625. 

Fixes # (issue)

title: Feature: Add random sampling function to help users use Kùzu for training GNNs

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Kùzu is mentioned in the following paper about using a graph database as a backend while training GNNs.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.11375

As described in Figure 4 of the paper, one of the key steps during training is to perform random sampling of the returned nodes from a 2-hop query as follows:

```cypher
MATCH (node_0:$NODE_TYPE)
WHERE node_0.id IN $SEED_NODES
OPTIONAL MATCH (node_0)-[rel_1:$REL_TYPE]->(node_1:$NODE_TYPE)-[rel_2:$REL_TYPE]->(node_2:$NODE_TYPE)
WITH node_0, node_1, node_2
ORDER BY rand()
LIMIT $MAX_NEIGHBOURS
RETURN
    node_0.id as src_id,
    node_1.id, node_1.features,
    node_2.id, node_2.features;
```

The `ORDER BY rand()` part is where the random sampling suffers on two counts:
- The randomness isn't truly random, as the `rand()` function doesn't offer a high enough level of randomness for the purposes of training (The author of the paper noted that they had to do some more workarounds to add more randomness)
- The above query is slow, as it's doing top-k (we could do better from a query performance perspective)

## Feature

Per the author's observations, the desired graph database feature would be to provide a function or some high-level utility in Cypher where the random sampling is pushed down to the database layer and isn't done by PyG in-memory. Could we add such a function that allows users to perform random sampling for the purposes of training GNNs using Kùzu?

title: Hash aggregate finalization parallelization
body:
Fixes kuzudb/internal#10 and #4547.

I switched back to having the partitioning hash table use linear probing, insert entries until a fixed capacity, and then empty and flush to the global partitions. The aggregation update code only works on the data within the vectors being inserted and requires that they are all available in the hash table at once, so kicking elements out of the hash table would require some complicated changes. I increased the default size of the hash table significantly to compensate as the performance was poor with hash tables of the default size.

It took a while to hunt down the bug in `BaseAggregateScan::writeAggregateResultToVector`. I've added an extra test to try and get slightly better coverage, but I think we really need some larger tests (the issue was caused by Vector re-use which previously we only would have encountered with results that have greater than `DEFAULT_VECTOR_CAPACITY` values, some of which must be null).

The performance isn't scaling well with the number of partitions at the moment. On workflows which don't need very many threads it's much faster if built with fewer partitions (e.g. on the query in #4547 I found that the total runtime was about 2x faster (3x for just the the HashAggregate code) with 16 partitions on a machine with 12 threads compared to 256 partitions (that query/dataset also seems to just be getting a maximum of ~14 worker threads, presumably due to the way that the input is being divided up). I've reduced the number of partitions to 128 as a compromise given that's the number of threads on our largest testing machine, but will work on improving that next (it should be possible to do the partitioning logically without physically partitioning the data to improve cache locality).

I've increased the default buffer pool size since anything involving aggregation was requiring a bunch of extra memory for constructing the `PartitioningAggregateHashTables`, but that should be able to be reverted with the optimization mentioned above as it would also reduce the minimum memory requirements.

### Performance

On the query from #4547 (msmarco v2.1 1st segment with the query `MATCH (b:doc) WITH tokenize(b.segment) AS tk, OFFSET(ID(b)) AS id UNWIND tk AS t RETURN STEM(t, 'porter'), id, count(*);`.
Run on a 128 thread machine (But see earlier note about not scaling past 14 threads).

- Before: 36GB peak memory usage; runtime 83.5s
- After: 21GB peak memory usage; runtime 63.5s
- Limited to 14 partitions: 24GB peak memory usage; runtime 47.8s 
  (as an example of the performance improvements we might expect to achieve with better cache locality)

Note that memory usage has improved significantly since before the per-thread AggregateHashTables would be filled first, and exist in-memory simultaneously with the final merged global AggregateHashTable. Now the per-thread tables get merged into the global ones in small chunks.

I'd run some benchmarks using queries from [ClickBench](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/) and seen an improvement of about 2-5x (I'll update with more details later).

title: Feature: Extend `LOAD FROM` clause with `TYPE` option

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
### API

C++

### Description

# Motivation:
## Current Implementation:
When kuzu scans from files, file extension is used to sniff the file format. 
For example: `LOAD FROM 'test.csv'`,
Kuzu uses the file extension `.csv` to infer the file type of `test` is in `CSV` format.

## Issue caused:
1. CSV files may end with a different extension name other than `.CSV` . (e.g. `.tsv`, '.xlsx')
`LOAD FROM 'test.tsv'`. => Exception
2. Certain file formats store data in a directory rather than a single file. Inferring those file formats is quite difficult. (e.g. delta lake, iceberg)
`LOAD FROM 'person-delta-lake'`

# Solution:
I propose that we extend our `LOAD FROM` grammar to accept an additional option: `TYPE`, which indicates the type of the file in the `LOAD FROM` clause. 

## Grammar:
1. Load from
```
LOAD FROM <file_path> (type=<file_format>)
RETURN XXXX
```

2. Copy from
```
COPY FROM <file_path> (type=<file_format>)
```

## Example:
```
LOAD FROM '/tmp/student' (type=delta)
RETURN name, age
```

```
COPY student FROM '/tmp/student' (type=delta)
```

We can make `TYPE` optional, meaning that kuzu still tries to infer the file format when the `TYPE` option is not provided. So:
```
LOAD FROM '/tmp/university.csv'
RETURN name, age
```
still works. However, kuzu should throw an exception when the type inference is impossible:
```
LOAD FROM '/tmp/student'
RETURN name, age
```

title: HNSW-based vector index
body:
# Description

This is the first version of the two-layer HNSW-based vector index. We keep two layers, each of which is a graph and is stored as a forward only rel table.

## Usage
### Basic Usage
We support creating vector indexes over a single float array column in node tables.
Here is an example node table for demonstration.
```sql
CREATE NODE TABLE embeddings (id int64, vec FLOAT[8], PRIMARY KEY (id));
```

We provide three functions: `CREATE_HNSW_INDEX`, `QUERY_HNSW_INDEX`, and `DROP_HNSW_INDEX` to create, query, and drop the index, respectively.

#### CREATE_HNSW_INDEX
The syntax for creating a vector index is as follows:
```
CALL CREATE_HNSW_INDEX('table_name', 'index_name', 'column_name', [option_name := option_value]);
```

We support following options during index creation.
| option name | description |
| ------------ | ------------ |
| mu                | max degree of nodes in the upper graph |
| ml                 | max degree of nodes in the lower graph |
| pu                | percentage of nodes sampled into the upper graph |
| metric       | metric (distance computation) functions. supported are cosine, l2, l2sq, and dotproduct. by default, the distance function is cosine. |
| efc               | The number of candidate vertices to consider during the construction of the index. A higher value will result in a more accurate index, but will also increase the time it takes to build the index. |

In our example, we create a vector index over the  `vec` column from `embeddings` table.
```cypher
CALL CREATE_HNSW_INDEX('embeddings', 'e_hnsw_index', 'vec', metric := 'l2');
```

**Note that for optional params in the function, we use `:=`, instead of `=` to specify values.**

#### QUERY_HNSW_INDEX
```
CALL QUERY_HNSW_INDEX('table_name', 'index_name',  vector, k, [option_name := option_value]) RETURN nn.id ORDER BY _distance;
```

We support following options during index search.
| option name | description |
| ------------ | ------------ |
| efs                | The number of candidate vertices to consider during the search phase of the index. A higher value will result in a more accurate index, but will also increase the time it takes to perform a search. |

In our example, we search the created vector index with a vector.
```cypher
CALL QUERY_HNSW_INDEX('embeddings', 'e_hnsw_index', [0.1521,0.3021,0.5366,0.2774,0.5593,0.5589,0.1365,0.8557], 3) RETURN nn.id ORDER BY _distance;
```

#### DROP_HNSW_INDEX
```
CALL DROP_HNSW_INDEX('table_name', 'index_name');
```

In our example, we can drop the newly created index with following statement:
```cypher
CALL DROP_HNSW_INDEX('embeddings', 'e_hnsw_index');
```

### Show Indexes
We can list all created indexes with `CALL SHOW_INDEXES() RETURN *`. Please see more details [here](https://docs.kuzudb.com/cypher/query-clauses/call/#show_indexes).

### Filtered Search
We allow search over filtered node tables with the index.
This is done by combining the use of projected graph and hnsw index functions.

A projected graph is a virtual view of a subset of node and rel tables in the database with (or without) some simple filter predicates.

An example is as follows, where we want to search over the `embeddings` table based on its `id` property.
```cypher
// Create a projected graph over the embeddings node table, with a predicate filter of `id < 50`.
CALL CREATE_PROJECTED_GRAPH('e_graph', {'embeddings': {'filter': 'n.id < 50'}}, []);
// Search over index based on the filtered node table defined in the projected graph.
CALL QUERY_HNSW_INDEX('e_graph', 'e_hnsw_index', [0.1521,0.3021,0.5366,0.2774,0.5593,0.5589,0.1365,0.8557], 3) RETURN nn.id ORDER BY _distance;
```

Note that in the use case of filtered search, for now, we only allow the passed in projected graph consisting of a single node table, and without any rel tables.

### Python API: Python array as the query vector
We support prepare and execute through Python API for the `QUERY_HNSW_INDEX` function to pass in a Python array
as the query vector.

An example can be found [here](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/master/tools/python_api/test/test_vector_index.py)

## Tech Details
### Query Plan
#### Index creation
The index creation follows a similar way as how COPY REL works. The `CREATE_HNSW_INDEX` call statement is compiled into three pipelines. The first one constructs in-memory index,  which consists of upper and lower layer graphs, and will convert the lower and upper in-memory graphs to flat tuples consisting of src and dst node offsets, respectively, which are shared with the second and third pipelines.
The second and third pipelines are reusing 'RelBatchInsert' to organize tuples from lower and upper layer graphs into node groups and flush them as rel tables.

Note that the above procedure assumes that we creates two rel tables for the upper and lower layer, respectively. This is done through the `rewriteFunc`, which generates a query string that is executed before the actual index create function.

Also, in this PR, to simplify the design and improve the performance, we cache the whole embedding column from the node table. Note that this can potentially improve the performance by avoiding random reads from disk, but reduces the scalability of the index in the longer term. For example, assume embeddings are not compressed, for FLOAT[1024], a single embedding is 4KB, which is a reasonable size to read from disk, while caching 10M embeddings of such in memory will cost 40GB of memory.

#### Index search
The index search (`QUERY_HNSW_INDEX`) is compiled into a hash join. The build side is the table function which does searches in the index, and return `k` tuples, and the probe side is scan of the base node table. Note that we will force semi mask to be passed from the build side to the probe side to reduce unnecessary scans, assuming `k` is small. But eventually we should let optimizer to figure out based on cardinality which side is build side and whether to pass semi mask or not.
Also, potentially we will replace the hash join with lookups instead, but not in this first initial PR.

----
**For reviewer:**
Pointers to important changes in the PR:
- src/function/table/call/hnsw/: implementation of create/query/drop index table functions.
- src/include/function/table/hnsw/hnsw_index_functions.h: definition of all hnsw index related table functions.
- src/include/storage/index/: core hnsw index data structures and algorithm implementation.

1. Have the flexibility to design graphs as separated as needed. Instead of designing DBs as 1 big graph, we could start thinking graphs as standalone DBs.
2. Split one DB into multiple DBs, while still having the possibility to query all the DBs as 1 whole.
3. Help introduce some level of "role based user access" patterns, by having one DB per user for example, and let the application layer route transactions to the relevant DB for this user. (or all sorts of logical separation of concerns)
4. Help with scaling and load balancing: we could easily deploy DBs across multiple nodes/servers

title: Fix VersionInfo SelectionVector creation
body:
Fixes #4271.

The issue was that `VersionInfo::getSelVectorForScan` (and `VectorVersionInfo::getSelVectorForScan`) append repeatedly to a `SelectionVector` and in certain circumstances it will turn a non-empty unfiltered SelectionVector into a filtered one without preserving the former values and then just appending to the end. My solution was to add a new makeDynamic function that copies the old selectedPositions into the mutable buffer before switching them.

E.g. this can occur when the first few VectorVersionInfos have no deletions, such that the first branch is taken in `VectorVersionInfo::getSelVectorToScan` and it just increases the length of the unfiltered SelectionVector, but then later VectorVersionInfos have deletions, taking the second branch where there is no check for unfiltered data (since it has to be converted to filtered at that point).

title: Optimization: `yy_json` memory allocation improvement

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

C++

### Description

Internally, we use the library `yy_json` to parse `json` strings. 

`yy_json` uses the system default allocator: `malloc` to allocate memory if no allocator is provided. However, fragmentation can be easily caused when the number of allocations is large. To resolve this issue, Duckdb implemented their own allocator which allocates memory from their own `memoryManager` and pass to `yy_json`.

I suggest we do something similar as duckdb to solve this issue.

title: Question: why is the rust build in the Makefile using the MSVC "Debug" Runtime?
body:
0.7.0

in Makefile

```
rust:
ifeq ($(OS),Windows_NT)
	set CFLAGS=/MDd
```

`/MDd` means using Debugging-Runtime as DLL (that means the Runtime is doing the typical more deep testing like Debug-Heap etc. )

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/reference/md-mt-ld-use-run-time-library?view=msvc-170

Debug builds should(could) use `/MDd`
but Release builds should use `/MD` - without the `d`

Microsoft MSVC behavior is different to Linux here because they provide Debug and Release Versions of Runtime - which are different in speed and active testing (same like with STL - which does in Debug builds also more testing at runtime)

also is the Debug-Runtime only installed when VStudio is also installed

title: Bug: SelectionVector bug in windows
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

MAC M1

### What happened?

1. `isContinuous` triggers an assertion failure(cant dereference out of range vector iterator) on windows debug build: 
```
bool isContinuous() const {
        return selectedPositions >= &*INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.begin() &&
               selectedPositions <= &*INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.end();
    }
```
According to this post:
[cant dereference out of range vector iterator](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57928328/cant-dereference-out-of-range-vector-iterator-whats-the-problem)
Looks like `&INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.end()` is unsafe in windows.

2. `isUnfiltered` is not safe in windows:
```
    bool isUnfiltered() const { return selectedPositions == INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.data(); }
```
We use pointer based arithmetic in windows to determine a vector is filtered or not, where `INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS ` is a static field in selectionVector.
However, the initialization of static fields behaves differently than linux/mac.
```
 (lldb) p selVector.INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS.data()
(const unsigned long long *) $49 = 0x00007ffff97b6290 {libfts.kuzu_extension!std::array<unsigned __int64,2048> const kuzu::common::SelectionVector::INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS} {0}
(lldb) p selVector.selectedPositions
(unsigned long long *const) $50 = 0x00007ff74d420080 {e2e_test.exe!std::array<unsigned __int64,2048> const kuzu::common::SelectionVector::INCREMENTAL_SELECTED_POS} {0}
```
I suggest we use an enum to indicate whether it is filtered or not.

title: Wasm buffer manager support
body:
This adds a simple alternative implementation to the BufferManager that allocates pages using malloc (via unique_ptr) and stores the page pointer in the PageState object. 

### Performance
There is a small performance penalty, pinning pages appears to be ~2-5x slower with this method, however even when doing a lot of new pins (i.e. where it's also allocating; there should be little difference for pins of pages which are already in memory) the overall cost is minimal.

E.g. summing the float edge property in the LDBC datagen-9_0-fb dataset took ~700ms using the normal buffer manager and ~900ms using this variant (obviously not a webassembly build; I overrode the macro used to enable/disable this feature).

Interestingly, it was actually faster when comparing the following query on the much larger graph500-30 dataset: 
`kuzu kugraph500-30 -d512 --noprogressbar --read_only <<< 'MATCH (v:N)-[e:E]->(:N) RETURN SUM(v.ID);'`, where the original runtime was ~4s, and improved to ~2.8s with this change (also on a machine with 128 threads; the difference may be that this approach scales better or has less of a setup cost, even though the allocation cost is higher; I'll look into it and try and see what the difference is).

### Outstanding Webassembly bugs
Unfortunately it appears that this is not the issue with the web assembly tests which were running out of memory. They are still running out of memory with this change, so I have left them disabled; as far as I can tell the huge memory allocations in those tests are unrelated to the BufferManager/MemoryManager.

### Other changes of note
I also lowered the default buffer pool size for testing back to 64MB. This should have been lowered before, but I guess was missed after it was raised when I was adding ColumnChunk memory to the tracked limit. With the higher limit most tests never do buffer manager evictions (including some of the tests which are disabled on webassembly due to this memory issue).

labels.name: type: feature

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Python 3.13 includes a [free-threaded mode](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.13.html#free-threaded-cpython) which does not enable GIL by default. This should make Python more performant when running multi-threaded code. The free-threaded mode uses a different executable called `python3.13t`. We have been building pre-compiled bins for `python3.13t` on Linux (see https://pypi.org/project/kuzu/0.6.2.dev29/#files) but did not really test whether it works correctly. We should test it and fix any potential error, then extend the support to all platforms as it may benefit users who use multi-threading in Python.

title: More ALP bug fixes
body:
# Description
- ALP chunks contain two types of pages: one for storing bitpacked data and one for storing exceptions. When determining if we can update in place, we should only use the number of pages to used bitpacked data to determine if we can perform updates (insertions) in place. Before we also included the number of pages for storing exceptions, giving a larger capacity than expected which caused some overflow errors.
- Modify the ALP vector size to match column chunk (rowgroup) size. For ALP we find a single set of parameters per column chunk and the disagreement between the ALP vector size and our column chunk size could potentially cause the parameters to be selected incorrectly.
- Have `ALPEncode::encode_value()` return int32_t if encoding `float` types (instead of `double`). This ensures that doing an encode then a decode of the return value will properly reflect the success of the operation. Before `encode_value()` always returned int64_t which caused us to miss some failed encode + decode for floats (which should be bitpacked as int32_t).
  - Technically always encoding as `int64_t` can be correct. However, we encode `float` as `int32_t` so that we can decompress the bitpacked values using the same memory that we return the decoded `float` values in, allowing us to avoid heap allocations.

# Contributor agreement

title: Refactor end-to-end testing framework to go through `query` instead of `prepare` and `execute`
body:
### Description

Right now, our end-to-end testing framework runs queries through `prepare` and `execute` interfaces, instead of directly through `query`, to accommodate the needs of enumerating plans and take in encoded joins during testing.

However, this can hide unexpected problems when running queries through the `query` interface. An example is #4502.
Moreover, plan enumeration and encoded joins should now be reworked with `hint` along with the query when we write the test cases. `prepare` and `execute` should be tested separately in the API level.
