title: Optimization: FactorizedTable Writes or Recursive Join/GDS Writers
body:
### Description

I'm working on the new recursive joins and I am seeing the following numbers on my machine, which indicate that we should be able to optimize when writing data to FactorizedTable.
I am running several versions of this query:
```
PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL all_sp_paths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c; 
```
The `{all/single}_sp_{paths/lengths/destinations}` functions materialize all of their output to an intermediate FactorizedTable. I'm measuring how much memory allocation these FactorizedTable do through the MemoryManager (by keeping some extra fields in FactorizedTable in my branch). I see the following numbers:

This query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL all_sp_lengths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` writes 5.5GB and the query takes 5.1s. If I remove the writing part with a hack to only write a few tuples (so think of this as writing 0 bytes), then the query takes ~0.8s.

This query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL all_sp_paths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` writes 7.8GB data and takes 13.3s. If I do the same hack of writing 0 tuples, the query takes 0.8s. 

For reference, his query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL single_sp_lengths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` takes 1.1s and writes 170MB of data. If I do the hack, it takes 0.7s.

Finally, for reference, this query: `PROJECT GRAPH PK (ljNode, ljRel) MATCH (a:ljNode) WHERE a.ID = 0 CALL single_sp_paths(PK, a, 30, true) RETURN  count(*) as c;` takes 1.1s and writes 240MB of data. If I do the hack, it takes 0.8s.

I think we should look into what we can do to improve the write performance of FactorizedTable. I don't have a very good idea now unfortunately. We might consider changing some APIs that allow operators to write to FactorizedTable in a faster way, which usually should mean writing in bulk but not sure how to enable that. In my case, I'm writing one tuple at a time. We might instead have to write in bulk to FactorizedTable.

title: Make FactorizedTable threadsafe (especially the merge function)
body:
Currently FactorizedTable is not a threadsafe class. In particular it has a merge function to merge multiple FactorizedTables that delegates the responsibility of thread safety, i.e., acquiring the locks, to the caller. This makes the code harder to read as one needs to figure out the call stack to find whether or not a lock has been acquired. It also leads to duplicated lock acquisition code in cases when the only reason the caller uses a mutex and lock is to ensure FactorizedTable::merge's safety (which is currently what happens on ResultCollectorSharedState::mergeLocalTable and the GDS RJOutputWriterVC code in my branch).

Instead FactorizedTable should be threadsafe itself by keeping an internal lock. Even if an outside lock is acquired this is fine and in some cases, as in RJOutputWriterVC, this can help us remove the duplicated locking code from the caller. So we should refactor this.

title: Map GDS call is passing a FactorizedTable instead of a schema
body:
I was in the following situation. I'm parallelizing the writes of the GDS outputs. In this case, each thread needs to create a local copy of an FTable. The current PlanMapper::mapGDSCall passes an actual FTable instead of TableSchema down to the operators (putting this in the GDSCallSharedState). This left me in a situation where I wanted to copy or clone the FTable but there is no such function. 

Having talked to @acquamarin apparently normally the frontend passes just the schema and each operator that wants to do parallel writes, e.g., ResultCollector, use this schema to create its local copy with a line like this (see ResultCollector::initLocalStateInternal for an example):
```
    localTable = std::make_unique<FactorizedTable>(context->clientContext->getMemoryManager(),
        info.tableSchema.copy());
```

So maybe we should follow this style also in GDSCall. Or we can add a clone function to FTable and pass in FTable in other places too. Regardless, let's be consistent everywhere for code readability.

title: Exporting to NetworkX for a multi-edge graph contains duplicates
body:
This is from @kamalikaray's comment in #3640.

## Issue

When exporting a Kuzu graph that has multi-edges to NetworkX, it seems that there are duplicate edges being returned as NetworkX objects. It seems that we're not de-duplicating the edges appropriately prior to returning them as a NetworkX graph when there are multi-edges.

The actual graph in Kuzu contains the following data:

```
┌────────────┬───────┬───────────┬──────────────┬──────────┬────────────┐
│ a.username ┆ a.age ┆ c.name    ┆ c.population ┆ l.role   ┆ con.county │
│ ---        ┆ ---   ┆ ---       ┆ ---          ┆ ---      ┆ ---        │
│ str        ┆ i64   ┆ str       ┆ i64          ┆ str      ┆ str        │
╞════════════╪═══════╪═══════════╪══════════════╪══════════╪════════════╡
│ Adam       ┆ 30    ┆ Waterloo  ┆ 150000       ┆ Resident ┆ county1    │
│ Adam       ┆ 30    ┆ Waterloo  ┆ 150000       ┆ Worker   ┆ county1    │
│ Karissa    ┆ 40    ┆ Waterloo  ┆ 150000       ┆ Resident ┆ county1    │
│ Zhang      ┆ 50    ┆ Kitchener ┆ 200000       ┆ Resident ┆ county2    │
│ Noura      ┆ 25    ┆ Guelph    ┆ 75000        ┆ Worker   ┆ county2    │
└────────────┴───────┴───────────┴──────────────┴──────────┴────────────┘
```
However, the NetworkX results contain duplicate edges that have the same offset and table IDs and property information. For example, the `(City_Waterloo, County_county1)` edge appears three times in the results and contain identical information, including properties.

```
Edge (User_Adam, City_Waterloo) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Resident'}
Edge (User_Adam, City_Waterloo) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Worker'}
Edge (City_Waterloo, County_county1) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (City_Waterloo, County_county1) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (City_Waterloo, County_county1) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (User_Karissa, City_Waterloo) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 1, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 0, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Resident'}
Edge (User_Zhang, City_Kitchener) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 2, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 1, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Resident'}
Edge (City_Kitchener, County_county2) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 1, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 1, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
Edge (User_Noura, City_Guelph) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 3, 'table': 0}, '_dst': {'offset': 2, 'table': 1}, '_label': 'LivesIn', 'role': 'Worker'}
Edge (City_Guelph, County_county2) has properties {'_src': {'offset': 2, 'table': 1}, '_dst': {'offset': 1, 'table': 2}, '_label': 'PartOf'}
```

Perhaps we can utilize these IDs in combination with the property information to inform the `get_as_networkx()` method that the edges have the same source and destination and have identical properties? The de-duplication logic as we have it seems insufficient.

## Code to reproduce

Below is a minimal reproducible example:

```py
import kuzu
import shutil

# Initialize database
shutil.rmtree("./demo_db", ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database("./demo_db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# Create schema
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE User(username STRING, age INT64, PRIMARY KEY (username))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE City(name STRING, population INT64, PRIMARY KEY (name))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE County(county STRING, PRIMARY KEY (county))")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE LivesIn(FROM User TO City, role STRING)")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE PartOf(FROM City TO County)")

# Insert data
conn.execute('COPY User FROM "./user.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY City FROM "./city.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY County FROM "./county.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY LivesIn FROM "./lives-in.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')
conn.execute('COPY PartOf FROM "./part-of.csv" (HEADER=TRUE)')

# Execute Cypher query
query1 = """
    MATCH (a:User)-[l:LivesIn]->(c:City)-[p:PartOf]->(con:County)
    RETURN a.*, c.*, l.*, p.*, con.*
"""

result1 = conn.execute(query1)
print(result1.get_as_pl())

query2 = """
    MATCH (a:User)-[l:LivesIn]->(c:City)-[p:PartOf]->(con:County)
    RETURN a, c, l, p, con
"""

res2 = conn.execute(query2)
G = res2.get_as_networkx(directed=True)
for u, v, attr in G.edges(data=True):
    print(f"Edge ({u}, {v}) has properties {attr}")
```

title: Optimize version vector array
body:
# Description

This is on top of #4210.

Skip allocation of insertion/deletion versions array if all insertions and deletions are of the same version.
It's common that all values within the same vector are of the same version as they are inserted through `COPY FROM` statement, though all deletions of the same version happen only when all tuples within the vector are deleted.
The optimization is to keep a `sameInsertionVersion` and a `sameDeletionVersion` inside the `VectorVersionInfo`. Further, each `VersionInfo` can keep a global `sameInsertionVersion` and `sameDeletionVersion` too, though that won't contribute much to the reduction of memory usage.

I did a simple benchmark with lsqb-100 Comment table, which only contains only one property, `ID INT64`. The benchmarking is done under in-memory mode, the mem usage after COPY reduced from ~14GB to ~10G.

TODO:
- A common data structure for both insertion and deletion VectorVersionInfo.
- The `insertionStatus` and `deletionStatus` can perhaps also be simplified.

title: Bug: Kuzu wrongly output non-existing relations in certain cases
Spill to disk
body:
Based on #3743

This feature allows Column chunk data from the partitioner during rel table copies to be written to disk and freed (to save memory) if the ChunkedNodeGroup in question will no longer be needed until the end of the copy.
Every full ChunkedNodeGroup (in the InMemChunkedGroupCollection) gets passed to the Spiller, which stores them in a locked unordered_set (so they can be quickly removed once they are needed again; we could probably use an EvictionQueue to store them, but I'm not convinced that performance benefit would be noticeable).

Data starts to be spilled to disk when the buffer pool is full and at least 50% of the buffer pool is used by column chunks (though this calculation includes chunks which aren't in the fullPartitionerGroups set and can't be spilled).

When it comes time for the data spilled to be used, it gets loaded back into memory and removed from the fullPartitionerGroups set (which could cause other chunks to be spilled if there is not enough memory; ideally we could make sure to use all the chunks already in memory first, but that would be complicated). The memory is then freed afterwards (originally all the chunks would be held in memory until the end of RelBatchInsert execution, but that's no longer possible so we now need mutable access to that data and move it out of the partitioner shared state when processing it so that it can be freed).

### Future work
This is currently only enabled when the database is using the LocalFileSystem and it is not in in-memory mode. I feel like spilling to disk should not write to other types of filesystems, but it seems reasonable that this could spill to the local filesystem for databases stored on other filesystems. That will be more complicated though, and I don't know if there will be much demand for it.

title: Populate error source info (e.g. line number) for node batch insert if the source is a CSV file
body:
# Description

Partially Fixes https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/1872

Report line number, skipped line, and file path for PK-constraint related copy warnings. File sources other than CSV (e.g. numpy, RDF, parquet) will still report PK-constraint-related errors, but the additional warning information will not be provided.

Additional changes made to make the above possible:
- Pass any required reader-related metadata from the file reader to `IndexBuilder` for each scanned row via an additional data chunk. When a warning is reported by `IndexBuilder`, it will store such information in the raw warning and eventually flush them to the global `WarningContext`. Such metadata will only be populated if `IGNORE_ERRORS` is set to `true`.
- During finalize, the file reader populates all raw warnings in the global `WarningContext` using the information stored in each warning.
- Remove all error-handling functionality away from `SharedCSVFileErrorHandler`. It's purpose is now to primarily keep track of line numbers for a file as well as caching + throwing any errors that can't be thrown immediately in the `LocalCSVFileErrorHandler` (due to the line number not being calculable at the time)
  -  `LocalCSVFileErrorHandler` and `NodeBatchInsertErrorHandler` directly flush raw(unpopulated) errors to the global `WarningContext` when their local buffers are full.
I also added in some tests for reading from CSVs that span multiple blocks (or have lines that span multiple blocks) and fixed the reporting of line numbers in this case.

**Some quick sanity-check benchmarks can be found [here](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/pull/4184#issuecomment-2334802877)**

title: Backslashes are poorly supported in paths on Windows

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

labels.name: area: frontend
labels.description: Frontend, i.e., binder, parser, query planning-related issues

body:
Forward slashes work, but windows also uses backslashes as a path separator, but kuzu will give a cryptic parser exception if you attempt to use them.

I think it does work if properly escaped, however in some APIs that adds an annoying extra level of string processing (e.g. having to pass `\\\\` to get a single backslash in python).
And the error message is not very helpful. Either you get vaild escape sequences (resulting in it not finding the file) or something like the following:
```
Error: Parser exception: Invalid input <copy foo from ">: expected rule oC_Statement (line: 1, offset: 14)
"copy foo from "C:\Program Files\foo.csv""
```

So maybe we need some combination of support for backslashes in paths on windows directly, and improved error messages related to the incorrect use of escape characters.

Whenever someone issues a PR to add a new feature that requires documentation, they can mark it with the label "needs-documentation". Then the CI bot would kick in and create a new issue on our [docs repo](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu-docs), where it links back to the PR in this repo that adds the feature. This will help on two counts:

- We can link the docs issue directly back to the feature PR that implemented it (or the issue that was flagged) on our main repo

title: Pyarrow Performance Problem

labels.name: type: perf bug
labels.description: Issues related to a regression in the performance

body:
### Kùzu version

projection-py branch

### What operating system are you using?

_No response_

### What happened?

When scanning from large python dataframes, it seems like Arrow sources are noticeably slower than Numpy sources. For example, consider the following results, where we have a 100 million row table with two integer columns.
```
loadNumpy: 0.09682886581867933s
loadNumpyProj: 0.03378376178443432s

loadArrow: 0.4811821011826396s
loadArrowProj: 0.4280042313039303s
```
The query used for normal results is
```
LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0), max(col1)
```
Results suffixed by `proj` used the following query
```
LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0)
```
If we consider the absolute performance difference between not projecting and projecting, both sources improve by about 0.063s and 0.053s respectively, which is most likely the performance improvement gained from not scanning the second column, plus not attempting to determine the max value of the column. However, it looks like arrow scanning comes with a significant overhead. The most likely cause of this overhead is the binding process, though I can't be sure.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

The following script was used to generate results. It also contains commented out code for benchmarking json, but the performance results there are not expected to be significant.
```py
import kuzu
import os
import random
import pandas as pd
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
import time

conn = kuzu.Connection(kuzu.Database())
conn.execute("LOAD EXTENSION 'extension/json/build/libjson.kuzu_extension';")
# conn.execute("CALL THREADS=1")

random.seed(100)
datalen = 100_000_000
maxnum = 1_000_000_000
mp = {'col0': np.random.randint(maxnum, size=(datalen)), 'col1': np.random.randint(maxnum, size=(datalen))}
polarsDF = pl.DataFrame(mp)
pandasDF = pd.DataFrame(mp)
# open('test.json', 'w').write('[\n' + ',\n'.join(['{"col0": ' + str(mp['col0'][i]) + ', "col1": ' + str(mp['col1'][i]) + '}' for i in range(datalen)]) + '\n]\n')

def benchmark(func, params):
        begin = time.perf_counter()
        func(*params)
        end = time.perf_counter()
        return end - begin

def loadNumpy(conn, df):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0), max(col1)').get_as_pl()

def loadNumpyProj(conn, df):
        result = conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0)').get_as_pl()

def loadArrow(conn, df):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0), max(col1)').get_as_pl()

def loadArrowProj(conn, df):
        result = conn.execute('LOAD FROM df RETURN max(col0)').get_as_pl()

def loadJSON(conn):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM "test.json" RETURN max(col0), max(col1)').get_as_pl()

def loadJSONProj(conn):
        conn.execute('LOAD FROM "test.json" RETURN max(col0)').get_as_pl()

print(f'loadNumpy: {benchmark(loadNumpy, [conn, pandasDF])}')
print(f'loadNumpyProj: {benchmark(loadNumpyProj, [conn, pandasDF])}')
print(f'loadArrow: {benchmark(loadArrow, [conn, polarsDF])}')
print(f'loadArrowProj: {benchmark(loadArrowProj, [conn, polarsDF])}')
# print(f'loadJSON: {benchmark(loadJSON, [conn])}')
# print(f'loadJSONProj: {benchmark(loadJSONProj, [conn])}')

# os.system('rm test.json')
```

title: Fix JSON null handling
body:
# Description

JSON assigned NULL values to int8 as a placeholder. This doesn't work out too good if you try to put it through maxlogicaltype. 
```json
[
null,
{"col1": 1, "col2": 2, "col3": "asdf"}
]
```
In the above case, it would assign the first object to INT8, then the second object to STRUCT. It'd then combine the two to deduce that we're reading from a one column table and interpret the whole thing as string.

It now assigns nulls to be ANY, and then purges the result to turn any instances of ANY into STRING. The above example now works as expected.

title: BUG: Using `CTRL C` to interrupt a query exits the shell
body:
When running a query and printing query results in the CLI, if `CTRL C` is pressed it exits the shell instead of terminating the query and starting a new line to edit. 

This is due to the way we handle `SIGINT` for the `embedded_shell.cpp` code. 

https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/87de7f9128ff9946b95e62bad69bd8d8053a176c/tools/shell/embedded_shell.cpp#L304 https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/87de7f9128ff9946b95e62bad69bd8d8053a176c/tools/shell/embedded_shell.cpp#L429-L438

It seems like SIGINT is not being handled by this function or it still terminates afterwards. 

One possibility is switching to using [sigaction](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/2.4.0?topic=functions-sigaction-examine-change-signal-action) instead of `signal` for more flexibility but a different solution would be needed for Windows. 

Our `CTRL C` handling works in the `linenoise.cpp` file where we change the terminal modes to process the raw input. A similar solution may need to be applied to adjust the terminal mode to correctly send `SIGINT` to our signal handler.
https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/blob/87de7f9128ff9946b95e62bad69bd8d8053a176c/tools/shell/linenoise.cpp#L448-L519

title: Add external node table
body:
# Description

This is our initial PR to support directly execute cypher on relational database. It contains logic for node table only. Major changes including

### Nested catalog entry.

We add a new catalog entry type `ExternalNodeTable` which has a nested entry structure. At parent level, it maintains the logic view of properties which aligns with the columns in relational tables. At child level, it maintains another catalog entry which contains the primary key property only. This child entry aligns with our physical storage.

In the current design, we still need to materialize primary key and use it as join condition when we try to read a property that does not exist in storage. 

### Scan external table

When we run `MATCH (a:label)` where label points to an external relational table, we need to scan external relational table and the primary key column materialized in our storage and then perform a join on primary key.

Some sanity benchmark numbers are

**Setup**
LDBC10 Comment table storing in DuckDB database. 8 Threads.

DuckDB native scanning: 0.3s.
Kuzu scanning DuckDB: 2s.
Scanning external database: copy primary key (6s) + join (3s) = 9s.

Slower than DuckDB is expected as we need to first materialize DuckDB's result and then re-scan it. The major overhead is in us scanning DuckDB result which @acquamarin should see if we can further optimize this.

Another bottleneck is the copy of primary key. I'm fairly confident I can bring the time to ~2s with some optimization.

Fixes # (issue)

body:
This doesn't mean that it was always rebuilding everything, as it would still re-use the old build directory, but if you haven't touched the C++ sources, then it shouldn't be necessary to run CMake at all (outside of configuration changes of course), and Cargo is faster at detecting if anything needs to be rebuilt than CMake is (a build without changes went from ~6s to ~0.03s). This is a particularly common situation for anyone using the releases.

One of the files set to re-run if changed had an incorrect path, so Cargo was always re-running the kuzu build script as that's the behaviour if a file is missing. We were also missing rerun-if-changed instructions for the C++ sources.

title: Feature: Consider adding `BOOL` alias for `BOOLEAN` to help cross-language consistency

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Currently, for Python and Rust, which both use `bool` to denote the boolean type natively, we also specify these types in the Kùzu language bindings API.

- Python:  `kuzu.Type.BOOL`
- Rust: `Value::Bool(value)`

When defining a Python UDF, the user has to keep in mind the fact that Kùzu's internal type is named `BOOLEAN`, but the language (Python in this case) calls it `BOOL`. During DDL, we have to maintain this difference by specifying `BOOLEAN` for Kùzu types and `BOOL` for Python types.

Having an alias `BOOL` on Kùzu's side can help keep things consistent when working with Python/Rust. The user can just use `BOOL` everywhere and not have to mix and match.

Rather than changing the language API's naming to match with Kùzu's (which would be a breaking change and affect all tests), it makes more sense to add the alias, which is a minor change, improves usability and consistency, and doesn't break any tests.

title: Vacuum dropped columns during checkpoint
body:
# Description

The PR is to fix a bug due to not vacuum dropped columns during checkpoint. The bug happens when we recover after dropped a column and performed checkpoint. During the recovery, we will have some columns as nullptr, which lead to seg faults when we collect data types from table columns.

This PR solves the issue by always vacuuming dropped columns from storage during checkpoint. Note that the column ID inside property will be reset due to the vacuuming, that's why the checkpoint of catalog now happens after the checkpoint of tables. Letting storage modifies catalog may not be a good practice, alternatively, we can let `TableCatalogEntry` reset its column ids during checkpoint independently, which sounds like a better idea to me.

In the future, we should also reclaim disk pages of persistent column chunks being dropped during checkpoint.

A minor refactoring:
- aligned columnID for rel table properties (`nextColumnID` starts from 1 to skip the anonymous NBR_ID column inside `RelTableCatalogEntry`). thus removed the special implementation of `RelTableCatalogEntry::getColumnID`.

title: Bug: [Recursive, undirected relationship] Error: Runtime exception: Different path semantics for COUNT(*) optimization is not implemented. Try WALK semantic.
body:
### Kùzu version

nightly

### What operating system are you using?

Fedora 40

### What happened?

Example:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE V (id INT64, PRIMARY KEY(id));
CREATE REL TABLE links_to (FROM V TO V);
CREATE (v1:V {id: 1})-[:links_to]->(v2:V {id: 2})-[:links_to]->(v3:V {id: 3}), 
(v4:V {id: 4})-[:links_to]->(v2),(v4)-[:links_to]->(v5:V {id: 5}), (v6:V {id: 6})-[:links_to]->(v1),
(v8:V {id: 8})-[:links_to]->(v9: V{id: 9}), 
(v10:V {id:10});
```
![graph](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3b8ea6cb-c23e-43f4-95eb-ba6dc9cf55fd)

Given node `1` as input, I'd like to query the weakly connected components (directly and indirectly connected nodes neglecting the relationship direction).

Expected: `[2,3,4,5,6]`

One possible query leads to following error:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (:V {id: 1})-[:links_to*]-(v2:V) RETURN DISTINCT v2;
Error: Buffer manager exception: Failed to claim a frame.
```

The reason is (thanks @andyfengHKU for clarification), that by default `WALK` semantic is used for traversal, which allows arbitrary repeated nodes/edges. Hence this computation ends up costly performance-wise and produces a lot of results.

A temporary workaround - which does not solve mentioned performance issues and is more verbose - is to specify max hops:
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (:V {id: 1})-[:links_to*..10]-(v2:V) RETURN DISTINCT v2;
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ v2                           │
│ NODE                         │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ {_ID: 0:1, _LABEL: V, id: 2} │
│ {_ID: 0:5, _LABEL: V, id: 6} │
│ {_ID: 0:2, _LABEL: V, id: 3} │
│ {_ID: 0:3, _LABEL: V, id: 4} │
│ {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: V, id: 1} │
│ {_ID: 0:4, _LABEL: V, id: 5} │
└──────────────────────────────┘
(6 tuples)
(1 column)
```
Note there is also small deviation in semantics, as node `1` is included as well.

A better alternative is to use `TRAIL` semantic, which eliminates repeated edges:
```cypher
CALL recursive_pattern_semantic = 'Trail';
kuzu> MATCH (:V {id: 1})-[:links_to*]-(v2:V) RETURN DISTINCT v2;
```
But currently this will trigger following error:
> Error: Runtime exception: Different path semantics for COUNT(*) optimization is not implemented. Try WALK semantic.

Last I think, it would be best if user would not need to `CALL recursive_pattern_semantic = 'Trail';` manually for recursive relationships at all. Re-visiting edges in a recursive fashion via `WALK` - or hopping possibly infinite times between two connected nodes in case of an undirected relation query - probably does not make sense (ever?). Maybe take `TRAIL` as default for recursive relationships - or even globally? 

What might be worth to consider in this regard: Neo4j uses `TRAIL` semantic as default for one `MATCH` pattern. The openCypher standard states:
> While pattern matching, Cypher makes sure to not include matches where the same graph relationship is found multiple times in a single pattern.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

_No response_

title: Bug: CLI `:mode csv` not giving valid lists
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

_No response_

### What happened?

```
> :mode csv
> unwind [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] as col1 unwind [['a', 'b', 'c'], ['x', 'y', 'z']] as col2 return col1, col2;
```

gives

title: Feature: Support single-line comments in the CLI with syntax highlighting

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### Kùzu version

0.5.0

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

Currently, single line comments aren't parsed by the CLI:
```
kuzu> // This is a comment
..> match (n) return n.name;
Error: Parser exception: mismatched input '<EOF>' expecting {ALTER, ATTACH, BEGIN, CALL, CHECKPOINT, COMMENT, COMMIT, COPY, CREATE, DELETE, DETACH, DROP, EXPORT, IMPORT, INSTALL, LOAD, MATCH, MERGE, OPTIONAL, PROJECT, RETURN, ROLLBACK, SET, UNWIND, USE, WITH} (line: 1, offset: 44)
"// This is a comment match (n) return n.name"
```
Multi-line comments work.

```
kuzu> /* This
..> is a comment */
..> match (n:Person) return n.*;
┌────────┐
│ n.name │
│ STRING │
├────────┤
│ Alice  │
│ Bob    │
│ Carol  │
│ Dan    │
└────────┘
(4 tuples)
(1 column)
Time: 0.09ms (compiling), 0.25ms (executing)
```

## No issues in other clients

Kùzu Explorer has no issues and parses the single line comment correctly, presumably because it uses the Node.js client under the hood. The Python client also parses both kinds of comments correctly.

## Desired behaviour

The user should be able to specify single line comments in the CLI that span an entire line, just like they do in the other interfaces to Kùzu.

A simple rule could be "if line starts with `//` parse that entire line as a comment".

### DuckDB CLI supports this

To demonstrate expected behaviour, DuckDB's CLI supports single line comments.

```
❯ duckdb ./ex_db.duckdb
v1.0.0 1f98600c2c
Enter ".help" for usage hints.
D -- This is a comment
D CREATE TABLE person (name STRING PRIMARY KEY);
```

Also, DuckDB takes care of syntax highlighting the comments in the CLI (note how it's grey in colour):
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/134dac27-25ed-4df6-b83f-901cf02d002f)

Partially addresses #1872, adding the following features:

title: Fix updates to same row leading to incorrect write-write conflict errors

# Description

Adding a cpp test case for now. Eventually we should also cover the cases of not going through `prepare` interface in our testing framework.

Also, removed the useless param `requiredNexTx`, which is always set to false, from `executeAndAutoCommitIfNecessaryNoLock`.

body:
### Kùzu version

v0.5.0

### What operating system are you using?

MacOS

### What happened?

I'm using Kuzu 0.5.0 and tried to prepare a statement with a variable for the node type. It fails with the error below. If I hard code the node type instead of using the `$type` variable it works but won't be usable for my use case.

```typescript
const nodeStmt = await conn.prepare(`CREATE (n:$type {id: $id, label: $label})`);
```

```
node_modules/.pnpm/kuzu@0.5.0/node_modules/kuzu/connection.js:103
        return reject(new Error(preparedStatement.getErrorMessage()));
                      ^

Error: Parser exception: Invalid input <CREATE (n:$>: expected rule oC_SingleQuery (line: 1, offset: 10)
"CREATE (n:$type {id: $id, label: $label})"
           ^
    at node_modules/.pnpm/kuzu@0.5.0/node_modules/kuzu/connection.js:103:23
    at new Promise (<anonymous>)
```

This also fails using variables for the nodes in a `MATCH` statement as well. In this case it will fail on the node type variables and edge label variables so neither seems to be supported. 

```typescript
  const edgeStmt = await conn.prepare(`
    MATCH (n1:$source_type), (n2:$target_type)
    WHERE n1.id = $source AND n2.id = $target
    MERGE (n1)-[:$edge_label]->(n2)
  `);
```

title: Only commit memory when initially claiming the frame
body:
This fixes a fairly significant performance issue on Windows.

I was less familiar with our buffer manager when initially getting it to work on Windows. There's no need to ensure the memory is committed every time we call getFrame.

It was also necessary to skip evicted pages in updateFrameIfPageIsInFrameWithoutLock as it would otherwise segfault from trying to access uncommitted memory (it's not necessary to update them if they're evicted anyway).

title: Bug: READ_ONLY connection fails to read from database after ALTER TABLE is run
body:
### Kùzu version

0.5.0

### What operating system are you using?

macOS

### What happened?

The scenario under which this bug occurs is as follows:

- Copy from a Pandas DataFrame to a node table
- Alter node table to add a new column
- `LOAD FROM` a Pandas DataFrame and `MERGE` the new column to the existing Kùzu node table
- Open `READ_ONLY` CLI that tries to access the DB

The following error occurs when a `READ_ONLY` CLI is opened:

```
❯ kuzu ./test_db -r        
Error during recovery: Runtime exception: Failed to replay wal record from WAL file. Error: IO exception: Cannot write to file. path: ./test_db/data.kz fileDescriptor: 6 offsetToWrite: 45056 numBytesToWrite: 8 numBytesWritten: -1. Error: Bad file descriptor
```
The same error occurs with Kùzu Explorer as well.

When I change that to a `READ_WRITE` connection, either with the CLI or Kùzu Explorer, there's no error, and the process opens.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Consider this CSV file named `product.csv`:
```
"watch",200.0
"shoes",300.0
"wallet",150.0
```
Run this script:
```py
import kuzu
import shutil
import pandas as pd

shutil.rmtree("test_db", ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database("test_db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# create a table
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Product (item STRING, price INT64, PRIMARY KEY (item))")

df = pd.read_csv("product.csv", header=None, names=["item", "price"])

conn.execute("COPY Product FROM df")

# Alter a table
conn.execute("ALTER TABLE Product ADD has_discount BOOLEAN DEFAULT false")

df = pd.read_csv("product.csv", header=None, names=["item", "price"])
df["has_discount"] = pd.Series([True, False, True])

conn.execute(
    """
    LOAD FROM df
    WITH item, has_discount
    MERGE (p:Product {item: item})
    ON MATCH SET p.has_discount = has_discount
    """
)

res = conn.execute("MATCH (p:Product) RETURN p.*")
print(res.get_as_df())
```
The aim is to first copy from an initial DataFrame into a node table. Then, alter the node table to add a column. Finally, perform some other computations, and scan/merge from another DataFrame to the new node table column.

The script above runs to completion (no issues). The error is only *after* everything is done, when we try to open a `READ_ONLY` connection to the modified database.

title: Bug: IN clause does not find a node
body:
### Kùzu version

0.4.2, 0.5.0

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22

### What happened?

I modified a Your First Graph example by adding ID property and making it as primary key.
in a query  
```
   MATCH (a:User)-[r:LivesIn]->(b:City)
    WHERE b.ID in [1]
    RETURN a.*;
```
kuzu returns empty result, but
```
    MATCH (a:User)-[r:LivesIn]->(b:City)
    WHERE b.ID = 1
    RETURN a.*;
```
return the correct node. 

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

Code for reproducing:
```
import kuzu

# Initialize database
db = kuzu.Database("db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

# Create schema
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE User(name STRING, age INT64, ID SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY (ID))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE City(name STRING, population INT64, ID SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY (ID))")    
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE LivesIn(FROM User TO City)")

# Insert data
conn.execute('COPY User FROM "./user.csv"')
conn.execute('COPY City FROM "./city.csv"')    

conn.execute(f"""
        MATCH (a:User), (b:City)
        WHERE a.ID = 1 AND b.ID = 1
        CREATE (a)-[r:LivesIn]->(b)            
        RETURN r.*
        """)

# Execute Cypher query
response = conn.execute(
    """
    MATCH (a:User)-[r:LivesIn]->(b:City)
    WHERE b.ID = 1
    RETURN a.*;
    """
)
while response.has_next():
    print(response.get_next())

response = conn.execute(
    """
    MATCH (a:User)-[r:LivesIn]->(b:City)
    WHERE b.ID in [1]
    RETURN a.*;
    """
)
while response.has_next():
    print(response.get_next())
```

title: Make property case insensitive
body:
# Description

This PR contains the following changes

### Make property case insensitive

We have already make table name case insensitive, it does not make sense for our property to remain case sensitive. So we start applying case-insensitive-map everywhere when binding properties.

### Remove property_id_t

We use to have an `o_id` like identifier for property, i.e. `property_id_t`. Though I start to realize this is unnecessary. We could just use property name as the identifier since property should be unique within a table.

Fixes # (issue)

title: Join order with multiple variable names
body:
Can we give a better error for this case. I'm using b twice in the join order:
```
kuzu> explain match (a:Person)-[e1]->(b:Person)-[e2]->(c:Person) HINT (a JOIN (e1 JOIN b)) JOIN ((b JOIN e2) JOIN c) return *;
Error: Binder exception: Cannot resolve join condition.
```
The ideal error message should be: "The variable b is used twice in the join HINT. In HINT, each node and relationship pattern must appear exactly once."

title: Join hint with implicit variable names
body:
I have Person and Likes tables. I tried the following query (which I know won't work but I am testing what the system does):
```
explain match (a:Person)-[:Likes]->(b:Person)-[:Likes]->(c:Person), (a)-[:Likes]->(c) HINT a JOIN b JOIN c return *;
Error: Binder exception: Cannot find  in join hint.
```

We should give a better error message. Something like: "HINT clause requires every node and relationship table variable to be named. You have a relationship pattern with label Likes that does not have a named variable, e.g., -[:Likes]-> should be something like -[e:Likes]->." If the pattern does not have a label, you can change that part as: "...you have an unlabeled relationship pattern, ..., e.g., -[]->". 

If the problem is due to an implicit node variable, then the error message can be something like: "HINT clause requires every node and relationship table variable to be named. You have a node pattern with label Person that does not have a named variable, e.g., (:Person) should be something like (a:Person)." Similarly if the pattern does not have a label, you can change the error message accordingly.

In general it's very useful to give clear examples in error message that point users to the mistake. If you think there are many edge cases and don't want to give an error, you can just give a generic example. For example for the first one you can say: "..., e.g., -[:Foo]-> should be something like -[e:Foo]->." and similarly for the second one: "..., e.g., (:Person) should be something like (a:Person)".

body:
### API

Python

### Description

We currently allow attaching to a remote Kuzu db if its wal file is empty. However with the new MVCC mechanism, wal files will generally be non-empty. This means we cannot attach to (most) Kuzu dbs. There are two things to do here:
1. Remedy: A good remedy is to checkpoint before closing dbs and remove the wal file contents. We can assume that users would close external dbs before attaching to them. So, this should ensure that the external dbs we attach to  have empty wal files.
2. Solution:  Attach db functionality does not assume that the wal file is empty. This is apparently also doable.

If the remedy is easy to do, I suggest we just do that and keep this issue open until we have enough time to implement the actual solution. If they're about the same amount of work, we can go for the solution and not implement the remedy.

title: In memory mode
body:
# Description

Add the support for in-memory mode.  https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/1816.

## Feature
When the database path is omitted, set to empty or set to `:memory:` (follow duck's convention here), the database will be open under in-memory mode.

The main differences between on-disk and in-memory mode are:
Under on-disk mode, all data will be persistent on disk. All transactions are logged in WAL, in which changes will be merged into database files during checkpoint.
While under the in-memory mode, there is no writes to WAL, no data is persistent to disk and `CHECKPOINT` will do nothing. All data are lost when the process finishes.

Restrictions on in-memory mode:
- The database cannot be open as read-only.
- When use Httpfs extension, we don't support file cache.
- Attaching an in-memory database is not allowed. (maybe we should allow?)

## Implementation
After MVCC changes, supporting in-mem mode becomes much easier.
New pages in BMFileHandle are pinned in BM and only unpinned when BMFileHandle gets destructed. Accesses to these pages directly grab frames from BM.

## Benchmark
Did a few simple benchmarks on ldbc-100.
#### COPY
```
| table       | in mem (ms) | on disk (ms) |
| ----------- | ----------- | ------------ |
| Comment     | 14879       | 34696        |
| Person      | 513         | 749          |
| knows       | 1781        | 2123         |
| likeComment | 29246       | 34581        |
```

```
| space usage | in-mem mode | on-disk mode |
| ----------- | ----------- | ------------ |
| mem         | 56.7GB      | 32.2GB       |
| disk        | 0           | 29GB         |
```

#### Read only queries
```
Q1: match (c:Comment) return min(c.ID), min(c.creationDate), min(c.locationIP), min(c.browserUsed), min(c.content), min(c.length)
Q2: MATCH (a:Person)-[:knows]->(b:Person)-[:knows]->(c:Person) RETURN MIN(a.birthday), MIN(b.birthday), MIN(c.birthday)
Q3: MATCH (a:Person)-[r:knows* 2..2]->(b:Person) RETURN COUNT(*);

| query | in-mem | on-disk (cold) | on-disk (warm) |
| ----- | ------ | -------------- | -------------- |
| Q1    | 1896   | 5330           | 1791           |
| Q2    | 1004   | 948            | 893            |
| Q3    | 72133  | 84419          | 
```
#### Insertions
1M node insertions.

```
CREATE NODE TABLE Person (id INT64, name STRING, age INT64, net_worth FLOAT, PRIMARY KEY (id));

| 1M txn in-mem (ms) | 1M txn on-disk (ms) | 1 txn in-mem (ms) | 1 txn on-disk (ms) |
| ------------------ | ------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| 47814              | 79313               | 38895            | 40054               |
```
## TODO
- [ ] rewrite copy to / export tests (copy to should not rely on db path)

title: Fix or a better error message (not) attaching to external kuzu databases with non-empty wal files.

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
Now that we moved to MVCC, we do not checkpoint immediately after every transaction. Therefore, it is possible that users will connect and do writes to databases that will leave non-empty wal files. 

However we cannot attach to kuzu databases that have non-empty wal files. I get the following error:
`Error: Runtime exception: Cannot attach a remote kuzu database with non-empty wal file.`.

First, I feel this may be a result of the assumptions we made the pre-MVCC transaction manager. We should be able to connect to remote databases that have non-empty wal files. However, if there is a real concern here then, we should at least give a better error message that suggests a solution. In this case the solution is to ask the user to checkpoint the external database. So if we cannot fix the issue, let's update the error message to: `Error: Runtime exception: Cannot attach an external Kùzu database with non-empty wal file. Try manually checkpointing the external database (i.e., run "CHECKPOINT;").`.

title: ALP implementation
body:
# Description

Implements (ALP compression for floating-point values)[https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3626717]. The general idea of this compression algorithm consists of the following steps:
1. Pick values `e`, `f` (these can be found by sampling values, running the below steps, and picking the ones that provide the best compression ratio)
2. Floating point values are encoded to integers via the formula `encoded_value = float_value * 10^f * 10^(-e)`. We test if encoding and decoding a value will result in a loss of data. For values where there is no loss of data, the encoded integers are bitpacked normally. For values where there is a loss of data ('exceptions'), they are stored separately in uncompressed form.
3. Repeat the above steps for each chunk of values

Generally, the compression ratio will improve if all the values are in a similar range + have similar decimal precision.

This implementation deviates from the reference implementation (duckdb) in a few ways:
- DuckDB compressed one chunk for each segment. Since we don't have the concept of segments, we compress one chunk for each column chunk (which results in worse compression ratio since it is over a larger chunk of values).
- In the DuckDB implementation exceptions are directly appended to the each of each ALP chunk. This does not work for us as we rely on there being a constant number of compressed values in each page. Thus we store all the exceptions for a column chunk as a separate uncompressed chunk and iterate through the exception chunk (which we cache in memory during each checkpoint) while compressing/uncompressing the actual column chunk of floating point values. There is a performance cost of both reading/flushing the exception chunk and searching the exception chunk so we turn off compression if there are too many exceptions in a chunk.

The deviations generally negatively affect our performance and compression ratio; we should update our implementation once segmentation is done to follow the paper more faithfully.

title: Feature: Implement implicit cast from struct to map

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Users may want to provide a struct (e.g., a Python dict) as a node property. This currently fails with an implicit casting error.

```py
import shutil
import kuzu

shutil.rmtree("test_db", ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database("test_db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

conn.execute(
    """
    CREATE NODE TABLE Student (
        name STRING,
        grades MAP(STRING, INT64),
        PRIMARY KEY(name)
    )
    """
)

conn.execute(
    """
    CREATE (a:Student {name: "Karissa"})
        SET a.grades = {"math": 92, "physics": 91, "music": 78};
    CREATE (b:Student {name: "Adam"})
        SET b.grades = {"history": 81, "english": 87}
    """
)

res = conn.execute("MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.name, p.grades")
while res.has_next():
    result = res.get_next()
    print(result)
```
Currently throws an exception since we don't support implicit cast from `struct`->`map`

This is the exception:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/code/kuzu/test.py", line 21, in <module>
    conn.execute(
  File "/code/kuzu/tools/python_api/build/kuzu/connection.py", line 130, in execute
    _query_result = self._connection.query(query)
                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
RuntimeError: Binder exception: Expression STRUCT_PACK(math,physics,music) has data type STRUCT(math INT64, physics INT64, music INT64) but expected MAP(STRING, INT64). Implicit cast is not supported.
```

title: Bug: Kuzu could violate the relation uniqueness requirements of Cypher standard

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Kùzu version

v0.4.2

### What operating system are you using?

Ubuntu 22.04

### What happened?

Kuzu seems to violate the uniqueness requirements when matching relations, as specified in the openCypher standard, chapter "Pattern-Uniqueness"(https://s3.amazonaws.com/artifacts.opencypher.org/openCypher9.pdf):
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4e1594e5-4141-419c-8a3b-fb4d0cae5baf)


For example, suppose we build a database using the following queries:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE L0 (id INT64, PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE REL TABLE T0 (FROM L0 TO L0, id INT64);
CREATE (n0:L0{id : 2});
CREATE (n0:L0{id : 5});
MATCH (n0 {id : 5}), (n1 {id : 2}) MERGE(n0)-[r :T0 {id : 24}]->(n1);
MATCH (n0)-[r0]-(n1)-[r1]-(n2) WHERE true RETURN n0.id, r0.id, n1.id, r1.id, n2.id
```
And then run the Cypher query:
```cypher
MATCH (n0)-[r0]-(n1)-[r1]-(n2) WHERE true RETURN n0.id, r0.id, n1.id, r1.id, n2.id
```
There should be no result, as such a pattern does not exist if we do not count repetitive relations (assigning relation 24 to both r0 and r1), and other Cypher-based databases indeed follow this rule, for example Memgraph and neo4j:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7df01a3d-0a29-4b4e-84ed-e18598e2d5b8)

However, Kuzu violates this property and gives the result:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d8962a56-4df6-43a8-b7b1-714ce988db25)
Such inconsistency with the standard could cause trouble when programming with Kuzu. Fix would be very appreciated. Thank you!

This is how a `LOAD FROM` currently outputs a table in the Kùzu CLI.
```
kuzu> LOAD FROM 'test_data.csv' (header=true) RETURN *;
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
| id | amount   | counts | birthdate  | is_valid | comment                |
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

```

```
┌───────┬──────────┬────────┬────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────┐
│  id   │  amount  │ counts │ birthdate  │ is_valid │        comment         │
│ int64 │  double  │ int64  │    date    │ boolean  │        varchar         │
```

Here's how our query profile boxes look - it's already looking nicer than the CLI output does, and is arguably more readable. We already appear to be using continuous lines as table outlines, rather than chaining many hyphens.

```
││        Physical Plan         ││
│└──────────────────────────────┘│
└────────────────────────────────┘
```

title: CLI: Provide better error message when trying to open `READ_ONLY` connection when lock file is in use

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
Currently, we provide an error message that's not very helpful when a user tries to open a `READ_ONLY` connection to a database whose lock file is held by another process (e.g., a running Jupyter notebook or Python script).

This is our current CLI error message:
```
❯ kuzu ./db -r
Opened the database at path: ./db in read-only mode.
Enter ":help" for usage hints.
IO exception: Could not set lock on file : ./db/.lock
```
It just says "could not set lock on file", but that's not very helpful. Also, it says "opened the database" despite not doing so and producing an error, which is again, not helpful.

Instead, we could say something along the lines of the following:

```
❯ kuzu ./db -r
Error: unable to open database "./db": IO exception: Could not set lock on file : ./db/.lock
See the docs: https://docs.kuzudb.com/connections/concurrency for more information.
```
At least this would point the user to the actual cause and the docs page that helps them understand more.

Here's how DuckDB does it  -- it specifies the exact process ID that's conflicting and which user on the machine is the owner of that process, not sure if we can do that as well, but that would be great:

```
❯ duckdb ./test.duckdb --readonly
Error: unable to open database "./test.duckdb": IO Error: Could not set lock on file "./test.duckdb": Conflicting lock is held in /Users/prrao/.pyenv/versions/3.12.4/bin/python3.12 (PID 97844) by user prrao. See also https://duckdb.org/docs/connect/concurrency
```

title: UX: Allow read-only CLI when another process is holding the lockfile

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
### API

Other

### Description

## Use case
I have a common use case for Python data scientists as follows:
- User opens a Jupyter notebook and starts a `READ_WRITE` connection to Kùzu, and builds a graph
- User then wants to do one of the following: a) open Kùzu Explorer in `READ_ONLY` mode to query the graph visually, and/or b) open the CLI in `READ_ONLY` mode to query the graph interactively
- If there's something wrong with the data or if the data needs to be updated, the user runs more code inside the Jupyter notebook
- All this while, the lock file is held by the notebook (the same `READ_WRITE` connection and underlying process)
- To query the updated data, the user then closes and reopens the CLI or Kùzu Explorer, all the while taking care to specify `READ_ONLY` connection for these processes

## Issue
I'm going through this workflow and run into a problem with the CLI.
```bash
$ kuzu ./db -r
Opened the database at path: ./db in read-only mode.
Enter ":help" for usage hints.
IO exception: Could not set lock on file : ./db/.lock
```
Even though it says it's trying to open the DB in read-only mode, it fails to open the DB because the lock is held by the `READ_WRITE` process inside the Jupyter notebook. This seems far too strict - we're basically assuming the ultimate worst case (that the second process is also `READ_WRITE`, even though the user specified the `-r` flag when opening the CLI).

So from a user perspective, specifying the `-r` flag seems to do nothing when opening the CLI, or at least, doesn't do what it was aiming to do.

I think this is far too common a use case to resort to such a strict treatment where a CLI can't be opened if the lock file is held by a Jupyter notebook. To work around this, can we just assume that *any* process that is opened after an existing process holds the lock file should be read-only, and this is the user's responsibility to ensure that they don't open a second read-write connection? To make it more obvious, we could place a warning as follows:

```bash
$ kuzu ./db -r
Opened the database at path: ./db in read-only mode.
WARNING: The lock file ./db/.lock is being held by another process. This means that you are not guaranteed consistency of your data. To ensure proper consistency of your data, close the process that is holding the lock file and try again.
```
This would make it clear that any data corruption or lack of consistency is because the user ignored the warning and went ahead.

> [!NOTE]
> See the explanation below on why this is not a good idea, and is actually quite unsafe.

title: Optimization: `COUNT(*)` query takes a long time to complete
body:
### Description

I'm trying to count the number of relationships in the IMDB dataset once the data is fully ingested into Kùzu:
https://developer.imdb.com/non-commercial-datasets/

It has ~150M nodes and ~540M relationships.

```cypher
MATCH (n) RETURN COUNT(*)
```
The above query returns results almost instantly (<60 ms) for the ~150M nodes.

```cypher
MATCH ()-[]->() COUNT(*)
```

The above query to count the number of relationships takes much longer, ~3-4 mins to complete on my M3 Mac, and I get the answer of ~540M.

I think we should be able to replicate this relatively easily using LDBC, so that we can look to improve the performance of `COUNT(*)` when the user doesn't specify the relationship or node labels in the query.

### Description


**Description:**

Hi, I followed the documentation to build the LDBC dataset and performed SNB Interactive Queries. However, the query performance seems slower than expected as shown in this [paper](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p1011-jin.pdf). I would like to know if this behavior is expected or if I might be doing something wrong.

**Steps to Reproduce:**

1. Install Kuzu
 
I installed Kuzu by `pip install kuzu`, and the version is kuzu-0.4.2

4. Execute IC query ( I executed it with single-thread )

Take a simplified IC-6 as an example:
```
 MATCH  (p1:PERSON {id: 6597069812321})-[:PERSON_KNOWS_PERSON]-(p2:PERSON)<-[:POST_HASCREATOR_PERSON]-(m:POST)-[:POST_HASTAG_TAG]->(t1:TAG {name:'William_Wordsworth'}), (m)-[:POST_HASTAG_TAG]->(t2:TAG)  WHERE t2.name <> 'William_Wordsworth' RETURN t2.name;
```
It takes 3-4 seconds.


Questions:

1. Is this performance expected?
2. Could I be missing some optimizations or best practices (e.g., did I missing building necessary indexes)?
3. Are there any specific configurations or settings that might improve query performance?

**Environment:**
A Linux server with 52 cores, 371GB of RAM

title: Hash index support for MVCC
body:
Access to the hash index has been mostly moved into the node table so that it can handle visibility checks.
I've fixed a few (presumably) gcc-14-related compilation issues introduced by the mvcc-base branch.
I've also removed the dummy transactions in a couple places related to the hash index so that copying and lookups work properly.

I haven't benchmarked the performance impact of these visibility checks on the hash index yet. It should mostly affect lookups, since every positive lookup needs a visibility check, but since negative lookups don't, it shouldn't affect copy performance (except where there are lots of duplicate values from other transactions, but not the initial copy, or even multiple copies without anything in-between).

I also found dealing with access to the lowest level of the NodeTable a little confusing because of how the offset has to change each time to be relative to the beginning of each part, but they all basically take the same integer-based offset types as arguments (NodeTable->NodeGroup->GroupCollection<ChunkedNodeGroup>->ChunkedNodeGroup (and in this case to VersionInfo, but it would be similarly complicated to access the chunks)). In particular, one issue was that NodeGroup gives public access to its data through `getChunkedNodeGroup`, but I wasn't able to find the correct group without using the private `findChunkedGroupFromRowIdx`. I'll have to look in more detail at how everything is accessed, but it seems like having more restricted APIs for accessing the data would make them easier to work with and harder to make mistakes. Maybe using simple struct wrappers for the offsets so that they can't be confused. E.g. `struct GlobalOffset { offset_t offset; };` `struct NodeGroupOffset { offset_t offsetInNodeGroup; };`

title: Issue 3507
body:
# Description

We had faced many issues regarding parameter binding. I think it's just fundamentally hard to bind an arbitrary expression when the parameter type is not given (I.e. when we prepare the statement). I say "fundamentally hard" not because it's not doable but more because we have to go through all functions and expressions to handle & test the case. I don't think it's the right time to spend our engineering effort on this now.

I have moved to a new design where we skip the expression binding if we detect it contains a parameter expression whose data type is unknown. With this, we no longer need to worry about propagating ANY data type along expression binding.

I do anticipate more bug related to parameter because it may appear anywhere in a statement. So there must be missing pieces that we forget to handle. We can fix them as more bugs being report.

Fixes #3507 in a more proper way.

title: Feature: Auto-detect min/max values in DataFrame column to downcast integers

body:
### API

Python

### Description

Tested on 0.4.3.dev57

Say I have this input CSV (files attached as zip archive):
```
id,amount,counts,birthdate,is_valid,comment
a68a8af4-4a53-4420-9cb8-4a3e1fa0f324,3.635742,89,1990-01-01,true,"This is a test. "
55cfb01c-8cfc-4e3f-8408-05f362d7cf31,9.381905,57,2001-03-27,false,"This is another ""test"". "
9cddb5ae-e1d8-4382-b364-19b67e9a45a5,1.668131,29,2004-02-29,true,"This is (yet) another \"test\". "
```
I'd like to use the following schema for the node table that's created from the CSV:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE Item(
    id STRING,
    amount DOUBLE,
    counts INT32,
    birthdate STRING,
    is_valid BOOLEAN,
    comment STRING,
    PRIMARY KEY(id)
)
```
If I want the `counts` column to be INT32 instead of the default INT64, I have to manually cast it using `LOAD FROM` on the DataFrame as follows:

```
COPY Item FROM (
    LOAD FROM df
    RETURN
      id,
      amount,
      CAST(counts AS INT32),
      date
      is_valid,
      comment
)
```
There are two inconveniences here:
1. Just for casting the one column in the entire DataFrame, we have to explicitly write out every column name (which is verbose if we have 10+ columns, which is really common in real world data). If we don't do the manual casting, the `COPY` will fail.
2. The min/max integer information for a column in a DataFrame is already known beforehand, so Kùzu (in theory) can estimate the right integer type for this range, rather than the user having to manually cast the type by calculating their data ranges.

The provided code in the zip file shows how DuckDB does this - it seems to auto-detect the ranges of integers, downcasting the `INT64` type from Pandas/Polars DataFrame. Here's an example of DuckDB's output before (once the Polars df is read) and after (Outputting the results of a query and sending it to a Polars df).

Before:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┬──────────┬────────┬────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ id                              ┆ amount   ┆ counts ┆ birthdate  ┆ is_valid ┆ comment                        │
│ ---                             ┆ ---      ┆ ---    ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---                            │
│ str                             ┆ f64      ┆ i64    ┆ str        ┆ bool     ┆ str                            │
╞═════════════════════════════════╪══════════╪════════╪════════════╪══════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ a68a8af4-4a53-4420-9cb8-4a3e1f… ┆ 3.635742 ┆ 89     ┆ 1990-01-01 ┆ true     ┆ This is a test.                │
│ 55cfb01c-8cfc-4e3f-8408-05f362… ┆ 9.381905 ┆ 57     ┆ 2001-03-27 ┆ false    ┆ This is another "test".        │
│ 9cddb5ae-e1d8-4382-b364-19b67e… ┆ 1.668131 ┆ 29     ┆ 2004-02-29 ┆ true     ┆ This is (yet) another \test\.  │
└─────────────────────────────────┴──────────┴────────┴────────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
```
After (note how the `counts` column is now an `INT32`, which presumably came from DuckDB):
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┬──────────┬────────┬────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ id                              ┆ amount   ┆ counts ┆ birthdate  ┆ is_valid ┆ comment                        │
│ ---                             ┆ ---      ┆ ---    ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---                            │
│ str                             ┆ f64      ┆ i32    ┆ date       ┆ bool     ┆ str                            │
╞═════════════════════════════════╪══════════╪════════╪════════════╪══════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ a68a8af4-4a53-4420-9cb8-4a3e1f… ┆ 3.635742 ┆ 89     ┆ 1990-01-01 ┆ true     ┆ This is a test.                │
│ 55cfb01c-8cfc-4e3f-8408-05f362… ┆ 9.381905 ┆ 57     ┆ 2001-03-27 ┆ false    ┆ This is another "test".        │
│ 9cddb5ae-e1d8-4382-b364-19b67e… ┆ 1.668131 ┆ 29     ┆ 2004-02-29 ┆ true     ┆ This is (yet) another \test\.  │
└─────────────────────────────────┴──────────┴────────┴────────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
```

In Kùzu, we could potentially save a lot of user effort (and compress the data better, while also improving performance) if we auto-detect the integer ranges to downcast integer types to INT32 rather than defaulting to INT64 for every use case.

[files.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/16266357/files.zip)

### API

Python

### Description

Tried on version 0.4.3dev57.

When we return all properties in a `MATCH` query and we want to unpack the results into a DataFrame, the convention is to use the `.*` syntax as follows:

```py
conn.execute("COPY Item FROM df")
result = conn.execute("MATCH (n:Item) RETURN n.*")
print(result.get_as_pl())
```
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┬──────────┬──────────┬─────────────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ n.id                            ┆ n.amount ┆ n.counts ┆ n.birthdate ┆ n.is_valid ┆ n.comment                      │
│ ---                             ┆ ---      ┆ ---      ┆ ---         ┆ ---        ┆ ---                            │
│ str                             ┆ f64      ┆ i64      ┆ date        ┆ bool       ┆ str                            │
╞═════════════════════════════════╪══════════╪══════════╪═════════════╪════════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ a68a8af4-4a53-4420-9cb8-4a3e1f… ┆ 3.635742 ┆ 89       ┆ 1990-01-01  ┆ true       ┆ This is a test.                │
│ 55cfb01c-8cfc-4e3f-8408-05f362… ┆ 9.381905 ┆ 57       ┆ 2001-03-27  ┆ false      ┆ This is another "test".        │
│ 9cddb5ae-e1d8-4382-b364-19b67e… ┆ 1.668131 ┆ 29       ┆ 2004-02-29  ┆ true       ┆ This is (yet) another \test\.  │
└─────────────────────────────────┴──────────┴──────────┴─────────────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
```
The returned Pandas/Polars DataFrame will have header columns that always contain the variable name to which we bound the node type in the `MATCH` statement (`n.id`, `n.counts`, etc).

Here's how the same thing done in DuckDB will look:
```py
conn.execute("INSERT INTO item SELECT * from df")
result = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM item")
print(res.pl())
```
```
┌─────────────────────────────────┬──────────┬────────┬────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ id                              ┆ amount   ┆ counts ┆ birthdate  ┆ is_valid ┆ comment                        │
│ ---                             ┆ ---      ┆ ---    ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---                            │
│ str                             ┆ f64      ┆ i32    ┆ date       ┆ bool     ┆ str                            │
╞═════════════════════════════════╪══════════╪════════╪════════════╪══════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ a68a8af4-4a53-4420-9cb8-4a3e1f… ┆ 3.635742 ┆ 89     ┆ 1990-01-01 ┆ true     ┆ This is a test.                │
│ 55cfb01c-8cfc-4e3f-8408-05f362… ┆ 9.381905 ┆ 57     ┆ 2001-03-27 ┆ false    ┆ This is another "test".        │
│ 9cddb5ae-e1d8-4382-b364-19b67e… ┆ 1.668131 ┆ 29     ┆ 2004-02-29 ┆ true     ┆ This is (yet) another \test\.  │
└─────────────────────────────────┴──────────┴────────┴────────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
```

The column names are as per the input CSV file, which is convenient for downstream use.

## Desired outcome

Is it possible to automatically alias the column headers in Kùzu when using `a.*` to output all properties as tuples? This would make downstream usage so much easier as the user can just rely on the DataFrame column names being identical to the input CSV/DataFrames upstream.

title: MVCC checkpoint
body:
# Description

Enable checkpoint under MVCC changes. The auto checkpoint relies on the size of WAL file, which will be done in the recovery part.

The checkpoint is done as several steps: 1) flush out shadow files for catalog; 2) write shadow pages for node groups and hash indexes, also flush shadow metadata file (we now rewrite the whole metadata from scratch through serializer, which can be optimized later if we find this is becoming a bottleneck); 3) log CHECKPOINT record to wal;  4) replace shadow pages/files with original pages/files; 5) clear wal and clear all shadow files.
The checkpoint logic doesn't go through wal replay anymore.

Note that there are also minor changes to file names, during checkpoint, we flush out three shadow files: `catalog.shadow`, `metadata.shadow` and `.shadow`. The last one keeps all shadow pages for data.kz and index files.

The checkpoint is done in single thread for now, which can be optimized to be done in parallel for each node group in the future.
Replaying of shadow pages can also be done in parallel or in async I/O in the future.

Some refactoring along the changes:
- removed shadow pages from BMFileHandle. This simplifies BMFileHandle greatly.
- unified DUMMY_READ_TRANSACTION and DUMMY_WRITE_TRANSACTION into one DUMMY_TRANSACTION.
- added debugging interface for ser/deSer, which is annoying to debug. the interface can be optimized a bit more to propagate to all places in the codebase.

title: Fix lambda dependency analyze
body:
# Description

This PR reworks factorization dependency analyze so that we can evaluate lambda function properly. Consider the following example
```
-STATEMENT MATCH (a:person) WHERE a.ID < 6 RETURN a.age ,LIST_TRANSFORM([1,2,3], x->x + a.age)
---- 4
20|[21,22,23]
30|[31,32,33]
35|[36,37,38]
45|[46,47,48]
```
One of `x` and `a.age` needs to be flat. If `x` is flat, then we will fill result in the following order
```
[[21], [31], [36], [46]]
[[21, 22], [31, 32], [36, 37], [46, 47]]
[[21, 22, 23], [31, 32, 33], [36, 37, 38], [46, 47, 48]]
```

If `a.age` is flat, then the order if
```
[[21, 22, 23]]
[[21, 22, 23], [31, 32, 33]]
[[21, 22, 23], [31, 32, 33], [36, 37, 38]]
[[21, 22, 23], [31, 32, 33], [36, 37, 38], [46, 47, 48]]
```
We prefer the second case because write is sequential and easier to implement.

So this PR changes the dependency analyzer to make sure we always flatten `a.age` for lambda function.

title: Fix python struct and map type interpretation
body:
# Description

As desribed in #3814, python dictionaries are interpreted as `MAP` instead of `STRUCT`. This PR follows the duckdb way of translating python `DICT` to kuzu internal types.

The dict object can convert to either STRUCT(...) or MAP(..., ...) depending on its structure. If the dict has a structure similar to:
```
my_map_dict = {
    "key": [
        1, 2, 3
    ],
    "value": [
        "one", "two", "three"
    ]
}
```
Then we'll convert it to a MAP of key-value pairs of the two lists zipped together. The example above becomes a MAP(INTEGER, VARCHAR):
```
{1=one, 2=two, 3=three}
```
Otherwise we'll try to convert it to a STRUCT.
```
my_struct_dict = {
    1: "one",
    "2": 2,
    "three": [1, 2, 3],
    False: True
}
```
Becomes:
```
{'1': one, '2': 2, 'three': [1, 2, 3], 'False': true}
```


Fixes # 3814

title: Fix issue-3616
body:
# Description

Our RDF copy relies on the fact that literal primary key (SERIAL) aligns with row offset. Since we start materializing SERIAL and start parallel processing over SERIAL column. The  previous assumption no longer holds. I have set RDF literal copy pipeline back to single-threaded to enforce the assumption.

An alternative is to materialize literal primary key as INT64 instead of SERIAL. This however, will break `CREATE` because we will ask user to input a valid primary key for RDF literal instead of generating one internally. I found it quite a bit of work to do this internal generation so end up taking the easy approach.

The change of this PR is mostly refactor.

Adds a simple new GDSAlgorithm that reuses most of the shortest path logic that uses the PathLengthsFrontier and ShortestPathsAlgorithm. title: Optimize small rel table lookups
body:
Adds a random access version of `OnDiskGraph::scanFwd` which reads only the CSR header information necessary for the requested nodes.

I profiled `RelScanTestTwitter.TestRandomAccessScanMany` and compared it to a version using the other scan function, and `scanFwdRandom` was ~50 times faster `scanFwd` (I left the test since it covers some edge cases such as >2048 rels for a single node).

The underlying code in RelTableData still scans a single node at a time, and I think making it scan multiple could improve performance by an additional 50% or so when scanning multiple nodes within a single node group and there are few edges for the nodes scanned (currently initializeScanState is still taking >2x the time of the actual scan, and close to half of that is initialization which would be redundant for nodes in the same group). However that will be more complicated and the relative performance improvement is less significant than what this already achieves.

I've added a couple of simple unit tests that test OnDiskGraph directly, as none of the algorithms make use of the new function yet.

With demo dataset execute following query:

title: Making up for the lost worker thread in GDSTasks
Fix creation of new overflow slots when reserving space in the hash index
body:
When splitting slots to reserve space in the hash index it's possible (but unlikely) that the newly added slot will need an overflow slot, but adding such overflow slots was broken and keys put into them would be lost since the previous slot was not being set to point to them.
Unfortunately this is a quite rare occurrence and not easy to test.

*Should be testable using a bunch of keys (>1 slot) that collide for the hash index size used and rehash into a new slot. E.g. keys which hash into slot 0 with the default hash index size of 16 slots, and then all hash to slot 16 once enough other keys are added, forcing multiple slots to be created when slot 0 is split. My initial attempt was not failing on the master branch, so I suspect I made a mistake somewhere (Edit: initially forgot to make sure they all went into the same index)*.

title: Performance Bug: Scan rel is slow when bound node offsets are random
body:
### Kùzu version

master

### What operating system are you using?

_No response_

### What happened?

Currently, we assume scans of rel tables are sequential (bound node offsets are sequential), and cache the whole node group header (CSR lengths and offsets) ahead of actual scans. However, in cases like recursive joins and graph algorithms, the access pattern can be random and we lost the guarantee of sequential scans. 

Under these cases, we should take in a batch of bound node offsets (with the assumption that they are all sorted? this is to be decided by the caller, but this should be a reasonable gurantee to be provided), and have a smarter way of cacheing only necessary offsets and lengths from the node group header.

The optimization should be all done inside `initializeScanState` without the need of introducing another set of interfaces.

title: Fix issue-3730
body:
# Description

This PR removes the previous expression visitor and implement a new one that enables override. I start realizing different use case requires different way of visiting expression. For example,

when evaluating subquery, we don't collect subquery expression recursively. Instead we plan subquery recursively. E.g.
```
MATCH (a) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (a)->(b) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (b)->(c)}}
```

when collecting property, we do visit subquery expression recursively to find all properties.
```
MATCH (a) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (a)->(b) WHERE a.age = 10 AND EXISTS { MATCH (a)->(c) WHERE a.ID = 0}}
```

So the best approach is to abort the previous one-fit-all-purpose visitor.

Fixes #3730

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Based on David's [comment](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/2878#issuecomment-2212532367), when using the `DROP TABLE` command, it can be useful to check if the table exists prior to running the statement, otherwise it may result in a Runtime error.

title: Bug: Recursive relationship does not find node
body:
### Kùzu version

0.4.2

### What operating system are you using?

Fedora 39

### What happened?

Here is a minimal example:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE Topic (id UUID, PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE REL TABLE related (FROM Topic TO Topic);
CREATE NODE TABLE Tag (id UUID, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE REL TABLE GROUP has_tag (FROM Topic TO Tag, FROM Tag TO Tag);

CREATE (:Topic {id: gen_random_uuid()})-[:related]->(:Topic {id: gen_random_uuid()})
-[:has_tag]->(:Tag {id: gen_random_uuid(), name: "Kuzu"})
-[:has_tag]->(:Tag {id: gen_random_uuid(), name: "Database"});
```
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (n:Topic)-[*]->(t:Tag {name: "Database"}) RETURN n;
-----
| n |
-----
(0 tuples)
(1 column)
```
Expected: Both `:Topic` nodes are returned. Actual: None.

If I drop `related` rel table and its connected `:Topic` node, then results are as expected:
```cypher
CREATE NODE TABLE Topic (id UUID, PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE NODE TABLE Tag (id UUID, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (id));
CREATE REL TABLE GROUP has_tag (FROM Topic TO Tag, FROM Tag TO Tag);
CREATE (:Topic {id: gen_random_uuid()})-[:has_tag]->(:Tag {id: gen_random_uuid(), name: "Kuzu"})
-[:has_tag]->(:Tag {id: gen_random_uuid(), name: "Database"});
```
```cypher
kuzu> MATCH (n:Topic)-[*]->(t:Tag {name: "Database"}) RETURN n;
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
| n                                                                   |
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
| {_ID: 0:0, _LABEL: Topic, id: fbc994d8-4310-44ff-9ccf-36e7a90d1d3c} |
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
```

Issue seems not related to REL GROUPs - results are same, if I separate `has_tag` in two single relation tables.
Unfortunately I could not try with latest nightly cli, as there no x86_64 version.

title: Skip scanning null lists
body:
Null lists may have junk data in their offset/size which may not be safe to scan as it could be outside the bounds of the data (or produce underflows when calculating the extents)

I also removed the null columns on the offset/size as its duplicate information (which should actually make the data accurately store zeroes for null values, and zero-length lists are safe, but it would be useful to eventually allow the main null column to be used for storing offset/size column values).
