title: Feature: Support COPY from DataFrame

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Python

### Description

We currently support COPY from DataFrames via a subquery, whose syntax is a little inconvenient.
This works in v0.4.2:
```py
import shutil
import kuzu
import pandas as pd

shutil.rmtree("./testdb", ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database("./testdb")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'id': [1, 2, 3],
    'name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'age': [24, 25, 26]
})

conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE Person (id INT64, name STRING, age INT64, PRIMARY KEY (id))")
conn.execute("COPY Person FROM (LOAD FROM df RETURN *)")
res = conn.execute("MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.name, p.age")
print(res.get_as_df())
```
```
   id     name  age
0   1    Alice   24
1   2      Bob   25
2   3  Charlie   26
```

What we'd like to support at the earliest, is a more convenient way to directly populate the entire contents of a DataFrame (ideally both Pandas and Polars via the Arrow connector).

```py
# df could be either a numpy-backed Pandas DataFrame
# Or, df could be an Arrow-backed Pandas or Polars DataFrame
conn.execute("COPY Person FROM df")
```

title: Track ColumnChunk allocations through the BufferManager
body:
Implements #3660 (also see #3698)

I've merged the MemoryAllocator and MemoryManager; it wasn't obvious the purpose of the distinction (though it's occurred to me that we could have separate allocators for stuff using malloc like the ColumnChunks and our own allocator). Mainly I just wanted to avoid having to store separate references to the MemoryManager everywhere. The MemoryManager seemed better suited than the memory allocator to pass around to initialize column chunk buffers, however there wasn't an way of getting a MemoryManager from an existing buffer (just a MemoryAllocator). While I could have changed that, merging MemoryManager and MemoryAllocator seemed simpler.

Note that it was necessary to raise the buffer pool size used for the tests; that should be able to be lowered again once spilling to disk is implemented as part of testing that behaviour.

## Issues
I was having some issues with hanging instead of throwing exceptions when doing large rel copies with a restricted buffer pool size (looking at the behaviour when there is not sufficient memory). 
As far as I can tell, sometimes, with a large buffer pool of ~2000-3000 MB the hanging seems to be it continuously swapping out pages in the hash index. It may be that it will eventually throw an exception, but there sometimes is enough free memory for it to almost continuously try to do a small amount of work.

What's more concerning is that restricting the buffer pool size to the minimum 64MB on the same tests it will hang, and running it with backtraces will show a backtrace from a buffer manager exception (when looking up in the hash index; a couple of times it was the assert in freeUsedMemory), but that exception isn't stopping execution and it continues running with high CPU usage (possibly related to #3459).

I suspect that spilling to disk (#3698) will more or less solve these issues, as we generally shouldn't need to operate in such a memory restricted environment, and with spilling to disk ideally won't need to actually fail unless both disk and memory are full, but I'm concerned that we don't seem to be failing reliably in those circumstances.

title: Fix data race in eviction queue
body:
The candidate may be evicted by another thread between the first time it is checked (in `EvictionQueue::next`) and when it is loaded, in which case the pageState lookup will cause UB as the fileIdx will be out of bounds. 

After loading (and the check) it should be safe since even if the page is evicted in the background, we have a local copy of the candidate's data to safely look up the page state and the candidate will either be discarded for no longer being evictable according to the PageState, or get discarded in `tryEvictPage` once we notice it's already been evicted.

I also changed pagesEvicted to evictablePages for clarity, since they don't get evicted until the end of the function and the counter just tracks the number of candidates found.

title: Fix CI after lambda expression pr
Add list transform with lambda
body:
# Description

The `list_transform` function in openCypher (sometimes just called transform in some implementations) is a powerful list processing function that applies a transformation to each element of a list, returning a new list containing the transformed elements.

This PR implements `list_transform` with lambda function support.
The basic syntax is 
```cypher
list_transform(list, lambda_variable -> expression)
```

An example:
```cypher
RETURN LIST_TRANSFORM([5,28,92], x->x+ 10)
```

title: Deprecate CentOS 7 builder and restructure the build pipeline
body:
# Description

CentOS 7 has reached EOL on June 30 2024. GitHub self-hosted runner also [no longer supports CentOS 7](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners/managing-self-hosted-runners/about-self-hosted-runners#linux). This makes it impractical to maintain the CentOS 7 based self-hosted builders. In this PR we deprecate the CentOS 7 builders in favor of AlmaLinux 8. This change also causes some compatibility changes for the pre-compiled binaries:

- The produced binaries now requires at least Red Hat 8 / Debian 10 / Ubuntu 20.04 to run. Older distros are not supported.
- All of the produced binaries now uses new ABI. The support for old C++ ABI has been deprecated.

# Infrastructure Update
https://github.com/kuzudb/ci-deployment-compose/commit/2db6d11ba1ee40406085d661e56306fc15049dbc

This should be merged with the next release: 
https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu-docs/pull/173

title: Feature: Support negation in list operators

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Just tested in the latest nightly build (0.4.3dev41), and it seems like we do not support negation on the `IN` list operator.

Here's the query I want to run:

```cypher
MATCH (e)-[r]->(t)
WHERE r.type NOT IN ["IsFrom"]
RETURN *;
```

This should return all paths whose relation type is *not* `IsFrom`, but it produces the following error:

```
The evaluation of this query failed with the following error:
Parser exception: Query must conclude with RETURN clause (line: 1, offset: 0)
"MATCH (e)-[r]->(t)"
```

The following query, which is the reverse (returning only those relationships that are of type "IsFrom"), works:

```cypher
MATCH (e)-[r]->(t)
WHERE r.type IN ["IsFrom"]
RETURN *;
```

Can we also support negation on the `IN` operator?

title: Fix writing shared node groups to partially filled groups on disk in node batch insert
body:
Fixes #3714 

If every thread produces an incomplete node group, the shared node group will be used to write to the partially filled group on disk, which may need to write twice before the remaining tuples in the local node group can all be copied into the shared group.

I've also added a test that should be able to reproduce this with any number of threads.

title: MVCC for storage
body:
# Description

This PR reworks the storage and transaction for MVCC. 
We can support concurrent reads and writes at the same time. Though, we still restrict one writer at a time, which can be lifted later.
Besides, after this PR, write transactions won't trigger checkpoint right after they commit, instead, we checkpoint until: 1) a manual `CHECKPOINT` statement runs; 2) the size of wal file exceeds the checkpoint threshold.
This can greatly ease database size growth after write transactions and also increase the throughput of write transactions.

Two new options are introduced when starting the Database:
```cpp
bool autoCheckpoint = true, uint64_t checkpointThreshold = 16777216 /* 16MB */
```
These two options can also be configured through `CALL`.

## Main changes
The high level idea is described here (https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/2529).
In this PR, we organize the internal storage of node and rel table as `NodeGroup`s, which consists of `ColumnChunk`s. Each `ColumnChunk` can reside on disk or in-memory.
At the `NodeGroup` level, we maintain versioning info for creation and deletion of these tuples. And at the `ColumnChunk` level, we maintain update version chains. These are in-memory data structures to make sure we read the correct version of data in each transaction.
Introduced a separate `.shadow` file for checkpoint, and reworked how we write shadow pages.

## Minor changes
- Unifies `DUMMY_READ_TRANSACTION` AND `DUMMY_WRITE_TRANSACTION` into `DUMMY_TRANSACTION`.
- Removed `COMMIT_SKIP_CHECKPOINTING` and `ROLLBACK_SKIP_CHECKPOINTING` for testing, which instead now can rely on `CHECKPOINT` statement.
- `BufferedFileWriter` can now handle the case of writes larger than `BUFFER_SIZE`, which is needed for serializing large wal records.
- Added the infra of `writeDebuggingInfo` in Serializer. This can help with debugging our serializer and deserializer.

## TODO
- [x] This PR breaks the implementation of OnDiskGraph, which should be fixed in a later one.

title: GDS Parallelism Infrastructure
body:
# Description
This PR adds the mechanism to parallelize GDS Algorithms. This is done through static functions in a new GDSUtils class (gds_utils.cpp) using iterative frontier extensions. The overall execution paradigm is based on vertex-centric parallelism of graph algorithms of Pregel-like systems (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/1807167.1807184). Specifically the current abstraction is closer to Ligra's edgeUpdate function (https://people.csail.mit.edu/jshun/ligra.pdf).

Here are some details about the different interfaces:
- **GDSFrontier**: A frontier implementation that supports isActive, setActive functions to check if a node is in a frontier and put a node into a frontier. I named this GDSFrontier because there is a Frontier class in recursive_joins, which we will replace with GDS eventually. We should rename this simply to Frontier then. Assumed to support multi-label graphs.
- **Frontiers**: Maintains two GDSFrontiers, a current and a next one. Contains some auxiliary information, such as how many nodes are active in the next frontier and a helper function to getFrontierMorsels which are used by GDSUtils functions and GDSTask, which execute and parallelize GDS Algorithms. Contains some functions that require explanations, which I provided in code comments (e.g., `beginFrontierUpdatesBetweenTables(...)`). These are done for Frontiers implementations that may be using a single Frontier instance to store both the current and next frontier.
- **Graph**: This was already implemented and is the interface to scan neighbors of nodes. Assumed to support multi-label graphs.
- **FrontierUpdateFn** contains an` bool edgeUpdate(nodeID_t nbrID)`` function that implements the logic of what work to be done for a (u, v) edge, where u an active node and v is the neighbor. It describes the work to do for the neighbor. Eventually many new algorithms we implement will boil down to implementing this function or a similar function we are likely to add later called `vertexUpdate`. 
- **GDSUtils::runFrontiersUntilConvergence** & **GDSTask**: This is the main helper function to parallelize a GDS Algorithm that will run iterative frontier extensions until convergence or an upper bound number of iterations. The  inputs to `runFrontiersUntilConvergence` are `Frontiers frontiers`, `Graph* graph` and `FrontierUpdateFn& fu`. The function and FrontierTask implement the boilerplate logic of grabbing morsels from Frontiers and running the `fu.edgeUpdate` function on each (u, v) where u is an active node in the `curFrontier` of `frontiers`. More specifically, `runFrontiersUntilConvergence` breaks each iteration based on the one (src node table, rel table, dst node table) extension. That is if the input Graph (and Frontiers) is a multi-label, in each iteration i, for each rel table in the Graph, we do an extension. This is done so that when updating frontiers, we can fix the node table IDs of Frontiers from which we will read whether a particular node is active or to set a particular node active. 

Here is the main changes to shortest paths implementation. The functionality is still the same and only returns lengths. So this should really be called BFS. The main interfaces are:
- **PathLengths**: This is a dense GDSFrontier implementation that keeps a uint8_t for each possible node that can be in the frontier. A node u is active if its value is equal to `curIter`. Therefore, PathLengths needs to be given the `curIter` value from Frontiers class that wraps it, which is called `PathLengthsFrontiers`. To mark a node v as active, PathLengths sets its v's value to `curIter`+1.
- **PathLengthsFrontiers**: This is Frontiers implementation that uses a single PathLengths both as current and next frontier. There are several unintuitive consequences of this optimization. These are discussed in class comments.
- **ShortestPathsFrontierUpdateFn**: This is a simple function that basically marks the neighbor v active if and only if v is UNVISITED, which is represented with value 255 in PathLengths.

The rest of the code in shortest_paths.cpp is similar to before and connects this code to the frontend.

I have several questions to the reviewer about general coding style. The reviewer should look closely to whether the PR does the correct forward declarations and includes.

I'm keeping a list of next things to do here: https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/issues/3717

title: Optimization: Lightweight compression for in-memory materialized ColumnChunks
body:
### Description

`COPY` into a rel table can consume very large amount of memory for some large num of rels dataset. For example, https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~arb/data/colisten-Spotify/ and also the one mentioned in #3660.

The memory usage should mainly come from the design of partitioning and materializing all rel tuples first before constructing node groups in parallel, though more detailed profiling into memory usage is needed to figure out if we can squeeze unnecessary memory usage in some data structures.

To ease the peak memory usage, we should address/make several changes regarding to the rel batch insert pipeline:
- [x] Make memory allocation of ColumnChunk go through MM, thus the memory usage can be bound by BM (#3660).
- [x] Allow spilling to disk during partitioning, so we can sequentially read back each partition when constructing node groups in parallel. (Note that for the case a node group is very large, in the extreme case only one node group exists, we should optimize this further later with the segmenting design to chunk node group into more fine-grained storage units).
- [ ] Lightweight compression for in-memory materialized ColumnChunks. Either dynamically typed integer columns (i.e. switching between 8,16,32,64-bit integer values), or byte-packed integer columns (8, 16, 24, 32, ...). The advantage over bitpacking is that we would need to re-pack the data less frequently, and switching between natively supported types instead of packing could have a performance benefit. Both options would make interfaces more complicated since direct memory access would not generally work (e.g. unless we did the same thing with ValueVector, memcpy directly from ValueVector to ColumnChunk would not be possible since the types would have different sizes and we'd need to check the range of the new values).

title: Skip removing page candidates in the Database destructor
body:
Following up the issue mentioned in #3687, `EvictionQueue::removeCandidatesForFile` is somewhat slow, and running it on every open file when the database is destroyed slows things down noticeably (~200ms when I did a quick test creating an empty database, but probably more on DBs where data is in memory since it returns early once the eviction queue is empty). It should only be necessary when closing files if the BufferManager needs to continue being used, which is not the case when the Database is destroyed.
The same applies to removePageFromFrame since the memory region gets unmapped when the BufferManager is destroyed.

I don't particularly like this way of skipping the call, but the best alternative I can think of is to move the call out of the destructor and make it explicit when we remove files during normal database operations, but that will probably be harder to keep track of compared to automatic handling in the destructor.

title: Sqlite extension
body:
# Description
This PR implements sqlite extension with duckdb scanner as an intermediate.   The typing system in sqlite is completely different from us since sqlite only has the following types:

1. NULL. The value is a NULL value.
2. INTEGER. The value is a signed integer, stored in 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, or 8 bytes depending on the magnitude of the value.
3. REAL. The value is a floating point value, stored as an 8-byte IEEE floating point number.
4. TEXT. The value is a text string, stored using the database encoding (UTF-8, UTF-16BE or UTF-16LE).
5. BLOB. The value is a blob of data, stored exactly as it was input.

Sqlite is also using a [weakly typed database system](https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html), meaning that users can store a string in an int column. Duckdb currently throws an exception in such case.

Fixes #3682

title: Use 8-byte atomics in the eviction queue
body:
The new eviction queue from #3620 seems to have slowed down `BufferManager::removeCandidatesForFile`, in some cases significantly.
This may be more apparent on systems where libatomic (or whatever is providing std::atomic for 16-byte values) was not compiled with `-mcx16`/`-march=x86-64-v2` (or later microarchitectures) for use of the native cmpxchg16b instruction for 16-byte atomics. I'm not sure, but the macos runner is running particularly slowly, and this may be the cause (*edit: this seems to give a roughly 2x improvement on the macos runner for the tests in debug mode, so it's probably just really slow in debug mode in general; switching to release sped things up significantly; I'll change that in a separate PR*).

This PR removes the page ~~index~~ *state pointer* from the EvictionCandidate to make it an 8-byte atomic instead, and just uses the file and page index to look up the PageState.
It also makes removeCandidatesForFile return early if the queue is empty to minimize the cost of clearing files which haven't been used.

body:
### API

Other

### Description

DuckDB allows the [generation of date ranges](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/nested.html#date-ranges) using the `range` and `generate_series` functions. Below is an example for date range:

```
D SELECT * FROM range(DATE '2024-06-01', DATE '2024-06-03', INTERVAL '1' DAY);
┌─────────────────────┐
│        range        │
│      timestamp      │
├─────────────────────┤
│ 2024-06-01 00:00:00 │
│ 2024-06-02 00:00:00 │
└─────────────────────┘
```

It would be nice to support the `DATE` and `TIMESTAMP` type in the `range` function for cases where we want to quickly create a series with a start and end date without having to resort to datetime objects in the programming language.

#### Note

This would require that we also provide a grammar for the user to specify the interval between each value in the series, which may be a little more work, so this can be de-prioritized for later when we have the time.

title: Feature: Change `range` defaults and add `generate_series` function

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
## Features

- [ ] Change the default `stop` argument for `range` to be non-inclusive (similar to DuckDB and many programming languages)
- [ ] Add a `generate_series` function to allow the user to generate series inclusively (where the `stop` argument is the last value of the series)

### API

Other

### Description

Kùzu's `range` function is currently inclusive of the `stop` argument.

```
kuzu> RETURN range(1,3) AS r ;
-----------
| r       |
-----------
| [1,2,3] |
-----------
(1 tuple)
(1 column)
Time: 0.15ms (compiling), 0.30ms (executing)
```

This is not the case in DuckDB:

```
D SELECT range(1,3) AS r;
┌─────────┐
│    r    │
│ int64[] │
├─────────┤
│ [1, 2]  │
└─────────┘
```

For inclusive range, DuckDB provides an additional function `generate_series`, which behaves like our current `range` function in Kùzu.

```
D SELECT * FROM generate_series(1,3);
┌─────────────────┐
│ generate_series │
│      int64      │
├─────────────────┤
│               1 │
│               2 │
│               3 │
└─────────────────┘
```

title: [DO NOT REVIEW] Add create external table
body:
# Description

This draft is POC showing if we can directly model a graph from existing relational tables and querying them without loading entire dataset. It turns out we can if a load the following data

- primary key column of a (conceptual) node table
- foreign key columns of a (conceptual) relationship table

The former one is to create an internal node offset and a mapping from primary key to these offsets. The latter one is to create a CSR.

There are however, outstanding problems.

First, for columns in node table we can obtain by scanning relational table and join through primary key. But for relationship table we cannot do the same as there may not be a primary key column. We could do the same as our relationship table with is storing them together with CSR. The pros is it requires almost no additional work. While the cons is we end up materializing much more data internally.

Then we need to make a decision about if we want to build primary key index & CSR index only or we wanna build in-memory temporary table. The latter one makes more sense to me (or at least they require less change to the core).

Querying we multi-label is doable but probably require a specialized operator. I don't foresee us scanning tables from different database in one scan operator.

As for making it an extension, I suggest we do this at the very end. Although every component is extendable, we don't know what exact API needs to be extended until we solve the above problems.

title: Allow integer packing of numValues in a page that isn't a multiple of 32

### Description

Currently during integer bitpacking the number of values in a page must be a multiple of 32. This means that we leave extra space at the end of each page that could be used to store values, reducing our compression ratio.

title: Remove redundant CSRListEntries data
body:
The CSR offsets/lengths are also cached in the csrHeaderChunks. Pre-calculating them may have a slight benefit, as getCSRLength/getStartCSROffset handle a few edge cases which make them slower than just a memory lookup, but the differences are minor and pre-calculating them slows down small scans.

This reduces the cost of small rel table scans by more than half. E.g. in one query from the LDBC fintech sf1 dataset which was taking ~60s, largely as a result of doing many small rel table scans as part of a recursive join, this reduced it to ~30s in total (more improvements are possible; this was the easiest of them).

title: Dictionary compression is unnecessary for primary key columns
body:
E.g. copying the 41,652,230 IDs (as strings, but they're really just numbers) from the twitter-2010 dataset (warm copy to tmpfs) took 8.7s with compression enabled vs 5.7s with compression disabled. This isn't quite a perfect comparison, since that also disables compression on the integer columns storing the string indices and offsets, but the vast majority of the extra cost comes from checking for duplicates in the string data.

This isn't a huge amount of overhead in general, so it's acceptable for the most part, but for primary key columns it's unnecessary due to the constraint that primary keys are unique. However, there currently isn't an easy way of exposing that information to the copy pipeline.

title: Add compression for int128
body:
# Description

#3532

Add support for compression of int128_t using a bitpacking algorithm from [duckdb](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/main/src/storage/compression/bitpacking_hugeint.cpp).

Additionally, expanded the `int128_t` type + some utilities to support this.

# Testing

We have existing integration tests on the tinysnb dataset that use int128 or UUIDs (which are encoded with int128). There is no regression on these tests.

Additionally, unit tests were added (for example in `test/storage/compression_test.cpp`).

# Benchmarks

The INT128 benchmarks were conducted on two datasets, both with identical single-column schema `create node table person (ID INT128, PRIMARY KEY (ID));`. The results of the benchmarks will be compared to uncompressed + INT64 implementations.

The INT64 benchmarks were conducted on similar datasets but with column type INT64.

To conduct the benchmarks, a copy of the dataset is run and then a query.

```
PROFILE COPY person FROM "dataset/int128-db/vPerson.csv";
PROFILE MATCH (a:person) RETURN a.ID;
```

For the 1st dataset (constructed as **favourable for FOR + bitpacking**) the data column is `2^127 - NUM_NODES, ... 2^127 - 2, 2^127 - 1` so the bitpacking bitwidth should be appx. `log2(NUM_NODES)`

For the 2nd dataset (constructed as **unfavourable for FOR + bitpacking**) the data column is `1, 2^125 - 2, 3, 2^125 - 4...` so the bitpacking bitwidth should be 125 (For INT64, it will be 61).

Results are below, the logs referenced for the results are attached. I'll also summarize it in the comments.

title: [Draft PR] Parallel utils
body:
# Description

This is a draft PR for the Parallel Utils interface to be used for Algorithm library. `ParallelUtils` is the interface invoked to submit tasks to the main execution queue. All threads pick up the task pushed (function pointer saved inside the `GDSCallWorker` operator) and execute it.

Main files added for parallel utils:

(1) parallel_utils.cpp
(2) gds_call.cpp
(3) gds_call_worker.cpp
(4) parallel_shortest_path.cpp

- There is a main **GDSAlgorithm** class defined and all algorithms will override the **exec()** function. The exec function gets called from the `GDSCall` operator at runtime (only called by a single thread).  
- For parallel shortest path, we have 2 functions that need to be executed in parallel: **extendFrontierFunc** and **shortestPathOutputFunc**. We want both frontier extension and output writing to parallelize. 
- GDSCall is registered as a single threaded task, the first thread to register itself is the master that orchestrates the execution of the graph algorithm. It will call graphAlgorithm→exec() 
- **ParallelUtils** is defined inside GDSAlgorithm and gets called by the master thread to submit tasks to the task queue. To submit a task, **doParallel()** is called passing as arg the function to be executed in parallel.
- The other threads act as workers and pick up the new task from the queue. All local state for a thread is saved inside the `GDSLocalState` class (overriden later for algorithm specific state - `ParallelShortestPathLocalState`). 
- The return value for the executed function has to be the no. of tuples it wants to write to the Factorized Table. There are two FTables defined inside the GDSCallWorker - the localFTable and the main global results FTable (all threads have a reference to this through the `GDSSharedState`). 
- For the extend frontier parallel function, the threads do not explicitly write any results that need to be merged to the FTable, a `UINT64_MAX` val is returned to indicate this. In the parallel output case, threads return the no. of destination output values written to the value vectors. When no more morsels are present, a 0 is returned which indicates that the local FTable can be merged to the global FTable. 
 
### Parallelization Results (tested on spotify dataset)

Query - CALL shortest_path('spotify_n', 'spotify_e', 1, 30, 85) RETURN dst_offset, path_length;
Results - 3,592,911 tuples (unweighted bfs from node offset 85 to all nodes in the graph as destinations)

| Threads | Runtime (in seconds) |
|---------|----------------------|
| 1       | 16.91                |
| 32      | 2.15                 |

body:
### API

Other

### Description

Both Iceberg and Delta Lake are table formats for large, complex datasets. Both systems manage metadata, optimizes querying, and supports ACID transactions. They are designed to work on top of file formats like Parquet, ORC, or Avro. 

# Iceberg:
## Design goal: 
We are going to provide three utility functions to query: metadata, data, snapshot from a iceberg table.
1. Query individual iceberg table by providing the iceberg table path.  
`LOAD FROM iceberg_scan('data/iceberg/lineitem_iceberg', allow_moved_paths = true) RETURN *;`
2. Query the metadata of an iceberg table:
`LOAD FROM iceberg_metadata('data/iceberg/lineitem_iceberg', allow_moved_paths = true) RETURN *;`
3. Query the snapshot of an iceberg table:
`LOAD FROM iceberg_snapshots('data/iceberg/lineitem_iceberg') RETURN *;`
4. Together with HTTP extension, we could also scan from a remote iceberg table:
`LOAD FROM iceberg_scan('S3:/data/iceberg/lineitem_iceberg', allow_moved_paths = true) RETURN *;` 
## Feature to discuss:
5. Export to iceberg using cypher:
`COPY (MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(p1) return p, p1) to 'data/iceberg/lineitem_iceberg' (format=parquet)`

## Implementation:
We only have to implement three table functions and register them to the catalog using the `addFunction` API.
To make things simple, we are not going to implement the actual table functions by ourselves. We are going to use DuckDB as an intermediate layer instead.
When the user executes a Iceberg scan query, we are going to generate an equivalent SQL query. The SQL query is then sent to duckDB, and results will be converted to kuzu format.

# Delta lake:
I would suggest that we delay our implementation of Delta Lake since the support of Delta Lake on DuckDB is still experimental as well as the Delta Lake is still in its early stage.
## Design goal:
We only have to support the scan function for now:
`LOAD FROM delta_scan('file:///some/path/on/local/machine') RETURN *`

## Implementation:
Similar to Iceberg, we also use DuckDB as an intermediate instead of implementing one by ourselves.

title: Optimization: Scan rel optimization
body:
### Description

There are quite a few performance improvement left on table for scan rel, especially on sparse graphs, when the average size of csr list is small.

Optimizations can be done in two phases:
1. In the storage side, when we scan from rel table, currently, we only scan one csr list and at most 2048 tuples at one time. This is bad when the csr list is small, and usually they are smaller than 2048. The simple optimization we can do is to batch the reads of several csr lists altogether to 2048 tuples at a time, and the ScanRel operator can make use of SelVector to still output one csr list at a time into the pipeline.
2. The optimizer should be aware of the degree distribution and decide to not factorize, instead vectorize the scan, in which case we don't need to output one csr list at a time from ScanRel operator.

We should get the first optimization done first, which can give us some level of robustness guarantee in terms of scan performance against various graph distributions.

title: Feature: Unify REL TABLE GROUP with REL TABLE

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### Description

Back in the day, we added `REL TABLE GROUP` because our `REL TABLE` cannot have multiple `FROM,TO` pairs. While in practice, users do want to have one (conceptual) `REL TABLE` that connects multiple `NODE TABLE`s.

The expected usage of `REL TABLE GROUP` is to be a drop-in replacement for `REL TABLE` except for `COPY` (see the note below). We have issues like #3608 and #2929 asking about different behaviours between `REL TABLE GROUP` and `REL TABLE`. We can (and should) implement them. As I plan to get started on them, I think we might just do what #2914 suggested, where we do not keep a difference between `REL TABLE GROUP` and `REL TABLE` on the user's end. Instead, we keep `REL TABLE GROUP` as an internal concept that is generated automatically we see multiple `FROM, TO` pairs when creating a `REL TABLE`.

> [!NOTE]
> The problem with `COPY` is that we need to ask user to provide table name for each row, otherwise it's impossible to resolve the table deterministically.

```
MATCH (a:person) WHERE a.ID = 0 PROJECT GRAPH PK (person, knows) CALL shortest_path(PK, a, 2) RETURN a.fName, dst, length
```

title: Use a clock-based Buffer Manager eviction strategy
body:
Instead of queueing potential pages to evict when unpinning, all pages currently in memory are kept in the evictionqueue. When more space is needed, pages are evicted if they haven't changed since the last time we scanned them. The eviction queue is now only accessed when fetching pages from disk and has no global lock.

Fixes #2137

Based on the hash table implementation in the VMCache paper, except that we store page states by reference and for simplicity store the eviction candidates in a circular buffer instead of a hash table since lookups aren't necessary.

While this isn't the first place we're using atomics, GCC at least depends on libatomic for 16-byte compare and swap because it's not generating the 16-byte compare exchange instruction (cmpxchg16b) directly (see [the open bug](https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=94649), and also the [atomic docs](https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/Atomic/GCCMM/LIbrary)). Even with libatomic, it won't use cmpxchg16b without custom flags and instead uses a fallback (the `-mcx16` flag is for this specifically, but `-march=native` will also enable it if your CPU supports it or `-march=x86_64-v2` or newer). Benchmarks with `-mcx16` were almost identical, so I don't think this is much of a bottleneck (using 8-byte atomic eviction and insertion cursors should make it rare that two different threads are trying to evict or insert to the same spot anyway).

Performance improvements are minimal when there is plenty of buffer room.
I tried running some large copy benchmarks (two copies of 60M integers) with a restricted buffer, and found that the master version kept throwing buffer manager exceptions if I didn't give it a buffer pool of at least 1.5GB. With this version it works with the minimum buffer pool size of 64MB, and there was also a significant performance improvement when running this version with a 1.5GB buffer pool compared to the original.

Benchmarks are fairly rough; I ran each at least twice and averaged them (times are the first/second copies, each of 60M integers).

|   | master (ba0a6020e610) | this pr (07fcd85f) |
| ------------- | ------------- | -- |
| Unrestricted BufferPoolSize (~38GB)  | 4.4s/8.0 s  | 4.4s/7.8s | 
| BufferPoolSize = 1.5GB | 4.5s/23s  | 4.4s/13s |
| BufferPoolSize = 64MB | exception | 4.9s/24s |

title: Feature: Json type support

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
# Design goal
1. Support json in the kernel and use as if it is an internal type in the system.
e.g. DDL: 
`CREATE NODE TABLE PERSON (ID INT64, DESCRIPTION JSON)`
       Data Insertion: 
`CREATE (p:PERSON {ID: 5, DESCRIPTION: '{ "family": "anatidae", "species": [ "duck", "goose", "swan", null ] }'})`
2. Json can be install and loaded as an official extension using cypher queries:
`INSTALL JSON;`  `LOAD EXTENSION JSON;`
3. Support load from/copy from/ copy to  a json file.
e.g. `LOAD FROM 'test.json' RETURN *;`  `COPY (MATCH (p:person) return p.DESCRIPTION) TO 'test.json'`
4. Support common json utility functions:
e.g.  `json_keys(json[, path])`   `json_array_length(json[, path])`

## DataType registeration
Json will be implemented as user defined type in kuzu and stored in the catalog using the existing user defined type framework. Json can be treated as an alias for kuzu built-in type string, meaning that we store `JSON` as string on disk.
Can be registered as simple as:
```
catalog->createType(trx, "json", *LogicalType::STRING());
```

## Json parsing and traversing
We are going to use `yyjson` which is a high performance JSON library written in ANSI C.
yyjson takes in a json string and converts it into a json document as well as providing multiple ways to traverse the keys and values.

## DDL statement & create statement
1. DDL: `CREATE NODE TABLE PERSON (ID INT64, DESCRIPTION JSON)`
2. CREATE: `CREATE (P:PERSON {ID: 5, DESCRIPTION: '{ "family": "anatidae", "species": [ "duck", "goose", "swan", null ] }'})`

## Load from/copy from/ copy to
We have to refactor the load from/copy from/copy to use our table function framework. #3414 
Json extension should register the read/write function as table function and binder can choose the correct read/write function based on file type.
1. Load from: `LOAD FROM 'test.json'(format = 'array', other options...)  RETURN *;`
3. Copy from `COPY PERSON from 'test.json' (format = 'array', other options...);`
4. Copy to: `COPY (MATCH (p:PERSON) RETURN *) TO 'test.json'`

## Casting between JSON and built-in types
We can cast kuzu built-in types to json or cast JSON to other kuzu built in types:
```
CAST('{"kuzu": 42}', 'struct(kuzu integer)')     Result:  {'kuzu': 42}
CAST('{kuzu: 42}', 'json')      Result:  {'kuzu': 42}
```

## Utility functions
1. Json creation functions:

| Function                 | Description                                                                                     |
|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `to_json(any)`           | Create JSON from a value of any type. LIST is converted to a JSON array, and STRUCT and MAP are converted to a JSON object. |
| `json_array([any, ...])` | Create a JSON array from any number of values.                                                  |
| `json_object([key, value, ...])` | Create a JSON object from any number of key, value pairs.                                      |
| `json_merge_patch(json, json)` | Merge two JSON documents together.                                                          |


2. Json extract functions:

| Function                                           | Description                                                                                                      |
|-----------------------------------|--------------------------|
| `json_extract(json, path)`        | Extract JSON from json at the given path. If path is a LIST, the result will be a LIST of JSON.                  |
| `json_extract_string(json, path)` | Extract VARCHAR from json at the given path. If path is a LIST, the result will be a LIST of VARCHAR.            |

3. Json scalar functions:

| Function                                | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `json_array_length(json[, path])`       | Return the number of elements in the JSON array `json`, or 0 if it is not a JSON array. If `path` is specified, return the number of elements in the JSON array at the given path. If `path` is a LIST, the result will be a LIST of array lengths. |
| `json_contains(json_haystack, json_needle)` | Returns true if `json_needle` is contained in `json_haystack`. Both parameters are of JSON type, but `json_needle` can also be a numeric value or a string, however, the string must be wrapped in double quotes.                                  |
| `json_keys(json[, path])`               | Returns the keys of `json` as a LIST of VARCHAR, if `json` is a JSON object. If `path` is specified, return the keys of the JSON object at the given path. If `path` is a LIST, the result will be a LIST of LIST of VARCHAR.                     |
| `json_structure(json)`                  | Return the structure of `json`. Defaults to JSON if the structure is inconsistent (e.g., incompatible types in an array).                                                                                    |
| `json_type(json[, path])`               | Return the type of the supplied `json`, which is one of ARRAY, BIGINT, BOOLEAN, DOUBLE, OBJECT, UBIGINT, VARCHAR, and NULL. If `path` is specified, return the type of the element at the given path. If `path` is a LIST, the result will be a LIST of types. |
| `json_valid(json)`                      | Return whether `json` is valid JSON.                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `json(json)`                            | Parse and minify `json`.                                                                                                                                                                                    |

## Features to discuss:
### Operators:
1. Retrive key value: `SELECT j.family FROM example;`
2. Extract the family key’s value with a JSONPath expression: `SELECT j->'$.family' FROM example;`
3. Extract the family key’s value with a JSONPath expression as a VARCHAR: `SELECT j->>'$.family' FROM example;`

title: Take null values into account for copy statistics
body:
I've added additional tests to the copy rel statistics test, and also fixed a typo in tinysnb ("temprature" -> "temperature").
I also added special handling for bools in `column.cpp:getMinMax` since it was treating bool data as uncompressed instead of bitpacked.

This also uncovered an issue with the list columns, where we're assuming its safe to read null lists, where in reality that's only the case if the size is 0. Unfortunately, compressing data with nulls may result in null values being non-zero after decompression due to frame of reference compression and, well, ignoring null values when determining the range used for compression.

Here I've just made the ListColumnChunk use a size of zero for any null offset, though it may be useful to remove null chunks for columns which don't need them like the list size and column.

Fixes #3572 (again)

title: Decimal datatype
body:
# Description

Adds Arithmetic and Casting for the DECIMAL datatype
Arithmetic: Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, Division*, Modulo, Negation, Absolute, Floor, Ceiling
Casting: (other numeric) <-> DECIMAL, STRING <-> DECIMAL, MaxLogicalType for DECIMALS

*For division, since finding a good resulting precision+scale pair was not easy or intuitive, and since DuckDB doesn't implement decimal division, decimal division is implemented but not enabled. Instead, decimals are implicitly casted to double, which is then used to compute division.
Similarly, decimal comparison isn't directly implemented. It defers to double comparison through implicit casting.

The Decimal Datatype hasn't been exposed on any API besides the arrow APIs. On top of that, the most straightforward way of accessing decimals fails:
```
RETURN CAST(123, 'DECIMAL');
```
gives a null result because of some unknown bug. The current workaround used in tests is
```
UNWIND [123] AS A RETURN CAST(A, 'DECIMAL');
```
Overall, the datatype is not complete.

Update: the bug has been fixed.

### Kùzu version

I'm using Python to load data dynamically and would like to do so in a single transaction. However, I can't link the nodes with serial primary keys, as such keys are not searchable until the transaction is over. See steps to reproduce with a Python code snippet.

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

```python
import kuzu

print(kuzu.version)

db = kuzu.Database("./demo-db")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE MyNode (uid SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY(uid))")
conn.execute("CREATE NODE TABLE MyOtherNode (uid SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY(uid))")
conn.execute("CREATE REL TABLE MyRel (FROM MyNode TO MyOtherNode)")

conn.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION;")

res1 = conn.execute("CREATE (n:MyNode) RETURN n.uid")
node1_id = None
while res1.has_next():
    node1_id = res1.get_next()[0]

res2 = conn.execute("CREATE (n:MyOtherNode) RETURN n.uid")
node2_id = None
while res2.has_next():
    node2_id = res2.get_next()[0]

# if these 2 lines are uncommented - the code will work
conn.execute("COMMIT;")
conn.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION;")

conn.execute("""
MATCH (i1:MyNode {uid: $from_node}), (i2:MyOtherNode {uid: $to_node})
CREATE (i1)-[:MyRel]->(i2)
""", {
    "from_node": node1_id,
    "to_node": node2_id,
})

conn.execute("COMMIT;")

results = conn.execute("MATCH (n:MyNode)-[:MyRel]->(m:MyOtherNode) RETURN n.uid, m.uid")

if not results.has_next():
    print("No results found")

while results.has_next():
    n_id, m_id = results.get_next()
    print(f"Found nodes {n_id} -> {m_id}")
```

title: Track variable sized memory manager allocations through the buffer manager

To follow up the missing part of #3243, this adds BufferManager tracking for variable-sized memory allocations made through the MemoryManager.

I also noticed that the buffer manager wasn't freeing the memory related to evictions if it fails to allocate the total amount of memory requested when claiming a frame. I don't know how much of our code at the moment can safely recover from failing to claim memory and continue allocations though, so it may not make a difference at the moment. I had noticed subsequent failures which seemed to be related to data not being successfully written in the multi copy test that was failing due to not having enough memory in #3557 (e.g. accessing out of bounds in a hash index disk array, which I think would have been in bounds if the data had been updated correctly), so at the moment it may not always be possible to continue using the database after such a failure.

title: String and List Column Structure

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
String and list columns currently have an int column as their primary column (uint64 and uint32 respectively). That means that in a number of places we have code to handle the fact that `PhysicalTypeID::STRING` and `PhysicalTypeID::LIST` are actually handled like integer columns.
It would simplify the code in a bunch of places if the main columns (for strings it's the index column, for lists its the offset column) were moved into child columns (similarly to the existing data/offset/size columns), and the main columns were instead empty like for struct columns.
This would also make it possible to store statistics for string columns, since the statistics are currently being used for integer compression, and would free up the metadata on the main string column to store the minimum and maximum string indices.

title: Disk array packed headers
body:
Packs the disk array headers into as few pages as possible (each header page points to the next one to support adding new disk arrays to the disk array collection) and packs the hash index headers into two pages.
I've also fixed some padding issues related to #3484, but there still seems to be a small amount of uninitialized data in the main hash index file (either due to something in the slot, or maybe related to the disk array write iterator).

A new class DiskArrayCollection gets passed around with the MetadataDAHInfo structure since the indices no longer refer to individual pages that can be easily read independently. Instead the DiskArrayCollection reads all the headers when initialized and the MetadataDAHInfo provides the index of the header for a particular chunk and an easy way of constructing the disk array.

title: Proposal: ListAggregate framework

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
### API

C++

### Description

This proposal is to improve the performance and deduce code duplication of list aggregation. Our ultimate goal is to reuse the aggregate functions on list aggregations.

## Current design of aggregate operator:
(Let's use sum as an example):
1. Init stage:
When the compute starts, each thread will firstly init a local buffer called aggState, which stores intermediate state during computation. For example:  
```
    struct SumState : public AggregateState {
          T sum;
    };
```
2. Update stage:
For each input value, we are going to update the state using the `update` method of the aggregate function. For sum, we only have to add the sum to the input value.
3. Finalize stage:
When a thread has exhausted its input, it is going to call the `finalize`  method to finalize its state and wait for combine stage.
4. Merge stage:
Finally, when each thread has finished computation, we are going to merge the aggregagte state using the `combine` method of the aggregate function.

## Feature1.
Add a new function: `list_aggregate(list, aggregate_type)`.
The aggregate_type parameter can be any aggregate function that we currently support: sum, avg, collect.
Implementation:
1. Frontend:
    a. Register list_aggregate to catalog
    b. Bind the aggregate function based on the aggregate_type. (TODO: XIYANG)
2. Backend:
Implement a new execFunction for list_aggregate:
```
void listAggExecFunc(
        const std::vector<std::shared_ptr<common::ValueVector>>& params,
        common::ValueVector& result, void* dataPtr);
```
The first vector in the params should store the list while the dataPtr stores the aggregate function pointer.
Similar to the aggregate operator, 
1. Init stage:
Initilaize a vector of aggregate states whose size equals to the number of lists in the vector.
2. Update stage:
We are going to loop through each element of each list, and update the agg state using the `update` method.
3. Finalize stage:
We loop through each aggreagte state, and call `finalize` on them. 
4. Finally, we write the finalized state to the output vector.

## Feature 2.
Frontend should rewrite all list aggregate functions (e.g. `list_sum`, `list_avg`) to reuse the `list_aggregate()` function.

title: Rework scan node
body:
## Description

Rework scan table's task morsel from a Vector to a NodeGroup.
More detailed items:
1. Removed ScanNodeID operator. Scan over node tables are no longer driven by node offsets, instead by the combination of node group id and the vector id within the node group.
2. Unify scan single label and multi label node tables into a single operator `ScanNodeTable`, which is now a source operator.
3. Removed `originalSize` from `DataChunkState` and `isSequential` from `ValueVector`. These two fields were used to indicate the size of a scan, and if the scan turns out to be point lookup, respectively. They were difficult to understand and no longer make sense now.

## Fixes
- #2257 and #2647. We no longer read more than actual data from committed persistent storage.

## Minor changes
- Cleaned the organization of `TableScanState` and `TableDataScanState` a bit.
- Removed `numBytesPerFixedSizedValue`, which was a legacy field used by `StorageDriver`, from `Column`.
- Try to add more `const` qualifiers.

## What's broken/disabled and what's to be further optimized
- [x] Filter push down on node tables. This should be reworked altogether with the zonemap optimization.
- [x] Index scan optimization. Will turn this back soon. Should separate `scan` and `lookup` interface in the storage side as callers are always sure which one they want. (currently we encapsulate both into `read` interface, which is no longer necessary).
- [x] Semi mask. Will add this back soon.
- [x] Read of node properties within the recursive join computation is broken.
- [x] Update pk (or columns with indexes) should scan its original values along the scan of node offsets. Original values are required as keys to update the indexes.
- [x] Rework ScanRelTable to scan one vector at a time.
- [x] String dictionary cache. When the dict is small, we should cache the dict chunks in advance when we initialize the scan state.

## Benchmarks
Done on `uw5` under `ldbc100` dataset and default settings from shell.

```
Q1: MATCH (comment:Comment) RETURN MIN(comment.length), MIN(comment.locationIP), MIN(comment.browserUsed), MIN(comment.content);
Q2: MATCH (p:person)-[e:likeComment]->(c:comment) RETURN MIN(e.creationDate);
Q3: MATCH (c1:comment)-[e:replyOfComment]->(c2:comment) RETURN COUNT(*);
```

|  | Cold Run (master) | Cold Run (this) | Hot Run (master) | Hot Run (this) |
-- | ---- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Q1 | 5436ms | 4304ms | 1149ms | 1027ms |
| Q2 | 1058ms| 1057ms | 139ms | 603ms |
| Q3 | 12094ms | 2224ms | 5460ms | 621ms |

title: Unexpected slowness: Self join
body:
### Kùzu version

v0.4.0

### What happened?

As a toy example, I tried a self join (Python snippet below). I'm interested in creating edges when some sets of columns are equal.

I found that with a 100k row table, I ran out of patience with KuzuDB, but DuckDB handled it in ~10s. 

Out of context snippets:

```
# KuzuDB join
MATCH (n:{left_table}), (m:{right_table})
WHERE n.{left_key} = m.{right_key}
CREATE (n)-[:{rel_table}]->(m)
```

```
# DuckDB join
    join_pl = duckdb.sql(
        "SELECT left_pk, right_pk FROM left_pl JOIN right_pl ON right_key = left_key"
    ).df()
    conn.execute(
        f"COPY {rel_table} FROM (LOAD FROM join_pl RETURN *)"
    )
```

### Are there known steps to reproduce?

# 1. Make PersonData100k.csv

```
# python make_persondata100k.py > PersonData100k.csv
from random import randint
from faker import Faker
fake = Faker()
def Person():
  return (
    fake.first_name(),
    fake.last_name(),
    randint(18, 100),
  )
data = [Person() for _ in range(100000)]
# print data as csv
print("first_name,last_name,age")
for row in data:
  print(",".join(map(str, row)))
```

# 2. Create a node table for PersonData100k.csv and import the data

```
# kuzu ./test
CREATE NODE TABLE PersonData100k(first_name STRING, last_name STRING, age INT64, rowid SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY(rowid));
COPY PersonData100k FROM "PersonData100k.csv" (HEADER=true, DELIM=",");
```

# 3. Use the sample code to compare duckdb_join and kuzudb_join

Uncomment one of the lines at the end.

```
import kuzu
import duckdb

db = kuzu.Database("./test")
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

def duckdb_join(left_table, left_pk, left_key, right_table, right_pk, right_key, rel_table):
    left_result = conn.execute(
        f"MATCH (n:{left_table}) RETURN n.{left_pk} as left_pk, n.{left_key} as left_key"
    )
    left_pl = left_result.get_as_pl()
    right_result = conn.execute(
        f"MATCH (n:{right_table}) RETURN n.{right_pk} as right_pk, n.{right_key} as right_key"
    )
    right_pl = right_result.get_as_pl()
    join_pl = duckdb.sql(
        "SELECT left_pk, right_pk FROM left_pl JOIN right_pl ON right_key = left_key"
    ).df()
    try:
        conn.execute(
            f"CREATE REL TABLE {rel_table}(FROM {left_table} TO {right_table})"
        )
    except:
        pass
    conn.execute(
        f"COPY {rel_table} FROM (LOAD FROM join_pl RETURN *)"
    )

def kuzudb_join(left_table, left_pk, left_key, right_table, right_pk, right_key, rel_table):
    try:
        conn.execute(
            f"CREATE REL TABLE {rel_table}(FROM {left_table} TO {right_table})"
        )
    except:
        pass
    conn.execute(
        f"""
        MATCH (n:{left_table}), (m:{right_table})
        WHERE n.{left_key} = m.{right_key}
        CREATE (n)-[:{rel_table}]->(m)
        """
    )

import time
start = time.time()
# Uncomment one of these lines
#duckdb_join("PersonData100k", "rowid", "first_name", "PersonData100k", "rowid", "first_name", "SELF_JOIN_DUCKDB")
#kuzudb_join("PersonData100k", "rowid", "first_name", "PersonData100k", "rowid", "first_name", "SELF_JOIN_KUZUDB")
end = time.time()
# Print seconds
print(end - start)
```

title: Binary datasets
body:
Instead of storing binary datasets in the git repository, it might be a better idea to generate them as CI artifacts and share them between pipelines when they are used for compatibility tests. 

That would remove the need to regenerate them and clutter the repository with large binary artifacts (and also mean that the compatibility tests could use larger datasets more easily).

On the other hand it will add some CI pipeline dependencies that overall may slow down the pipelines (the job generating the database would need to be run before other jobs which use the database are started, and that job will need to build kuzu), but it looks like most of the build steps are only taking about a minute, so it shouldn't be too much of a slowdown.

*Edit: It's also really annoying to have to deal with the binary database tests locally when making changes which break storage, as short of updating the version number every time you make a change, there's nothing preventing it from running on the old database and potentially allocating arbitrarily large amounts of memory when data isn't where it should be. It might be better to have those tests be disabled by default and just run in CI*

title: RuntimeError: Binder exception: Variable __existence already exists.
body:
Hi, above error can be reproduced by following snippet:

```python
import kuzu
from uuid import uuid4
import tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as dbpath:
    conn = kuzu.Connection(kuzu.Database(dbpath))
    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE NODE TABLE T (id UUID, PRIMARY KEY(id));
        CREATE NODE TABLE U (id UUID, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY(id));
        CREATE REL TABLE has (FROM T TO U);
        """,
    )
    # Prerequirement: existing :T
    tid = uuid4()
    conn.execute("CREATE (t:T {id: $id}) RETURN t;", {"id": tid})

    # Merge :U from memory (new here, but might already exist)
    uid = uuid4()
    conn.execute(
        """
        MATCH (t:T {id: $tid}) // (1)
        MERGE (u:U {id: $uid}) // (2)
        SET u.name = $name     // (3)
        MERGE (t)-[e:has]->(u)
        RETURN t,u,e;
        """,
        {"tid": tid, "uid": uid, "name": "foo"},
    )
```

Some background for clarification:
Goal was to construct a simple kind of object graph mapper (OGM) with `MERGE`: Given entities `T`,`U` with composite relation `(:T)-[:has]->(:U)`, try to merge a new or existing `U` from memory.
(1) ensures `:T` exists
(2) merges an `:U` by its identifier (otherwise `MERGE` would try to create a new entity, if any property has changed)
(3) update all `:U` properties in database (assuming object memory has most recent version or creates new entity)

Kuzu 0.4.2

title: Fix serial csv reader
body:
This PR solves a bug in the serial csv reader.
[Cause]
uint64_t numRows = reader->parseBlock(0 /* unused by serial csv reader */, outputChunk);
We pass block 0 to reader::parseBlock, however the block number is used by reader in the following way:
When the csv file has a header and the block number is 0, we are going to skip the first row in that block.
As a result, the serial csv reader will always skip the first row of each row.

[Fix]
We have to distinguish whether it is the first block. We can tell this by fileoffset of the reader.

Closes #3504

title: Serial vs. parallel COPY FROM yield different node counts when importing from CSV file

labels.name: area: import-export
labels.description: Issues related to data importing or exporting, such as copy to/from statements

body:
The number of lines in this CSV files as output by `wc -l` yields 14196 lines (excluding the header).

[postcode.csv](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu/files/15326739/postcode.csv)

However, when we read the CSV file into Kùzu using `COPY FROM` with parallelization disabled, the counts do not add up -- we obtain only 14190 nodes (6 nodes are missing). When parallelization is enabled in the CSV reader, the node count is correct, i.e., we get 14196 as expected.

## Code to reproduce

### Serial copy

```py
import shutil
import kuzu

shutil.rmtree('./db', ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database('./db')
conn = kuzu.Connection(db, num_threads=1)

conn.execute("""
CREATE NODE TABLE PostCode(
    node_id STRING,
    code STRING,
    PRIMARY KEY (node_id))
""")

# import nodes
conn.execute('CALL THREADS=1')
conn.execute('COPY PostCode FROM "./data/postcode.csv" (HEADER=true, PARALLEL=false)')

queries = [
    'MATCH (n:PostCode) RETURN count(n)',
]

for query in queries:
    results = conn.execute(query)
    while results.has_next():
        print(results.get_next()[0])
```
Result (Incorrect):
```bash
$ python test.py
14190
```

### Parallel copy

```py
import shutil
import kuzu

shutil.rmtree('./db', ignore_errors=True)
db = kuzu.Database('./db')
conn = kuzu.Connection(db, num_threads=0)

conn.execute("""
CREATE NODE TABLE PostCode(
    node_id STRING,
    code STRING,
    PRIMARY KEY (node_id))
""")

# import nodes
conn.execute('COPY PostCode FROM "./data/postcode.csv" (HEADER=true)')

queries = [
    'MATCH (n:PostCode) RETURN count(n)',
]

for query in queries:
    results = conn.execute(query)
    while results.has_next():
        print(results.get_next()[0])
```
Result (correct):
```bash
$ python test.py
14196
```

title: Make serializer tool able to be run standalone
body:
The serializer tool now works on the datasets in the dataset directory by using `schema.cypher` and `copy.cypher` if they are available. Argparse is used for a more readable CLI, and it should be compatible with the original arguments as their order hasn't changed (the log directory is now optional, and there's a new argument for single-threaded mode).

Also adds a script to generate the binary db, both for #3484 and because it needs to be updated for #3498 (which breaks the storage format) as I noticed there isn't any easy way to update the dataset.

The changes in the output included here are I think from #3471. The catalog also seems to have flipped the order of the "User" and "Follows" tables. I suspect this is because they are stored in memory in an `std::unordered_map` and serialized in the order produced by iteration, which won't be consistent across different stdlibs.

title: Disk array builder cleanup
body:
This separates the InMemDiskArrayBuilder from BaseDiskArray, renaming both to BlockVector and DiskArray, respectively.
The Hash index disk arrays are now initialized more similarly to the ColumnChunkMetadata disk arrays, using `addDAHPageToFile` instead of relying on flushing an empty builder.
It was necessary also to remove the reserved element 0 of the overflow slots (so that the overflow disk arrays can be initialized just with the headers). Invalid overflow slots are now represented by `UINT64_MAX`.

The Hash index headers are now being handled separately instead of using the disk arrays since they don't need the ability to be resized (removing the need for a header page and page index page for each header, which reduces disk usage a bit; I have further changes to reduce header sizes to follow this PR).

title: Binary Reproduceability
body:
In addition to testing databases created on one platform on different platforms, it would be useful to do direct binary comparisons between the databases (when produced in single threaded mode). That will help cover gaps in the coverage of the binary database tests, and can also enforce that kuzu's output is deterministic and the data is being properly initialized.

It could be implemented by creating a new database alongside the binary database tests, and comparing them with something like `diff -r` from GNU diffutils. An older version of diffutils is available for windows [here](https://gnuwin32.sourceforge.net/packages/diffutils.htm) (or via chocolatey).

title: Python UDF and C++ UDF improvements
body:
Changes:
- UDFs now evaluate to null by default when any one of the parameters is null. This is changeable via the `default_null_handling` parameter
- Exceptions can now be caught from python functions via the `catch_exceptions` parameter. When an exception is caught, the function is evaluated to null
- UDFs can now be removed, both in the C++ and in the python API via `removeUDFFunction` and `remove_function` respectively.

C++ UDF API now supports zero parameter functions, but this is an experimental feature (ie. not tested very well)

title: Merge the HashIndex bulkstorage with the local storage for inserts
body:

It was necessary to make the InMemHashIndex support deleting keys, which maintains the lack of gaps in the in-memory hash index by swapping deleted entries with the last entry.

title: Binder Exception when reading ARRAY type from Parquet (for embeddings)

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
I'm pushing typecasting to the limit here 😅. Am basically trying to ensure I have fine-grained control over each column's data type all the way from Python to Parquet and then into Kùzu. My aim is to replicate a typical Python workflow that would be used in similarity search.

## Dependencies

I'll be using `sentence-transformers` to generate embeddings from raw text, as is common in many real-world scenarios. 

```sh
pip install pyarrow polars kuzu sentence-transformers
```

## Code

I first write out the vectors computed by an embedding model (from `sentence-transformers`) alongside the raw data to Parquet, so that I can bulk-import the data to Kùzu (computing vectors/embeddings via a model is expensive, so this would be pre-computed in a real scenario).

Note that I explicitly typecast the integers from Python (by default `INT64`) to `UINT64` so that I can have unsigned integers in Kùzu per the graph schema below.

```py
import os
import shutil
import kuzu


def create_db(conn):
    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE NODE TABLE Person(
            id UINT64,
            name STRING,
            age UINT8,
            PRIMARY KEY (id)
        )
        """
    )

    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE NODE TABLE Item(
            id UINT64,
            name STRING,
            vector DOUBLE[384],
            PRIMARY KEY (id)
        )
        """
    )

    conn.execute(
        """
        CREATE REL TABLE Purchased(
            FROM Person
            TO Item
        )
        """
    )


def write_data_to_parquet():
    import warnings
    import polars as pl
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

    model = SentenceTransformer("Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-xs")

    persons = [
        {"id": 1, "name": "Karissa", "age": 25},
        {"id": 2, "name": "Zhang", "age": 29},
```

title: Refactor ftable schema
body:
- Split `FTableSchema`, `FactorizedTableUtils` into their own files.
- Move `dataChunkPos` out of `ColumnSchema`. The previous design simply doesn't make sense. We now maintain this information at `FTableSchema`. The high level idea is that `FTableSchema` contains multiple `ColumnSchema` and also multiple `Group`. Each `ColumnSchema` belongs to one `Group`. If multiple `ColumnSchema` belongs to the same `Group` then they must share the same `Group` metadata, i.e. flat information. There is still more work to do, for example we should make `GroupID` consecutive instead of using `DataChunkPos`. But this needs to be done progressively.
- Remove unnecessary unique_ptr
- Protect implicit copy with EXPLICIT_COPY macro.

title: Silent failure in Postgres extension when using unsupported type

labels.name: type: usability
labels.description: Issues related to better usability experience, including bad error messages

body:
I'm noticing silent failure of the Postgres table scan when using an unsupported type (Kùzu doesn't tell me there's an issue, but the table isn't listed as available even though it exists in Postgres)

I have a Postgres schema in which I want to use the `DECIMAL` data type to represent money values correctly with exactly two decimals, and with 6 significant digits. Here's my desired schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS wines(
    wine_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(1028) NOT NULL,
    variety VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    points SMALLINT,
    price DECIMAL(6, 2)
)
```

When I load this data into Postgres, I verify that the table exists, and my SQL query to list the data works.

However, when I list the table in Kùzu's Postgres extension via `CALL show_tables() RETURN *`, the table doesn't appear (it's not accessible via the schema cache, presumably because Kùzu doesn't correctly cast the `DECIMAL` type in Postgres to our internal representation of `DOUBLE`).

I know this is the case, because when I replace the `DECIMAL(6,2)` with a `FLOAT8`, i.e., the following schema, it works:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS wines(
    wine_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(1028) NOT NULL,
    variety VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    points SMALLINT,
    price FLOAT8
)
```

Then, the table appears in Kùzu as follows:

```
┌────────────────┬──────────┬────────────────┬─────────┐
│ name           ┆ type     ┆ database name  ┆ comment │
│ ---            ┆ ---      ┆ ---            ┆ ---     │
│ str            ┆ str      ┆ str            ┆ str     │
╞════════════════╪══════════╪════════════════╪═════════╡
│ wines          ┆ ATTACHED ┆ wine(POSTGRES) ┆         │
└────────────────┴──────────┴────────────────┴─────────┘
```

## Desirable behaviour

If, for some reason, the table that exists in Postgres can't be scanned in Kùzu, we should display an appropriate error so that the user knows something is wrong. In this case, it's not clear why switching the price schema from `DECIMAL(6,2)` to `FLOAT8` actually worked, so that's something to test out.

In the longer run, we should extend support for specialized Postgres data types (like `NUMERIC` or `DECIMAL`) as handling money values in Postgres should never be done with `FLOAT4` or `FLOAT8` as it's fundamentally imprecise due to floating point precision limitations.
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15726535/which-datatype-should-be-used-for-currency

Not only was the type of the value being used for the bit shift not wide enough (the characters are `char`s, but the result of a bitshift seems to always be at least `int`), but it was signed, and signed bit shifts may add new bits as 0 or 1 depending on the implementation, which I think is causing the difference among the platforms.

title: Attach remote kuzu database design

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
# Attach remote database design

**Design goal:** Allow user to execute read-only queries on a remote kuzu database which can be stored on S3 and accessed via `https`. We are not going to allow users to attach multiple kuzu instances at a time, and users are not allowed to query the original local kuzu database after attaching. The reason why we set this restriction is to keep the feature simple and straightforward.

## Prerequisite
The `httpfs` extension should be installed and loaded beforehand using:
```
INSTALL httpfs;
LOAD EXTENSION httpfs;
```

## Feature:
### 1.  User can attach/detach a remote database using attach/detach statement as follows:

Attach:

`ATTACH 'S3://kuzu_data/db' as uw (type kuzu)`

Detach:

`DETACH uw`

a. After attaching a remote database, users can no longer query/access the original local kuzu database.

b. Users can only query the original local kuzu database after issuing the detach statement.

c. Only one remote database can be attached at a time. meaning:
```cypher
ATTACH 'S3://kuzu_data/db' AS uw (type kuzu)
ATTACH 'S3://kuzu_data/db1' AS uw1 (type kuzu)
```

The second attach statement will cause an exception.

d. The Kuzu database will be attached in read-only mode, meaning write queries will be rejected. If the database path is an invalid Kuzu path, an exception will also be raised.

### Implementation
- Attach: After the user issues the attach statement, we reconstruct the fields in the database class using the provided remote file path.
- Detach: After the user issues the detach statement, we reconstruct the fields in the database class using the original file path (the one provided on startup).

### 2.  Querying
We allow users to attach a remote kuzu database and query it the same way as they would a local kuzu database.

Example:
```cypher
// Assume person is a valid table in uw database
ATTACH 'S3://kuzu_data/db' AS uw (type kuzu)
MATCH (p:person) RETURN p.*
```

> [!NOTE]
> Write queries are not allowed.

### 3. Benchmark Result
I am calling the HTTPFileSystem::read() and LocalFileSystem() read APIs to peform a sequential read of ldbc100 comment.csv file (21GB) to evaluate the read peformance under different filesystems.(results measured in seconds)
Block size means: the number of bytes to read for each FileSystem::read() call.
| Block size    | http file system read time (sec) | local file system read time (sec) |
| -------- | ------- | ------- |
| 4KB  | 145    | 5    |
| 64KB | 86     |  3    |
| 256KB    | 87    | 3    |
| 512KB    | 105   | 3    |
| 1MB| 86  | 3    |
| 4MB    |  32    | 3    |

# Downloading/Caching Optimization
Let us also have a version where users can choose to download the entire database from s3 with a single s3 call to a local temporary directory, so we cache the remote database locally. I think we should keep a map of which remote directory has been mapped to which local directory, so that if a user attaches and detaches multiple times during a session, we don't keep downloading these remote databases over and over again.

Manually deleting cached database: Users may want to refresh a cached database from time to time. We can provide a command to "clear the cached remote Kuzu db". That is we can have a function similar to clearning Postgres/DuckDB schema cache `CALL clear_cached_remote_kuzudb(`S3://kuzu_data/db`) RETURN *;` This function should be called after the user detaches from `S3://kuzu_data/db`. Otherwise it should fail. If the user has detached from this database, then this function can remove the local directory to which we cached the database.

When to delete the locally cached database automatically: The rule should be that if any behavior of the system leads to the extension to be uninstalled then we should delete the local temporary directory. For example, if crashing means that the remote Kuzu extension (or https extension) is uninstalled, then we must have deleted all data related to the extension during crashing or during recovery.

Warning/feedback when user attaches to a cached database: When user calls `ATTACH 'S3://kuzu_data/db' AS uw`, if this database has been cached, it would be good to give some feedback to the user: "Attaching to the cached version of the database S3://kuzu_data/db in /tmp/kuzu/attached-kuzu-dbs/uw/. So the user knows that they have attached to a local copy and can manually remove the cached version if they have to.

We should write tests to test these manual and automatic cache removals and write documentations for these cases.

title: [Draft PR] Parallel Utils
body:
This is a draft PR for the Parallel Utils interface to be used for Algorithm library. 
I am reusing some of the demo functions added by Xiyang. Since the front end interface is not ready, I have a defined an operator **AlgorithmRunner** that orchestrates execution of the function. 

Main files added for parallel utils:

(1) parallel_utils.cpp
(2) algorithm_runner.cpp
(3) graph_algorithms.cpp
(4) shortest_path.cpp

- There is a main **graph_algorithm** struct defined and all algorithms will override the **compute()** function. The compute function gets called from the AlgorithmRunner operator at runtime.  
- Currently TableFunctions store a reference to a "**tableFunc**" that gets executed at runtime (like a function pointer). 
- I have extended this to support a list of functions that need to get executed in parallel (for eg. in shortest_path algorithm, there are two functions **extendFrontierFunc** and **shortestPathOutputFunc** for frontier extension and parallel output writing executing in parallel). 
- AlgorithmRunner is registered as a single threaded task, the first thread to register itself is the master that orchestrates the execution of the graph algorithm. It will call graphAlgorithm→compute() 
- **ParallelUtils** is defined inside AlgorithmRunner and gets invoked by the master thread to submit tasks to the task queue. To submit a task, **doParallel()** is called with a copy of the Sink operator (in this case AlgorithmRunner). 
- The other threads act as workers and pick up the new task from the queue. Since they need access to local state (value vectors, ftable), unlike the master they will do initLocalState.
- **runWorker()** method is reserved for worker threads, the functions are invoked from here. The return result is the no. of tuples processed by the thread, if it is non-zero then the results need to be merged to the local FTable. Once a function returns 0, it indicates no more morsels remain. The local FTable's results are merged to the global FTable.
 
### Parallelization Results (tested on spotify dataset)

Query - CALL shortest_path('spotify_n', 'spotify_e', 1, 30, 85) RETURN dst_offset, path_length;
Results - 3,592,911 tuples (unweighted bfs from node offset 85 to all nodes in the graph as destinations)

| Threads | Runtime (in seconds) |
|---------|----------------------|
| 1       | 16.91                |
| 32      | 2.15                 |
