title: Implement popBack in DiskArray
body:
Currently DiskArrays can only grow in size through pushBack. Implementing popBack is tricky because it requires thinking hard about how to avoid dangling pages if we support pushing_back and popping back within the same transaction. Consider the following case: 
1) We push back enough to create ArrayPage with apIdx 2 and say with arrayPageIdx 5. Suppose this creates a WAL version for page 5 of the fileHandle at WAL page 22.
2) Then within the same transaction we truncate one page. At this point, fileHandle's numPages need to be updated to 4. However, we have already logged a WAL record saying that page 5 of the file has been inserted with WAL version of the page at WAL Page 22. This may be OK, if we insert a new log record saying that page 5 is now deleted.
3) Now suppose we push back again to create a new array page. That will have page 5. Now should we re-use its previous WAL version? Probably not and we should generate a new WAL version and group but what to do is not obvious.  In general we need to guarantee/prove that replaying the WAL record many times will lead to the same database, i.e., that replaying the wal leads to idempotent operations.

title: Make InMemDiskArray use BufferManager for in-memory Array Pages
body:
Currently InMemDiskArray manages the ArrayPages directly through the OS memory. This allows faster access to these pages, but we can achieve something similar by using BM but always pinning in-memory pages. This has the following benefit: During updates, we currently create 3 versions of pages for any storage structure that uses InMemDiskArray: 1 in the InMemDiskArray, 2 in the BufferManager when calling StorageStructureUtils::createWALVersionOfPageIfNecessary(). This is so, because we have utility functions like createWALVersionOfPageIfNecessary, which were developed
for updating Columns transactionally and we wanted to reuse them. iIf we make InMemDiskArray use BufferManager, we would solve this redundancy.

InMemDiskArray also contains some logic to either read values directly from in-memory array page or BM, which might simplify if all pages were BM-backed.

In general, we should consider having a BufferPool for in-memory always pinned pages, which in-memory implementations of storage structures can use to avoid any pins.

title: DiskArray Multi Element Updates

Once this feature is implemented to DiskArray, we should change our update functions (e.g., CSR reconstruction algorithms) to use it when possible.

title: Implementing transactional updates to Disk Array
body:
This PR adds two functions: `updateForWriteTrx(uint64_t idx, U val)`  and `pushBackForWriteTrx(U val)` to BaseDiskArray, which support "transactionally" updating DiskArray classes (BaseDiskArray and InMemDiskArray). So callers (e.g., my next PR that will implement updates to UnstructuredPropertyLists) can use these functions to change these disk arrays and when a user commits or rollbacks, we can commit and rollback all the changes to the DiskArrays (though of course UnstructuredPropertyLists might have to do some commit/rollback work too).

Additionally, the PR could break the benchmarks because it now makes all node tables have by default unstructured property lists even if nodes in this table do not have any unstructured properties. I did this as part of this PR because I needed a way to get access to a DiskArray that would be transactionally checkpointed/rolledback by our WALReplayer logic and UnstructuredPropertyLists' List Header was the simplest way to get access to such a DiskArray. This is also what we should do for the near future because the logic to create a new unstructured property lists when the first unstructured property is inserted would be very difficult to implement. So this will simplify our lives.

 
Also fixes a very hairy bug in the BufferManager, surfaced because of the WAL file-BufferManager interaction, where there was a codeline that unswizzled a page p from the FileHandle FH that was in a Frame F, but did not clear F. Therefore when the BM was trying to evict from F, if FH was for example truncated (so p > numPages), we would make an invalid memory access.

And sorry that disk_array.cpp and disk_array.h looks completely new. They moved folders and I shuffled many functions.

title: Enhance InMemDiskArrayBuilder with a to simplify population of lists in_mem_node_builder/in_mem_rel_builder

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently InMemNodeBuilder uses InMemUnstructuredLists unstrPropertyLists, which uses its own structures to populate the actual lists of lists, such as InMemFile. This is not true for ListMetadata and Lists, which uses InMemDiskArray. If we switch to using DiskArray and InMemDiskArrrayBuilder for the actual lists too some of the loading code can simplify. In particular, parts of code that are populating InMemFile work at a low-level abstraction, where they figure out where the actual page locations they need to update. Instead, if we worked at the abstraction of an array or vector, which can be supported by DiskArray, and had utility functions, such as copy(uint64_t beginOffset, uint8_t* from, uint64 numBytes) or push_back<T>(element), where T is the type of DiskArray etc, and the DiskArrayBuilder figured out exactly which pages to update could be much simpler.

As a concrete example, at a high level, the InMemNodeBuilder::putUnstrPropsOfALineToLists code, reads a line of csv, parses each unstructured property and copies to a particular offset in an array. But the code looks lower level and the following function calls happen
```
1. InMemNodeBuilder::putUnstrPropsOfALineToLists: unstrPropertyLists->setUnstructuredElement(...)
2. InMemUnstructuredLists::setUnstructuredElement:  InMemUnstructuredLists::setComponentOfUnstrProperty(...)
3. Inside InMemUnstructuredLists::setComponentOfUnstrProperty, we find the in-mem page or pages that need to be updated etc.
``` 
All this complexity can be hidden if we make lists to use DiskArrays enhance InMemDiskArrayBuilder to have several utility functions that automatically writes the given data to the correct in-memory locations and are saved to disk correctly as well.

title: fix encode null bits; make stopThreads safe
body:
This PR fixes a potential concurrency bug in the loader with null bits.
Previously, we directly set null bit in a page through `setElementAtPosToNonNull`, in which is changing the value of a null entry, i.e., uint64_t integer (`uint64_t* nullEntries;`). However, multiple threads might happen to set the null bits inside the same null entry. For example, T1 sets null for position 5, and T2 for 6, so they happen to write the same null entry concurrently, which causes bugs.
In this PR, I add an array for each value in a page to be null or not (no two threads will set the same value) and encode the array to the page when we flush it.

Also, this PR changes the `stopThreads` in TaskScheduler to atomic, so it's thread-safe. Practically, it is unnecessary for now, because we only set `stopThreads` to false once, and we don't care much when other threads will stop. But I want to fix this as it introduces minimal overhead and makes the code more robust for any future changes.

title: Fix the deadlock for hash index parallel insertions
body:
This PR fixes the deadlocks in hash index parallel insertions.
Previously, we perform fined-grained locks on each primary slot (pSlot) or overflow slot (oSlot) as needed (instead of locking the whole chain at a time) when we are traversing the chain of the primary slot. However, that potentially can trigger deadlocks. To illustrate the problem, I first list the main data structures in our current master:
```
    shared_mutex sharedLockForSlotMutexes; // coordinating resizing and accessing of slotMutexes.
    vector<unique_ptr<mutex>> slotMutexes;  // lock of each slot (both pSlot or oSlot)
```
 An example is like this, suppose we have a primary slot pSlot2 which is full already. Now both T1 and T2 are trying to append an entry to pSlot2. Their coordination is like:
- T1 grabs the shared lock of `sharedLockForSlotMutexes`;
- T1 locks pSlot2 exclusively;
- T1 releases the shared lock of `sharedLockForSlotMutexes`;
- T2 grabs the shared lock of `sharedLockForSlotMutexes`;
- T1 needs to allocate a new oSlot, thus it is trying to get the exclusive lock of `sharedLockForSlotMutexes` to resize the slotMutexes. The exclusive lock conflicts with T2.
- T2 needs to lock pSlot2 next, which is held by T1 currently, so it waits for T1 to release it. However, before releasing the lock of pSlot2, T1 is blocked by getting the exclusive lock of `sharedLockForSlotMutexes`, which conflicts with T2, who holds the shared lock of `sharedLockForSlotMutexes`. Thus, there is a deadlock.

In this PR, I chose to simplify the problem in the easiest way, that we lock the whole chain at a time. So we don't lock oSlots anymore, instead, every thread needs to grab a exclusive lock of a pSlot, and hold it until it finishes all changes to the chain.

To implement the idea above, two new data structures are added, `SlotArray` and `SlotWithMutexArray`, the former one is for oSlots, and the latter one is for pSlots right now.

**TODO**
Besides the above changes, there are two main todos that are on the way:
1. some code are duplicated right now in InMemHashIndexBuilder and HashIndex, which I'm gradually refactoring.
2. the hash index requires a logic of keeping mappers of logical to physical pages, which should use (InMem)DiskArray for it, which is also left to following prs.

title: Add vector hash operations
body:
Currently, we don't use UnaryOperationExecutor when calculating the hashes of a valueVector. 
For maintainability, we should refactor the hash operations to use UnaryOperationExecutor.
The difficulty is that:
Suppose we want to compute the hashValues of two flatVectors: A, B (A, B are on different dataChunks with different curIdx).
We first use unaryOperationExecutor to calculate the hashValues of A and store the result in a resultValueVector(which should share the same datachunk as A).
Then we need to combine the resultValueVector with B, however the unaryOperation executor assumes that the input and result valueVector share the same datachunk. So we may get incorrect results.

title: Node deletions and insertions
body:
Implements a new class NodesMetadata, which contains per each node table, a NodeMetadata, which is used to delete and insert nodes. Node deletions are allowed only for nodes that don't have any edges. The two important classes are:
NodesMetadata
Gives access to the NodeMetadata of each node table.
Ability to read and write to disk. The disk image is stored in nodes-metadata.bin.
rollingback and commitIfNecessary(): commitIfNecessary commits (in memory) each NodeMetadata for each node table that has had either a node addition or deletion. Rollback undoes any such changes (again in memory)
The full rolling back committing logic appears in Database::commitAndCheckpointOrRollback. During commit, we add a simple NODES_METADATA_RECORD into the wal indicating that there is a change to NodesMetadata. Then we serialize the entire updates NodesMetadata to nodes-metadata.bin.wal (so effectively part of the log appears as a separate file). This is simpler because we don't need to handle >4KB log records in case the new serialized NodesMetadata is larger than that. The recovery logic appears in the constructor of StorageManager (where we have to actually first see if there is a NODES_METADATA_RECORD in the wal and if so, before deserializing NodesMetadata, first copy over the file. This differs from the rest of the recovery mechanism which happens after NodesStore and RelsStore fields of StorageManager is constructed before recovery. Why this is needed is explained inside the StorageManager's constructor. (As I am writing this, I also noticed that I have not tested the recovery logic, so I should add a test for this; you can add a comment).

NodeMetadata:
Contains the public functions:

To add and delete nodes and the rolling back and committing these in memory. The rolling back and committing is done by keeping two separate NodeOffsetsInfo classes, one for readOnlyTransactions and one for write transactions (nodeOffsetsInfoForReadOnlyTrx and nodeOffsetsInfoForWriteTrx). For example, when committing, we simply copy nodeOffsetsInfoForWriteTrx to nodeOffsetsInfoForReadOnlyTrx;

Functions to query about getMaxNodeOffset. We also have a function for getLabelID to not pass labelID to the classes that already have access to NodeMetadata: Node, and ScanNodeID.

NodeOffsetsInfo:
Contains the maxNodeOffset and deletedNodeOffsets and a vector hasDeletedNodesPerMorsel, which keeps a boolean to quickly know (without looking at any sets) that a morsel does not have any deleted nodeOffsets.

Removes numNodes statistics from Catalog as this should be computed if/when needed and computing this requires knowing deleted nodes. Moreover, if this statistic was kept in Catalog, whenever nodes are added or deleted, we would have to write-ahead-log the catalog, which contains a lot of other things.

Adds basic tests in absence of frontend into node-insertion-deletion-tests.cpp.

This feature is inevitably half done and many things remain:

The frontend support is missing. Should be added by @andyfengHKU .

title: Implements the storage side of node deletions and insertions
body:
- Implements a new class NodesMetadata, which contains per each node table, a NodeMetadata, which is used to delete and insert nodes. Node deletions are allowed only for nodes that don't have any edges. The two important classes are: 
**NodesMetadata**
- Gives access to the NodeMetadata of each node table.
- Ability to read and write to disk. The disk image is stored in nodes-metadata.bin. 
- rollingback and commitIfNecessary(): commitIfNecessary commits (in memory) each NodeMetadata for each node table that has had either a node addition or deletion. Rollback undoes any such changes (again in memory)

The full rolling back committing logic appears in Database::commitAndCheckpointOrRollback. During commit, we add a simple NODES_METADATA_RECORD into the wal indicating that there is a change to NodesMetadata. Then we serialize the entire  updates NodesMetadata to nodes-metadata.bin.wal (so effectively part of the log appears as a separate file). This is simpler because we don't need to handle >4KB log records in case the new serialized NodesMetadata is larger than that. The recovery logic appears in the constructor of StorageManager (where we have to actually first see if there is a NODES_METADATA_RECORD in the wal and if so, before deserializing NodesMetadata, first copy over the file. This differs from the rest of the recovery mechanism which happens after NodesStore and RelsStore fields of StorageManager is constructed before recovery. Why this is needed is explained inside the StorageManager's constructor. (As I am writing this, I also noticed that I have not tested the recovery logic, so I should add a test for this; you can add a comment).

**NodeMetadata:**
Contains the public functions:
  1. To add and delete nodes and the rolling back and committing these in memory. The rolling back and committing is done by keeping two separate NodeOffsetsInfo classes, one for readOnlyTransactions and one for write transactions (nodeOffsetsInfoForReadOnlyTrx and nodeOffsetsInfoForWriteTrx). For example, when committing, we simply copy nodeOffsetsInfoForWriteTrx to nodeOffsetsInfoForReadOnlyTrx;

  2. Functions to query about getMaxNodeOffset. We also have a function for getLabelID to not pass labelID to the classes that already have access to NodeMetadata: Node, and ScanNodeID.

**NodeOffsetsInfo:**
Contains the maxNodeOffset and deletedNodeOffsets and a vector<bool> hasDeletedNodesPerMorsel, which keeps a boolean to quickly know (without looking at any sets) that a morsel does not have any deleted nodeOffsets.

- Removes numNodes statistics from Catalog as this should be computed if/when needed and computing this requires knowing deleted nodes. Moreover, if this statistic was kept in Catalog, whenever nodes are added or deleted, we would have to write-ahead-log the catalog, which contains a lot of other things.

- Adds basic tests in absence of frontend into node-insertion-deletion-tests.cpp.

This feature is inevitably half done and many things remain:
- The frontend support is missing. Should be added by @andyfengHKU .
- We do not verify that reading structured properties of a node returns null (I should add a test for this; please add a comment).
- We do not clear any unstructured property of a deleted node. Should be added after we start supporting updates to lists. Would be next for me. Similarly when adding a node and allocating the necessary headers and empty unstructured lists.
- We do not support removing the edges of a node. Similarly when adding a node, we do not add the necessary headers and empty adjacency lists.
- We do not remove the primary key of a deleted node. Should be added after @ray6080  supports updates to the hash index.

Also add a PR comment to remove any changes to tiny-snb-variant, which I was using in tests but removed.

title: orderBy string optimization
body:
This PR does the following optimizations for orderBy string column:
1.  OrderByScan: 
- Instead of encoding 6 bytes for tupleIdx and 2 bytes for factorizedTableIdx. We do: 4 bytes encoding for factorizedTableBlockIdx, 3 bytes encoding for factorizedTableBlockOffset, 1 byte for factorizedTableIdx. This can accelerate the fetching the string from the factorizedTable because we no longer need to do a division and mod operation to calculate the tuplePtr in factorizedTable. The drawBack is that the 1 byte encoding limits our maximum number of threads to 256.
- We encode one more byte for strings to indicate whether this string is a long or a short string. The new encoding length for string will be 14 bytes (1byte null + 12 bytes prefix  + 1byte long/short flag)
- EncodeTuples() for loop optimization

2. Radix sort:
- Instead of fetching the actual string from factorizedTable for each string comparison in quickSort, we can utilize the encoded long/short string flag to minimize the number of string fetch from factorizedTable.
- FindTies() for loop change to minimize the number of multiplications.

3. KeyBlockMerger:
- Minimizes the number of times of fetching strings from factorizedTable by utilizing the long/short string flag in compareTuplePtr().

4. FactorizedTable:
- Table schema now stores the numBytesPerTuple. We don't need to calculate the numBytesPerTuple dynamically during getNumBytesPerTuple().

title: Updates to string node properties, i.e., OverflowPages
body:
Implements the ability to update OverflowPages. Main changes are to:

StringPropertyColumn, OverflowPages, and WalReplayer: The actual logic of how we update are contained in these classes. - StringPropertyColumn::writeValueForSingleNodeIDPosition. This almost re-uses the same logic as the Column::writeValueForSingleNodeIDPosition. This common logic is abstracted in two functions that is now in Column::updateFixedLenPartAndReturnUpdatedPageInfoAndWALPageFrame and StorageStructure::unpinPageInWALAndReleaseOriginalPageLock. The main logic of Column::updateFixedLenPartAndReturnUpdatedPageInfoAndWALPageFrame is in StorageStructure::getUpdatePageInfoForElementAndCreateWALVersionOfPageIfNecessary. 

- OverflowPages::writeStringOverflowAndUpdateOverflowPtr: This handles writing a new string to the overflow file. Currently the logic is very simple and leaves holes in the pages of OverflowPages. We keep a single pointer called nextBytePosToWriteTo. This keeps track of the last available position in the pages where an overflow string can be written (can be used for lists too). Then we simply write to this space and increment nextBytePosToWriteTo. So this pointer monotonically increases and when previous overflows become "dangling" we don't have a mechanism to reuse them.

- WALReplayer: This change is minor. The only additional change is that modifications to string can create new page insertions. We need to treat page insertions differently than updates because if an insertion rolls back, we want to "undo" the insertion by truncating the fileHandle back to its previous size. Note that this truncation logic is currently very simple: Since we assume there is only a single write transaction in the system at any point in time, if we are undoing the insertion of page 5, we can truncate the file directly to 5 pages. That is suppose page 5 and page 6 were added during a transaction but then the transaction rolls back. In the WAL, when we replay, we will first see page 5 insertion. When we see page 5 insertion, we can directly remove both page 5 and page 6 from the fileHandle. This is because we assume that any further new page additions, i.e. those with higher page indices, must also be part of the rolling back transaction, so we can simply remove those pages from the MultiVersionFileHandle for the StorageStructure too. This is also explained inside a comment in WALReplayer.

Main Abstraction Changes:
MultiVersionFileHandle: This takes the logic of keeping pageLocks and pageVersion info data from Column to a new class MultiVersionFileHandle. This allows us to also keep one lock per page, instead of two locks. Previously we had a class called PageVersionInfo, which kept a second lock for each page P in a page group PG that had at least one update. This second lock was stored in the pageLocksAndVersionsPerPageGroup field of PageVersionInfo and was not necessary. MultiVersionFileHandle is meant to be used for any storage structure whose pages might be backed up by WAL pages. Although Lists don't yet need MultiVersionFileHandle, to simplify the class hierarchy, by default any storage structure, so Column, List, or OverflowPages (see the note below that OverflowPages also now extend StorageStructure), have a MultiVersionFileHandle instead of a FileHandle. 

Related to the changes in the FileHandle: FileHandle also now contains new functions to decrease the numPages (and resize the managed data structures). These were not needed before. They are now needed in case a transaction makes updates, which may increase the number of pages in the overflows but then rolls back, so we need to take the filehandle back to its previous state.

BaseColumnOrList: Previous StorageStructure is now called BaseColumnOrList. This class further extends another class called StorageStructure. This class holds some common fields between Column, Lists, and OverflowPages, such as bufferManager, wal, fileHandle, isInMemory. This was initially needed to share some update logic between Column and OverflowPages but once we needed yet even a more basic class, I used it to store common fields as well.

OverflowBufferUtils: Moved the utility functions in TypeUtils that handled overflow-related operations from TypeUtils to a new class OverflowBufferUtils. This was needed because OvrerflowBuffer depends on BufferManager which depends on something etc. and was causing a circular dependency when OverflowPages included type_utils.h

Also removes AdjColumnFileID related log structs from wal_record.h. These were not used and slows us down as many abstractions change as we figure out the right classes to abstract the general logic of transactions.

title: checkpointing logic
body:
Adds checkpointing logic for a committed transactions. The logic is currently implemented in database.h temporarily. That is because in absence of the frontend, the current tests do not use the connection class to interact with the db using transactions. Instead, we manually create transactions by calling transactionManager::beginWriteTransaction etc. Ideally this logic should go to connection.cpp. The logic is this:

For a write transaction that is committing:
1. write ahead the wal to disk
2. wait until all other running (read-only) transactions leave the system
3. commit (but keep the active transaction alive because currently each commit is immediately followed by a checkpoint)
4. storageManager::checkpoint()
5. truncate the wal to empty (by calling wal::clearWAL.
6. clear active transaction
7. allow new transactions to come in the system

For a write transaction that is rolling back:
only steps 6 and 7 run.

We currently have the logic to error and rollback if waiting for existing transactions to leave the system. This will be better tested when we start testing transactions through connection. For example we don't currently test that after this error the transaction is rolled back and wal is cleared etc, which will automatically happen through the connection. 
 
Checkpointing Algorithm:
This is implemented in a new WALReplayer (wal_replayer.h/cpp) class and is straightforward: We loop over each log and redo during checkpointing.  WALReplayer is also used for rolling back to undo some operations and these two algorithms share code. Although database files are guaranteed to not be updated during WAL, other structures, such as PageVersionInfo, can be updated and need to be undone. WALReplayer can be constructed either in checkpoint or rollback mode and in both modes call the same replay() function which for checkpointing does the extra work of copying over updates from WAL pages to the original db files and in both modes replay() also undoes the changes to the PageVersionInfo (and later possibly other structures).

title: Hash index concurrent insertions
body:
This PR adds support for concurrent insertion after `bulkReserve` in HashIndex.
Also, cached blocks are changed to be managed through BufferManager. During flushing, cached blocks are marked as dirty, and will be flushed to disk by BufferManager.

The insertion locking scheme is that:
for each primary and ovf slot, there is a mutex, i.e., `primarySlotMutexes`, and `ovfSlotMutexes`. Access to a slot during insertion requires a lock first.
When a key is to be inserted, we first calculate its primary slot id, based on which, we will require its lock and read its header. Remind that the way we organize our slots is each primary slot is chained with a list of ovf slots. So during insertion, to find the correct slot for insertion, we follow the chain by acquiring the nextOvfSlot's lock, and releasing the previous one. In this way, we can minimize the impact of locking.

Ovf page allocation:
During insertion, when a primary/ovf slot is full, we need to allocate a new ovf slot to address the hash confliction. The allocation happens in two cases: 1) there are empty ovf slots available in a ovf page, we require a global lock, and increment the current soltId to the empty one; 2) there are no empty ovf slots available, we need to allocate a new ovf page. We first require a global lock, then acquire a lock on `ovfSharedMutex`, which coordinates accesses to ovf pages, i.e., `ovfCachedBlocks`. The double locking design is to minimize the conflict between reading a slot from `ovfCachedBlocks`, and allocating a new ovf page.

# Phyiscal Operators
## Set
The physical set operator itself is a pipelined operator which updates a property column to an expression evaluation result for each input nodeID. This initial implementation only supports node structured property. To avoid undefined behavior as stated in the design doc. We append a ResultCollector and a FactorizedTableScan before each sink.

## ResultCollector
Add getMorsel() interface to allow multi-thread scanning from factorized table

## BaseTableScan, FactorizedTableScan and UnionAll
Abstract common table scan interface in to BaseTableScan operator. FactorizedTableScan scans from 1 factorized table while UnionAll scans from multiple factorized table.

# Logical Operators
## Remove logical result collector
In our design pattern, sink and scan operators are generated together. The only exception is a result collector will also be appended at the very end of a physical plan. Therefore, we should not define a logical result collector.
## LogicalSinkScan
This operator represents the ResultCollector and FactorizedTableScan we append before Set operator. Its name is subject to change.


# For Reviewers
- See if removing logical result collector decision is justified.
- Review all changes under physical_plan/operator
- Review if it makes sense to have ResultCollector and FTableScan as its own operator instead of making Set being able to sink/scan.

title: Inconsistent flat data chunk information between planner and mapper for optional match.
body:
Both planner and mapper maintains flat information by themselves. This is needed because flat information is changing as new operators being appended. So we can not maintain a global shared flat information. 

Ideally only flatten operator is allowed to change flat information. However, for optional match, because we are referencing data chunks (see comment in planOptionalMatch() in enumerator.cpp), a referenced data chunk could directly be flat without a previous flatten operator. This is a quite annoying bug, two possible solutions are

- Avoid referencing and deep copy from one data Chunk to another. Flat data chunk can be copies into unFlat ones whose size always equals to 1.
- Switch to HashJoin type of optional match. Personally I prefer this one which should be a more principled design and will also fix issue #438

title: Update of structured properties and basic WAL functionality
body:
Implements the backend for updating structured node properties. Gets in some infrastructure code to ensure updates are logged to a WAL and writer transactions see what they wrote without affecting read transactions.

Main New/Modified Classes:
WAL, WALIterator and WALRecord: Implement log record structures needed for updating columns and a library to write log records and iterate over log records.
Column: is modified to take as an argument during construction a WAL. Column also now has a function that can update the column, which leads to possibly writing a page to WAL and logging a record to WAL. Columns read functions also take in a transaction now, which is used to know which version of a page a transaction should read: readOnly transactions read the default page in the db file, while the writing transaction reads possibly from the WAL. 
PageVersionInfo: Is used to keep track of whether a particular page in a Column has multiple version or a single version. Implements the existing design.
There are several tests for these classes.

Medium Level Change:
Catalog: Catalog's way of holding information for Properties used to be in a class called PropertyDefinition that stored its string name, id, data type, and whether the property is the primary key or not. This is also used by the loader and several fields would be empty or not used previously. We needed to pass more information to Columns to log the ID of the file that Column uses to store data. We could use the string name but it would mean that we log the string in the wal logs. This could be fine but does not look right. To pass the necessary information to Column we need to pass the label of the nodes and when the column stores single multiplicity edges, i.e., the column is an adj column or holds properties of such single multiplicity edges, then also the rel label. This PR implements a new struct Property that stores more information about a property and passes it down to the coluimn.

The PR also solves a separate bug that I ran into, in which we were not reading the NULL bits for node offsets > 8 in the columns and directly setting their values to null. This bug is fixed and the PR modifies some input datasets we use to contain nulls in their structured properties to test this case now.

title: Making the scheduling thread wait for all threads to finish during errors.
body:
We used to remove a task in which at least one worker thread errored from the task queue. This means that by the time the application is notified that there is an exception in the query another worker thread could still be working on a pipeline of this query. This can be a problem when we implement transactions. For example, when we implement transactions, the connection could rollback a transaction but the "continuing worker thread" can still have a handle to this transaction and use it to scan data etc. 
This PR does the safer thing and ensures that no worker thread is working no any task related to the query before the application is notified.

title: Transactions Warm Up
body:
This PR adds basic support for beginning, committing, and rolling back transactions. Major classes that are added or modified are:
- TransactionManager
- Connection

The general behavior is explained in the comment above TransactionMode inside connection (copy pasted as it is in the current version of the PR):

    /**
     * If the connection is in AUTO_COMMIT mode any query over the connection will be wrapped around
     * a transaction and committed (even if the query is READ_ONLY).
     * If the connection is in MANUAL transaction mode, which happens only if an application
     * manually begins a transaction (see below), then an application has to manually commit or
     * rollback the transaction by calling commit() or rollback().
     *
     * AUTO_COMMIT is the default mode when a Connection is created. If an application calls
     * begin[ReadOnly/Write]Transaction at any point, the mode switches to MANUAL. This creates
     * an "active transaction" in the connection. When a connection is in MANUAL mode and the
     * active transaction is rolled back or committed, then the active transaction is removed (so
     * the connection no longer has an active transaction) and the mode automatically switches
     * back to AUTO_COMMIT.
     * Note: If connection is closed() and the connection has an active (manual) transaction, then
     * the active transaction is rolled back.
     */

title: Node degree function

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
I see many users of GDBMSs and in particular Cypher want to do query processing ignoring nodes with high degrees. We need a way for users to specify this. Queries can look like:
MATCH (a)-[:friend]->(b)
WHERE a.degree (or degree(a)) < 10
RETURN b.

We can add a new clause to our version of Cypher or probably more easily a node function that computes this. This information is stored in our list indexes, so we can compute this quickly.

I'm also open to moving to phase 1. My guess is that it is actually a very useful feature.

As a consequence, we remove expression types that are specific to a particular aggregate function and instead treat them all as AGGREGATE_FUNCTION.

title: Remove unnecessary overload, refactor comparison and string functions
body:
## Change function overloading signatures
For overloaded functions with known output type (e.g. `sin(INT) -> DOUBLE`  & `sin(DOUBLE) -> DOUBLE`), we use to have unstructured overloding signature as `sin(VALUE) -> VALUE`. This PR changes the signature to `sin(VALUE) -> DOUBLE`

## Change Cypher grammar-defined arithmetic and string functions to use function framework.
Previously we bind Cypher grammar-defined arithmetic and string functions (i.e. `+, -, *, /, %, ^, CONTAINS, STARTS_WITH`) with its own logic. This PR generates signatures for these functions and bind them through our new framework. As a consequence, we remove their expression type and treat them as regular functions. 

We did a similar change to Cypher grammar-defined  comparison functions (i.e. `=, <>, > , >=, <, <=`). But we keep their expression type.

title: VarLenExtend pattern matching front end
body:
We should allow the user to omit the lower bound/ upper bound of the variable length extend query.
If the user omit the lower bound of the query:
eg. (a)-[*..5]->(b), the front end should put 1 as the lower bound.
If the user omit the upper bound of the query:
eg. (a)-[*3..]->(b), the front end should put MAX_VAR_LENGTH_EXTEND_PATH as the upper bound.

https://neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/current/syntax/patterns/

title: Make variable-length joins non-pipelining only for long path queries

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
In our current design of variable-length joins that @acquamarin is implementing now, during query plan generation we blindly put in a variable-length join sink + variable-length join operators. This allows us to parallelize the frontier extensions that start from a single node. However, we should only execute this way: (1) if the variable-extend is guaranteed to start from a single prefix; and (2) the maxLen of the path is very long (e.g., contains > 4 edges and each edge is over one/many-to-many). Another smarter way could be to use the average degree of an edge label and make this decision based on that (e.g., if avg-deg^{maxLen} > 1M).

We should have a more standard completely pipelining variable-length join operator that we use if at least the 2nd condition fails. That is if the max-length of these conditions do not hold. For example one approach could be the following: 
Consider this example: MATCH (a:Person)-[:Knows..2...4]->(b:Person). So minLen = 2 and maxLen=4. Suppose we scanned (a) variable. We could add 1 regular Extend operator and then add 3 StandardVariableExtend operators. A high-level description of StandardVariableExtend is:

StandardVariableExtend (SVE): Contains 2 valueVectors: (i) to store the (b) values; and (ii) to store a temporary valuvector, which can be extended to (b). Let's call this temporary vector's variable _tmp. SVE first checks if the (b) vector has data in it. If so, it just passes it to the next operator. If not, it checks if _tmp has data in it. If so, it flattens the values in _tmp and extends it to (b) and calls the next operator. If both (b) and _tmp are empty then that means there are no more extensions to do. 

The pipelining version of varLenExtend is implemented in these two PRs:
1. VarLenAdjListExtend: #527 
2. VarLenColExtend: #537

title: Changing in memory db mode to not use BM instead of OS memory
body:
Fixes the first item in https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/issues/494. 

When we run the system in memory mode, the FileHandles to the database files used to use a unique_ptr<uint8_t[]> buffer; and read a file directly into this buffer. For example, if a column takes 1G, we'd acquire a 1G array through the OS. Instead we now pin the pages of this file in the BM when constructing Column and Lists. Then the rest of the access to these pages go through the BM as before. 

Note that we are losing some performance here because we still acquire locks when accessing the page but we do not do any I/O, so a cache hit is guaranteed. So the performance is similar to when we have a large BM. 

For now, I made this decision to go for simplicity. If later we decide to be very careful about the performance of the in-memory db mode, there is an easy buffer manager interface extension that can avoid any locks. We would have a separate pinInMemoryPage function, which would pin the page once and be called (as in this PR) from DataStructure's base constructor. Then we would have special case if (isInMemory) branches into the original pin and unpin function in BufferPool. For example, for unpin, as was done previously, if the file isInMemory, we'd just return. pin would require a bit more work. Probably we'd skip over the part of pin that acquires the page lock and the rest would be the same.

As an independent change 1: I had to test the BM's behavior through the embedded shell, so added a few new commands to the shell to see debug information about the bm and the system overall. I also changed how command line arguments are parsed in the shell_runner to make it more robust to order of arguments. I used the command line argument parser library that was done in the loader (@Taywee_args).

As an independent change 2: Renames data_structure folder and build package to storage_structure.

title: Multi page size bm
body:
This PR changes several things about the BufferManager's (BM) internals and how it can be used: 

- BM now supports 2 different page sizes: DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE and LARGE_PAGE_SIZE, both defined in configs.h. Currently these values are 4K and 256K but can be configured. This is done by extracting the main functionalities of the BM to a BufferPool class, and having the BufferManager class wrap 2 BufferPools. 
- Extends Frames with isDirty flag, which needs to be set explicitly through the BM. This leads to the BM writing these pages to disk when evicting.
- FileHandle has two new fields: 1) whether the pages of the file are largePaged or not; 2) whether the file is a new temporary file. These are done through a flag implementation, where several common flag configurations are added as constant in FileHandle.
- MemoryManager (MM) remains but for now has a new functionality to acquire its memory blocks through the BM.  This is only supported for fixed LARGE_PAGE_SIZE memory blocks. The previous functionality of acquiring memory through the OS still remains for now and should eventually be deprecated (adde these TODOs). So users can call MM::allocateBMBackedBlock, which will give to the user a page of size LARGE_PAGE_SIZE. These memories are never spilled to disk and the MM keeps them pinned. So the callers are guaranteed that these memory blocks will remain in memory. The implication of this is that MM has an internal FileHandle (that is configured to be isNewTmp and isLargePaged). When allocateBMBackedBlock is called, it sees if there is a free page in the file, and if so, just pins the page. Then a separate MM::freeBMBackedBlock function needs to be called to give these memories back to the system. MM will then unpin these pages.
- As an example of how to use BM-backed memory during query processing, StringBuffer is reimplemented to now use MM's allocateBMBackedBlock functions instead of allocateOSBackedBlock (which is a rename of the previous allocateBlock function).
- As part of these changes, makes BM and MM usage through shared_ptr's. This was needed primarily because some tests, that were constructing their own BufferManager and MemoryManagers were failing, because it is not easy to understand/control which sequence of destructors are called across FileHandle, StringBuffer, MM, and BM, when these are raw pointers. The problem was that the BM or MM would be deconstructed before StringBuffer, which would then try to free pages, which would cause seg faults. Keeping shared pointers guarantees that BufferManager and/or MemoryManager cannot be deconstructed before StringBuffer.
- As an independent change, makes BufferManagerMetrics local to BufferManager instead of a query-specific metric. This has not been useful so far and I don't expect it to be very useful for a while. We were passing all around just so that a few operators would need to call pin/unpin through Column/List, and it has been slowing down our implementation speed.

More work needs to be done in the system to move large all OS-backed memory allocations (excluding small a few KB allocations, e.g., those done in ValueVector) to BM-backed ones again using MemoryManager. These are listed here: https://github.com/graphflowdb/graphflowdb/issues/494.

title: Parallel distinct aggregate
body:
Currently, distinct aggregate is only executed with single thread because it's unsafe to perform thread-local aggregation without first taking distinct values. Imagine the following example of calculating COUNT(DISTINCT a.age) with 2 threads. Both threads t1 and t2 get input 20. 20 is a distinct value in their own thread so both threads have COUNT = 1. However, when we combine the state between t1 and t2, we lose track of input vectors and thus lead to the wrong aggregate value.

## Solution
A possible solution is to first calculate thread-local distinct values in parallel which is the same as the current implementation of DISTINCT. Then during task finalize, we first obtain global distinct values by merging all thread-local distinct hash tables. Then we loop through the global distinct hash table and update aggregate states for each row.

title: Use an efficient way to solve orderBy multiplicity problem
body:
Currently, we encode a tuple multiple times if it's multiplicity is not 1. This is not an efficient way to encode tuples.
We should have a flag about whether multiplicity is guaranteed to be 1 or it could change. Maybe we can always encode the multiplicity with the keys. But the frontend should check if multiplicity is guaranteed to be 1 or not and: 
1) use this information to set whether the output of order_by_scan should be unflat or flat (if multiplicities of output tuples is not guaranteed to be 1, we cannot output unflat vectors)
2) give this information to order_by_scan, so that order_by_scan knows whether or not it's scanning to flat or unflat datachunk/resultset and if it's scanning into flat datachunk/result set, it should also put the multiplicity back into the datachunk. But regardless of what we end up doing, in in order_by, each row r should get stored in localRowCollection once and the key columns of r should get encoded once.

The current solution is enough to solve this problem, so I close this issue.

title: Order by rules from user's perspective
body:
ORDER BY IN RETURN: Always works.

ORDER BY IN WITH. Only allow "Top k" type queries with LIMIT and/or SKIP. That is an ORDER BY clause can follow a WITH if and only if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP following ORDER BY. And if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP, the LIMIT and SKIP will consume its input/result set according to the given order. But any operator after that ignores the order. 

If a query uses ORDER BY IN WITH and is not followed with a LIMIT or SKIP, we error.

title: ordering of tuples after orderBy operator
body:
The ordering of tuples can't be guaranteed after the orderBy operator if we multi-threaded the execution of following opeators.

We defined some rules of the behaviour of operators after orderBy:
1. ORDER BY IN RETURN： the ordering of result tuples is preserved.
2. ORDER BY IN WITH:  Only allow "Top k" type queries with LIMIT and/or SKIP. That is an ORDER BY clause can follow a WITH if and only if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP following ORDER BY. And if there is a LIMIT and/or SKIP, the LIMIT and SKIP will consume its input/result set according to the given order. But any operator after that ignores the order. 
If a query uses ORDER BY IN WITH and is not followed with a LIMIT or SKIP, we error (or we should ignore the ORDER BY clause but ignoring could be harder to do. Erroring is more explicit. 

Currently, we just make the opeartors after orderby single-threaded.

title: problem with stringBuffer life cycle in pipelines
body:
Currently, the valueVector owns the string buffer. If the valueVector goes out of scope, the stringBuffer will be destroyed. 

As a result, there is a problem for the string overflow buffer lifecycle between two pipelines.

For example:
Pipeline 1 : Scan(a.ID)->ORDER BY(a.name)   (valueVector1)
Pipeline 2: ORDER BY SCAN(a.name)  -> ResultCollector (valueVector2)

The valueVector1 stores the overflow buffer for a.name. When pipeline1 goes out of scope, the overflow buffer will be destroyed. Thus the orderByScan operator in pipeline2 will read invalid strings from the overflow buffer.

We should reconsider the lifecycle of string overflows.

title: Subquery plans with multiple pipelines

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Exists and LeftNestedLoopJoin operators contain an outer-plan and a subquery plan. Currently, subplans can only be executed entirely as part of another pipeline that has been wrapped around in a ProcessorTask. This is because the pipeline that contains Exists of LeftNestedLoopJoin needs to call sub-plan in the middle of a pipeline, and the TaskScheduler currently cannot start a new task/pipeline without finishing an existing task/pipeline. It is also not clear if we ever want to decompose sub-plans into tasks and have worker threads execute them separately. This does not like a good design. 

The practical implication for us right now is this: we cannot have a sub-query plan (SQP) that consist of more than 1 pipeline, where one of the pipelines of SQP requires the call on finalize. This is because, since SQP is are part of an outer plan OP, worker threads will call finalize on OP and not SQP. So the pipeline of SQP that requires finalize will never be called. So SQP needs to be a single pipeline that does not require finalize to be called.

One general idea to fix this, which is probably the right way is that we never parallelize sub-plans as we do (which I think is the right thing for the foreseeable future), but we add a flag to operators to indicate whether they are part of a subquery, which means they are guaranteed to be executed with only one thread. And then at the end of execute() calls or maybe some other operator function, we can check whether this is an operator that is guaranteed to be executed by a single thread, in which case we can make any necessary finalize calls. 

The other fix we need is that if SQP consists of multiple pipelines SQP1 and SQP2, say SQP1 ends with a HashJoinBuild, and SQP2 is the HashJoinProbe pipeline. Now currently we will decompose SQP into SQP1 and SQP2 and we will execute SQP1 first by calling HashJoinBuild::execute(), which completes and constructs its hash table and then we will execute SQP2 by calling ResultCollector::execute(). Now because SQP's root operator is ResultCollector, we somehow need to be able to call HashJoinBuild::execute() first. It is not clear how to do this without a significant change to our current query plan execution architecture.

For now, we need to ensure that the enumerator never uses a HashJoin or an aggregation or anything else that is not a single pipeline. So we should focus on scans, extends and filters.

title: New task scheduler that merges loader and processor thread pools.
body:
This PR does two things (the main contribution is 1) but 2) was a bug observed when testing 1), and I'm putting it in the same PR for now):

1) Addresses Issue #304. It merges the two thread pool components of loader and processor into a TaskScheduler that is under src/common. The TaskScheduler.h provides a detailed description of how different components (possibly other than loader and processor) can use the TaskScheduler to schedule a set of tasks that worker threads can execute in parallel. I am copy pasting it here:  


/**
* TaskScheduler is a library that manages a set of worker threads that can execute tasks that are
 * put into a task queue. Each task accepts a maximum number of threads. Users of TaskScheduler
 * schedule tasks to be executed by calling schedule functions, e.g., scheduleTask or
 * scheduleTaskAndWaitOrError. New tasks are put at the end of the queue. Workers grab the first
 * task from the beginning of the queue that they can register themselves to work on. Any task that
 * is completed is removed automatically from the queue. If there is a task that raises an
 * exception, the worker threads catch it and store it with the tasks. The user thread that is
 * waiting on the completion of the task (or tasks) will throw the exception (the user thread could
 * be waiting on a tasks through a function that waits, e.g., scheduleTaskAndWaitOrError or
 * waitAllTasksToCompleteOrError.
 *
 * Currently there are two ways the TaskScheduler can be used:
 * (1) Schedule a set of tasks T1, ..., Tk, and wait for all of them to be completed or error
 * if any one them has raised an exception (but only the exception of one (the earliest scheduled)
 * task will be raised. We do not currently re-throw multiple exceptions from multiple tasks. Ex:
 *      schedule(T1);
 *      ...;
 *      schedule(Tk);
 *      waitAllTasksToCompleteOrError();
 * (2) Schedule one task T and wait for T to finish or error if there was an exception raised by
 * one of the threads working on T that errored. This is simply done by the call:
 *      scheduleTaskAndWaitOrError(T);
 *
 * TaskScheduler guarantees that workers will register themselves to tasks in FIFO order. However
 * this does not guarantee that the tasks will be completed in FIFO order: a long running task
 * that is not accepting more registration can stay in the queue for an unlimited time until
 * completion.
 */

2) A minor-looking but important change to SimpleAggregate and SimpleAggregationScan, which were moving a shared pointer of their SharedState objects when cloning themselves. This meant that the reference physical plan P from which worker threads in the previous thread pool and current task_scheduler would clone, when cloning twice would run into segmentation or other errors. This is because after the first clone is called on the reference SimpleAggregate/SimpleAggregationScan, the move of the shared pointer removes the reference's co-ownership of SimpleAggregate/SimpleAggregationScan from the SharedState, so e.g., shared_ptr<AggregationSharedState> could be nullified. Therefore the second time clone is called, which happens when number of worker threads that can work on P is > 1, we would error. This bug existed in the previous thread pool, so is not related to the main change in this PR.

title: Refactor init() and initResultSet()

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Currently, we have resultSet being created and given to a Sink operator during mapping phase. Sink then calls init which initialize the resultSet for its pipeline before execution. This design is no longer true for LeftNestedLoopJoinOperator where the subPlan does not have a sink operator but still requires a different resultSet.

The new design is to have one initResultSet() function that returns the resultSet after initialization. The signiture will be
`share_ptr<ResultSet> initResultSet()`

For unary operators, the logic would be,
```
resultSet = prev.initResultSet()
insert vectors into resultSet as necessary 
```

For binary operators, the logic would be
```
leftResultSet = left.initResultSet()
rightResultSet = right.initResultSet()
merge left and right resultSets
```

Also, we should protect the calling of initResult() within operators only.

For example, when pushing property scanners into the subPlan of logicalNestedLoopJoin, we need to update the schema for the subPlan.

Therefore, we might choose to move property push down optimization back into enumerator. The design is stated as follows
- Populate all properties to read based on a static evaluation of the query.
- Once a property's ID is matched, we apply all property scanners.

title: Scalable RETURN all unstructured properties of node
body:
Currently, when a user asks the query:
```
MATCH (a:Person)
WHERE a.firstName = "Ramon"
RETURN a
```
And we are given a graph that has 1000 different possible unstructured properties across Person nodes (which is an information kept in the catalog), we will try to construct a plan with 1000 property readers, what will try to read each possible property one after another, and put a null or a value in one ValueVector. So for a node that has only 1 unstructured property, we will try to read 1000 possible properties. In addition, we will output 999 nulls.

Instead, we should have a special ValueVector (possibly of dataType Map or currently we can call it UnstructuredPropertyMap) that and a special AlllUnstructuredPropertiesReader that reads all unstructured properties of a node and puts it into a single ValueVector.

title: ID constraints and errors in loader.
body:
changes layout of file headers to follow neo4j's design. 

Earlier, header of a file used to be like `a:A,b:B,c:C` for both the node and rel files, where property a has dataType A and b has dataType B. Also for node files, we used to specify the primary key in the metadata file. however, contrary to node files, in rel files, from and to nodes (foreign keys) were still positional, that is, first and second column of the file.

Neo4j's design enforces node file to have header like `:ID,a:A,b:B` where `:ID` column specifies the unique identifier (primary key). And rel file header to be like `:START_ID,:END_ID,a:A,b:B`. the advantage of having special tags like :ID, :START_ID etc is that the primary (in node file) and foreign keys (in rel files) are not positional and neither needs to be defined in the metadata file for each label. 

This PR hence forms the basis for the next which will add the check to skip relationships which has invalid src or dst node ids.
Skipping nodes with duplicate node ids is not intuitive since technically we create the nodeIDMaps after inserting the properties of nodes. (while inserting properties, we parallelly create the reverse nodeIDMaps ) 

Also adds checks to verify if the csv header is correct and subsequently add tests for each case.

title: add null support for rowCollection
body:
To represent the null values in RowCollection, we use a bitmap to represent the null fields in each row
1. For overflow columns, we use a large bitmap to represent the nulls in the whole overflow columns and stores it at the end of the overflow memory.
2. For all other columns, we just store a bitmap at the end of each row.

For example:
we have 3 columns: a1   a2(overflow)   a3 = (1   [null,4,6,7]  null)     

                       
Since the 3rd column is a null value, we set the 3rd bit(from right to left) of the first byte to 1.
The memory of the row Collection looks like: 
1  overflowPtrToA2  0 nullMap:4(00000100).

Since the 1st element in the overflow column is a null value, we set the 1st bit(from right to left) of the first byte to 1.
The overflow column memory looks like: 
3 4 6 0 nullMap:1(00000001).

title: Issue 397
body:
This PR solves issue #397 

This PR introduces a design pattern for merging result sets from different branches (pipelines). For example, hash join probe result set need to merge hash join build result set. We might follow a similar pattern when merging subquery or scanning aggregation/order by tables. The pattern is described as following.

Build side takes a schema (BuildDataInfo) describing what vectors should be materialized. It contains
-  DataPos keyIDDataPos: describes the position of hash key.
-  vector<DataPos> nonKeyDataPoses: describes the positions of all payload vectors.

Probe side takes a schema (ProbeDataInfo) describing how to append build side payload to probe side. It contains
- DataPos keyIDDataPos: describe the position of hash key. On probe side, this hash key is only used for probing.
- vector<DataPos> nonKeyDataPoses: describes the appending positions of payload vectors.
  -  Note that build and probe side nonKeyDataPoses have one-to-one mapping which means we should scan all columns that are materialized. Otherwise those columns should not be part of the payload.

title: Refactor Exists Subquery
body:
This PR refactor the logic of exists subquery evaluation.

Previously, we had ExistsSubqueryExpressionEvaluator which could be part of the expression evaluator tree. The new design introduces Exists operator which evaluates a subquery plan for each input tuple. The evaluation result is written as a new value vector with true/false values depending on whether the subquery plan has at least one result or not. Similar to aggregation, exists subquery expression is evaluated by Exists operator and later on treated as a leaf expression in the expression evaluator tree.

This new design has the following advantage.

- Decoupling expression and logical plan/operator.
- Decoupling expression evaluator and physical plan/operator.
- Decoupling expression mapper and plan mapper
- Leave the potential to optimize the subquery plan together with the outer query plan. (If we keep subquery plan in ExistsSubqueryExpressionEvaluator, then we can only optimize plan layer by layer )

title: Add RowCollection and refactor hash join to use it
body:
This PR introduces `RowCollection`, an intermediate row-based data structure for the query result. It stores data in a row-fashion, which is mostly used by hash tables, and sink operators such as OrderBy to materialize intermediate results. 

HashJoin has been refactored to use RowCollection in this PR.

Each `RowCollection` requires a `RowLayout`, which is a "schema" describing, for each field, the size and if the vector should be stored as an overflow (e.g., unFlat vectors in non-key data chunks should be stored as overflow during the hash join building phase).

The `RowCollection` provides three interfaces to handle the transformation between vector-based ResultSet and row-based data blocks.
```
void append(const vector<shared_ptr<ValueVector>>& vectors, uint64_t numRowsToAppend);
uint64_t scan(const vector<uint64_t>& fieldsToScan, const vector<DataPos>& resultDataPos, ResultSet& resultSet, uint64_t startRowId, uint64_t numRowsToScan) const;
uint64_t lookup(const vector<uint64_t>& fieldsToRead, const vector<DataPos>& resultDataPos, ResultSet& resultSet, uint8_t** rowsToRead, uint64_t startPos, uint64_t numRowsToRead) const;
```

`scan` and `lookup` will return actual number of rows that is scanned from the row collection.

`scan` is responsible for scanning from the given logical `startRowId` to at most `startRowId + numRowsToScan`.
`lookup` takes in an array of pointers to physical rows, it will be responsible to read rows from `rowsToRead[startPos]` to at most `rowsToRead[startPos + numRowsToRead]`.

Given a startRowId, the actual number of rows to read are computed as follows:
```
numRowsToRead = min(numRowsToRead, numRows - startRowId); // bounded by remaining rows after the startRowId
numRowsToRead = min(hasVectorOverflow ? 1 : DEFAULT_VECTOR_CAPACITY, numRowsToRead); // bounded by if fields has vector overflow
```


This PR also generalizes `MorselDesc` to prepare it to be used for scans other than ScanNodeID.

This PR removes the notion of leaf expression from the binder and enumerator.

Previously, leaf expression was defined as a set of expression types (PROPERTY, CSV_LINE_VARIABLE, ...) whose value is written to value vector before expression evaluation starts. This method is not correct since we could have an expression being aliased and become a leaf. For example, MATCH (a) WITH a.age + 2 AS newAge MATCH (b) RETURN b.age > newAge. In this case, newAge is a leaf expression when evaluating b.age > newAge.

This PR changes leaf expression to be an expression whose value exists in the schema, i.e., has been previously evaluated.  This is done through recursively check is a sub-expression exists in the schema or not

title: add encoder for order by
body:
Add encoder for order by operator.

The OrderByKeyEncoder encodes all columns in the ORDER BY clause into a single binary sequence that, when compared using memcmp will yield the correct overall sorting order.
On little-endian hardware, the least-significant byte is stored at the smallest address. To encode the sorting order, we need the big-endian representation for values.
For example: we want to encode 73(INT64) and 38(INT64) as an 8-byte binary string 
The encoding in little-endian hardware is:
73=0x4900000000000000 38=0x2600000000000000, which doesn't preserver the order. 
The encoding in big-endian hardware is: 
73=0x0000000000000049 38=0x0000000000000026, which can easily be compared using memcmp. 

In addition, The first bit is also flipped to preserve ordering between positive and negative numbers. 
So the final encoding for 73(INT64) and 38(INT64) as an 8-byte binary string: 
73=0x8000000000000049 38=0x8000000000000026 

If a string is too long, we only encode its prefix(12 bytes) and only look at the whole string if the prefixes are equal. 
With this binary string, we can now compare both columns at the same time by comparing only the binary string
representation.

To handle the null in comparison, we add an extra byte(called the NULL flag) to represent whether this value is null or not.
We currently add a null flag to all values, which affects the radix sort performance. We need to record whether or not a column has any nulls in catalog, so that we don't need add null flags to all values. Opened an issue about this #384.

title: Refactor Expression; Remove Alias Expression Type

  - uniqueName is the name used for internal processing and guaranteed to be unique for different expressions.
- Remove Alias expression type. We used to have an alias expression type which leads to de-aliasing during multiple processing stage (e.g. binding, planning and mapping). We now remove this expression type and kept alias as a field of expression and all alias related logic happens in binding. Note: node and rel automatically gets an implicit alias (same as their parsed name) if alias is not explicitly defined.

Minor change

title: Incorrect nullmask setting for the evaluation result of IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
body:
`IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` check if a value is `NULL` or not, and return `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each value.
Currently, we set the unary expression result to share the same nullmask with its child one, which causes incorrect output for `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`.
For example, given an input vector `[NULL, 10, 20]`, whose nullmask is `[True, False, False]`. When we apply `IS NULL`, the expected output is `TRUE, FALSE, FALSE`, while currently, due to the sharing of nullmask with the input, the actual output is `NULL,FALSE,FALSE`.

title: Add a system-level mechanism (possibly lock) to coordinate changes that might affect multiple components
body:
We are implementing several functionalities that change some components of the system, e.g., the buffer manager's buffer pool size, or updates, which affect the storage files. These need to be: (1) coordinated and; (2) happen when the system is idle, i.e., no queries, updates, or some system configuration changes are happening. We need a mechanism to coordinate these.

One idea is to have functions waitUntilSystemIsIdleAndAcquireSystemLock() and releaseSystemLock() somewhere, possibly in System. The first function could do two things: (i) acquire a system-level lock that the query compiler, BufferManager::resize(), and future components related to updates (e.g., transaction manager) can acquire before doing such changes; and (ii) monitor the query processor to ensure all query processing tasks have been completed.

labels.name: type: feature
labels.description: New features or missing components of existing features

body:
Consider the following query
`MATCH (d)<-(a)->(b)->(c) WHERE d.age = c.age`
We might enumerate join order abcd which leads to the following plan
`Scan(a)->Extend(b)->Extend(c)->Scan(c.age)->Extend(d)->Scan(d.age)->Filter`
Although Extend(d) and Scan(d.age) only depends Scan(a), this plan has to repeat the work for every flat (a,b) tuple which might be even worse for longer join path.

A possible solution is to embed the following optimization in join order enumeration.
When we match "a", we extend variables that depends on "a" at the same time. So Extend(b) and Extend(d) will happens together.

title: Refactor build files to avoid circular dependency of subquery expression.
body:
This PR refactor bazel build files to solve circular dependency introduced by subquery expression/evaluator.

### Circular dependency
Consider the case for expression_evaluator lib and physical_operator lib. 
- Expression_evaluator depends on physical_operator because subquery_evaluator requires the last operator of its subplan
- Physical_operator depends on expression_evaluator because filter/projection requires expression_evaluator
- In such case, bazel does know which lib to compile first.

### Solution
We create subquery_evaluator as its own lib. The updated dependency becomes
-  Physical_operator depends on expression_evaluator because filter/projection requires expression_evaluator
-  Subquery_evaluator depends on expression_evaluator
-  Subquery_evaluator depends on physical_operator
-  Compiling order becomes 
   -  expression_evaluator
   -  physical_operator
   -  subquery_evaluator
 
Same solution is applied to subquery_expression and logical_plan

### Additional change
Move clone() method from expression_mapper to expression_evaluator to decouple physical_operator and expression_mapper.
We used to compile physical_operator and expression_mapper together due to the clone() function. However, expression_mapper has to depend on subquery_evaluator while physical_operator can NOT depen on subquery_evaluator. So this decouple is needed.

title: Subquery evaluator
body:
This PR adds ExistSubqueryEvaluator and SelectScan operator

## General Subquery Design
Inner subquery takes n value vectors as input from outer query. These inputs must be flat. So we run the subquery once for each input tuple.

### ExistSubqueryEvaluator
Holds the last operator of a subplan. Each call of evaluate() return true if subplan has at least one tuple.  This evaluator does NOT evaluate unflat input.

### SelectScan
Takes a vector of flat value vector as input and put them in a single flat dataChunk which becomes the input of subquery. Because SelectScan assumes single tuple input, on the second call of getNextTuple(), it terminates the execution of subplan.

body:
Consider query ` MATCH (a:person) WHERE a.unstrNumericProp - 10 > a.unstrNumericProp2 RETURN COUNT(*)`
We will enumerate the following plan
```
LOGICAL_FILTER[a.unstrNumericProp - 10 > a.unstrNumericProp2]
LOGICAL_FLATTEN[_0_a.unstrNumericProp]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY[_0_a.unstrNumericProp2]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY[_0_a.unstrNumericProp]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_ID[_0_a._id]
```

title: Removes readBySettingFrame and simplifications to DataStructure, Lists, and Columns
body:
This PR does several refactoring and simplification at the interface of operators and storage, which is implemented in data_structure.h/cpp, lists.h/cpp, and column.h/cpp.

- Remove reading by settingFrame: All reads happen through copying. As a result we no longer need pageHandle.
- Fixes several hidden bugs in reading large lists due to how we were computing the sizeLeftToCopy for large lists. These fixes required introducing back the "originalSize" of data chunks before any filter for scans to use. If we push scans down this field may again become unnecessary. The core problem is that the we need to keep the vector sizes in data chunks the same length (which is the length of the original nodeIDSequence scan or the original 1-to-many extension). But if the scan happens after a filter, vectors become unaligned causing bugs. Adds some test data and tests for reading large property and adjacency lists. These bugs also highlighted a major performance bottleneck, for which I opened an issue #302, which should be fixed by pushing scans. See the issue for details.
- Removes templating from Lists and Columns: As part of this moves one common functions for columns, that was used by NodesStore and RelStore, into a ColumnFactory class.
- We still maintain what was called ListsPageHandle. This is now a wrapper around ListSyncState to support the "hasMoreRead" function which behaves differently if the ListSyncState is the state of an adj list or property list. This is now called LargeListHandle.
- Removes MAX_TO_READ. We always read as much as we can from a single page.


This PR also (and indepedently) fixes bugs in the threadpool that is used by the loader and the multi-threading code that is in the QueryProcessor. These classes do not use atomics any more and acquire locks before doing any operation and are written as libraries, so their fields are not exposed. In addition it fixes a minor bug in expression evaluator for unstructured properties (an rpos field should be lpos).

title: Push Scans of Properties down
body:
We have potentially a very bad performance scenario by not pushing down scans. 
Consider the following query: 
```MATCH (a)-[:e1]->(b)-[:e2]->(c) WHERE e1.date = e2.date RETURN *``` 
and the following plan: 

```Scan(a)->Flat1(a)->Ext1(b)->Flat2(b)->Ext2(c)->PR1(e1)->PR2(e2)->Filter.```
Let there be 3 datachunks: DC1(a), DC2(b, e1, e1.date), DC3(c, e2, e2.date). Suppose DC1
is flattened at currIdx=0, so a is fixed to say a0. Now suppose DC2 has 3 values (so a0 has 3
edges.) DC2 will be flattened iteratively to currIdx=0, 1, 2 and for each i, we will
read a0's forward (and possibly large) date property list over and over again.

To avoid this, we should either have a caching logic, possibly a boolean in adj_list_extend or read_rel_property_list to
ensure that the same list is not read over and over again. Or we should make sure scans are pushed down and happen immediately after joins or nodeIDSequence scans. For now I suggest simply pushing down scans.

title: Supporting extending to multiple destination node labels (related to queries with unlabeled node/rels)
body:
This feature is related to "Unlabeled Node and Rel Queries". We do not currently support extending through single relation label to nodes with possibly multiple labels. Our storage supports such lists and even our lists.cpp can read such adjacency lists into ValueVectors. But we don't seem to have the correct logic in the query plan and extend operators to handle this case. Specifically here is a test that should pass and currently fails.
The dataset under `dataset/read-list-tests/3-bytes-per-edge' is a dataset where there are both `animal` and `person` nodes and a `knows` relation over {animal,person} x {animal, person}. In this particular dataset there are 6000 person nodes and 1 animal node. person0 connectes to person0 to person5000 (so 5001 edges). animal0 connects to person6000 (all through `knows` edges). 

When I issue the following query: `MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)`,  the plan that stats scanning from b returns 5002 instead of 5001. Note that id here is an INT64 column (that also happens to be the primary key) and  exists for both animals and person. I did not look very closely but I am guessing that the filter that a should be a person does not seem to be passed along to the filter or extend to filter out the a:0 when the scan b scans p6000.

This is the plan that's failing:
```
LOGICAL_FILTER[a.id = 0]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY[_0_a.id]
LOGICAL_EXTEND[_1_b._id<-_0_a._id]
LOGICAL_FLATTEN[_1_b._id]
LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_ID[_1_b._id]
```
I believe LOGICAL_SCAN_NODE_PROPERTY scans a0's id column (this is not important but incidentally, I believe this operators is configured with the ID column of p, so in fact it's reading p0's id column, but regardless reads a 0) which passes the filter.

The following end to end test can be written for the 3-bytes-per-edge test. All of these should pass but the first one was failing, which is what triggered this issue.
```
-NAME NodeP0ExtendToPerson
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 5001

-NAME NodeP0ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:animal) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 0

-NAME NodeP1ExtendToPerson
-COMPARE_RESULT 1
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 1 RETURN b.id
---- 1
5000

-NAME NodeP1ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 1 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 1
0

-NAME NodeP5500ExtendToPerson
-COMPARE_RESULT 1
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 5500 RETURN b.id
---- 0

-NAME NodeP5500ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:person)-[:knows]->(b:person) WHERE a.id = 5500 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 0

-NAME NodeA0ExtendToPerson
-QUERY MATCH (a:animal)-[:knows]->(b:personerson) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN b.id
---- 6000

-NAME NodeA0ExtendToAnimal
-QUERY MATCH (a:animal)-[:knows]->(b:animal) WHERE a.id = 0 RETURN COUNT(*)
---- 0
```

This test can go under read_list_end_to_end_test.cpp.
```
class EndToEndReadLists3BytesPerEdgeTest : public DBLoadedTest {
public:
    string getInputCSVDir() override { return "dataset/read-list-tests/3-bytes-per-edge/"; }
};

TEST_F(EndToEndReadLists3BytesPerEdgeTest, 3BytesPerEdgeTest) {
    vector<TestQueryConfig> queryConfigs;
    queryConfigs =
        TestHelper::parseTestFile("test/runner/queries/adj-list-reading/3-bytes-per-edge.test");
    ASSERT_TRUE(TestHelper::runTest(queryConfigs, *defaultSystem));
}
```

title: Fix unsafe mem access and mem leak

This PR fix unsafe mem access and mem leak based on valgrind check
